teile.einleitung: A skyscraper is a particularly tall high-rise building that seems to reach up to the clouds. The first skyscrapers were built at the end of the 19th century in Chicago and New York; today the tallest ones are in Asia and the Middle East. The tallest building in the world, the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, is 828 metres high.
wichtigste: Only the safe passenger lift made tall buildings practical to use in the 19th century.
In 1885 the Home Insurance Building in Chicago became one of the first high-rise buildings with a steel frame.
In frame construction, a skeleton of columns and beams carries the weight.
A glass curtain wall is often hung in front of the frame.
The core of the building contains lifts and stairs and makes the building stiff.
The Empire State Building in New York was opened in 1931.
The Prime Tower in Zurich is about 126 metres high.

abschnitte.text: **Skyscrapers** are very tall high-rise buildings, often with many dozens of storeys. The word comes from English; the German word “Wolkenkratzer” is a direct translation of it. Skyscrapers are built mainly in big cities, where land is scarce and expensive. Instead of building outwards, people build upwards there, so that many people can live or work on a small area.

Before there were safe lifts, nobody wanted to walk up twenty floors. In the 1850s, the American **Elisha Otis** presented a passenger lift with a safety catch that stops the car if the rope breaks. The second important invention was **frame construction**: a skeleton of steel columns and beams carries the whole weight, and the walls no longer have to carry anything. In this way the Home Insurance Building was built in Chicago in 1885, which is regarded as one of the first skyscrapers.

In the middle of many high-rise buildings there is a stiff concrete **core**, which houses the lifts, stairs and pipes and cables. A glass **curtain wall**, which carries only its own weight, is often hung in front of the load-bearing frame. In strong wind, the top of a skyscraper sways slightly, because tall buildings are meant to be a little flexible; otherwise they would break. In the Taipei 101 tower in Taiwan, a huge steel ball of about 660 tonnes hangs inside and damps the swaying caused by wind and earthquakes.

The **Empire State Building** in New York was opened in 1931 and was the tallest building in the world for about 40 years. Since 2010 the **Burj Khalifa** in Dubai, at 828 metres, has held this record. Other well-known skyscrapers are the Petronas Towers in Kuala Lumpur and One World Trade Center in New York. Today many of the world’s tallest buildings are in China.

In Switzerland, high-rise buildings are much smaller than in New York or Dubai. The **Prime Tower** in Zurich was completed in 2011 and is about 126 metres high. The tallest buildings in Switzerland are the two Roche towers in Basel; the taller of them measures 205 metres. Whether tall buildings fit into the townscape is often hotly debated in Switzerland, and sometimes people even vote on it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A way of building in which a skeleton of columns and beams carries the weight.
An outer wall, usually of glass, that is hung in front of the load-bearing frame.
A stiff shaft inside with lifts and stairs that keeps the building stable.
A heavy mass that slows down the swaying of a high-rise building.

gewusst: The top of the Burj Khalifa is so high that you can still see the Sun there for a few minutes after it has set on the ground.
The Empire State Building was built in only about 13 months.
The huge damper ball in Taipei 101 is a sight that visitors can go and look at.

teile.einleitung: Pliers are a tool with two halves joined at a hinge. With them you can hold things, squeeze them together, bend them or snip through them. There are pliers for almost every job, from the workshop to the barbecue.
wichtigste: Pliers are used for holding and snipping.
The two halves of a pair of pliers are joined at a hinge.
The handles are longer than the jaws so that you have more force.
With pincers you pull out nails.
Needle-nose pliers have long, thin jaws for small parts.
With side cutters you cut through thin wires.
In the kitchen there are barbecue tongs and sugar tongs.

abschnitte.text: A pair of pliers consists of two parts that cross at a **hinge**. On one side are the **handles**, which you hold. On the other side are the **jaws**, which grip or cut through the workpiece. When you squeeze the handles together, the jaws close. Many workshop pliers have plastic-covered handles so that they sit comfortably in your hand.

Pliers are a double **lever**. The hinge is the pivot. Because the handles are much longer than the jaws, the force of your hand is multiplied. If you squeeze at the outer ends of the handles, several times that force arrives at the jaws. This way you can even snip through a wire by hand.

**Combination pliers** are all-rounders for gripping, bending and cutting. With **pincers** you pull nails out of wood. **Needle-nose pliers** have long, thin jaws with which you can grip small parts in tight spots. With **side cutters** you cut through thin wires. Water pump pliers can be adjusted and can also grip thick pipes and nuts.

abschnitte.titel: Pliers and tongs in everyday life
abschnitte.text: It is not only tradespeople who need pliers. With **barbecue tongs** you turn sausages and meat on the barbecue without burning your fingers. With sugar tongs you pick up sugar cubes without touching them with your hands. In the kitchen there are also salad tongs and spaghetti tongs. A very small relative of pliers is the pair of tweezers.

Pliers and tongs are among the oldest human tools. As early as the **Bronze Age**, smiths needed long tongs to take glowing metal out of the fire. That way they did not have to touch the hot metal with their hands. Over time, more and more special pliers were developed for different trades. Today you will find several pairs of pliers in almost every toolbox.

begriffe.erklaerung: The place where the two halves of the pliers are joined and turn.
The front parts of the pliers that grip.
A tool that turns around a point and multiplies force.
Pliers with sharp edges for cutting through wires.

gewusst: A pair of scissors works on the same principle as pliers, only with sharp blades.
Dentists also have special pliers for pulling teeth.
The further back you hold the handles of a pair of pliers, the more force you have.

teile.einleitung: A set of points is a device in the track that is used to send a train from one track onto another. Without points, trains could not branch off, overtake or run onto different tracks in stations.
wichtigste: A set of points steers a train onto another track.
Its moving rail parts are called switch blades.
Where two rails cross, there is the frog.
The check rail guides the wheels safely through the gap in the frog.
Modern points are moved with an electric point machine.
Many points in Switzerland have heating against snow and ice.
On the diverging track, trains often have to go more slowly.

abschnitte.text: A train cannot steer like a car, because its wheels always follow the rails. That is why a set of **points** decides whether the train goes straight on or turns off onto another track. In large stations there are hundreds of points, so that trains can reach every track. The points are controlled from a **signal box**.

abschnitte.titel: Parts of a set of points
abschnitte.text: The moving rail parts are called **switch blades**, and they lie close against one of the fixed rails. Depending on which side the blade lies against, the wheels are guided straight on or into the curve. Where two rails cross, there is the **frog**, with a small gap for the wheel flanges. Opposite it, a **check rail** makes sure that the wheels run safely through this gap.

In the past, a pointsman moved each set of points by hand with a lever or through wires. Today an electric **point machine** does this on command from the signal box. A lock holds the blades in place so that they do not move under the train. The signal box only clears a signal when all the points are in the right position and locked.

Snow and ice can block the blades so that the points no longer move. That is why many points in Switzerland have **point heating**, usually electric. It keeps the gaps between the blade and the rail clear. In the mountains, railway workers also clear them with brooms and shovels when there is heavy snowfall.

If a train enters the points from the side of the blade tips, they are taken in the **facing direction**, and the points decide where the train goes. If it comes from the other side, they are taken in the trailing direction, and the routes come together. The diverging track is a tight curve, so trains often have to go more slowly there. For high-speed lines, very long points with gentle curves are built, so that trains can travel fast even when turning off.

begriffe.erklaerung: A moving, tapering rail part of a set of points.
The place where two rails of a set of points cross.
An extra rail that guides the wheels safely at the frog.
The control centre from which points and signals are operated.

gewusst: With a double slip, a train can choose between four directions.
Points are regularly checked and greased so that the blades slide easily.
In English, depending on the country, a set of points is called a “switch” (in America) or “points” (in Britain).

teile.einleitung: Alan Turing was a British mathematician and is regarded as one of the fathers of computer science. As early as 1936 he described what a computer can calculate in principle, and in the Second World War he helped to decipher secret German radio messages. To this day, many terms in computer science bear his name.
wichtigste: Alan Turing lived from 1912 to 1954 and came from London.
In 1936 he described the Turing machine, a simple model of a computer.
He proved that the halting problem is undecidable.
In the Second World War he worked at Bletchley Park on breaking the Enigma code.
For this he helped to develop the Turing bombe.
In 1950 he described the imitation game, which became the Turing test.
Since 1966 the ACM has awarded the Turing Award, and since 2021 Turing has been on the 50-pound note.

abschnitte.text: Alan Mathison Turing was born in London on 23 June 1912. Even as a child he was very interested in mathematics and science. He studied at King's College in **Cambridge**. Later he also worked in Princeton in the USA and at the University of Manchester. He died on 7 June 1954, aged only 41.

In 1936 Turing described an imaginary machine that is now called the **Turing machine**. It consists of an endlessly long tape with squares and a head that reads and writes symbols and moves. This simple machine can calculate everything that can be calculated at all. Turing also proved that there are questions that no machine can solve, such as the **halting problem**. Programming languages that can do everything a Turing machine can do are called Turing-complete.

In the Second World War, the German armed forces encrypted their radio messages with the **Enigma**. Turing worked at the secret centre of **Bletchley Park** in England, where hundreds of people tried to crack these codes. He helped to develop the **Turing bombe**, a machine that quickly tried out possible settings of the Enigma. The deciphered messages helped the Allies a great deal. For a long time, nobody was allowed to talk about this work.

In 1950 Turing asked in an essay whether machines can think. He suggested a thought experiment that he called the **imitation game**. A person has a written conversation with an unknown partner and has to find out whether it is a human or a computer. This became the famous **Turing test**. It is still important today in discussions about artificial intelligence.

Since 1966 the professional society **ACM** has awarded the Turing Award, which is often called the “Nobel Prize of computing”. Since 2021 Turing has appeared on the British **50-pound note**. After the war he also worked on one of the first electronic computers in Manchester. Today he is regarded as one of the most important scientists of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary, very simple model of a computer.
The question of whether a program will stop at some point. No program can answer it for all cases.
A German encryption machine from the Second World War.
A test of whether you can tell a computer apart from a human in a conversation.

gewusst: Turing was a very good long-distance runner and ran a marathon in under three hours.
The new 50-pound note came into circulation on Turing’s birthday, 23 June 2021.
The work at Bletchley Park remained strictly secret for decades.

teile.einleitung: Hydropower is the energy of flowing or falling water, which people turn into electricity or movement. For Switzerland, with its mountains, lakes and rivers, it is the most important source of electricity.
wichtigste: Hydropower uses the energy of flowing or falling water.
Storage power stations use the potential energy of dammed water.
A run-of-river power station uses a river without a large reservoir.
A turbine turns, and a generator turns this into electricity.
In the record year 2024, Swiss hydropower supplied about 48 terawatt hours of electricity.
Valais and the Grisons produce the most electricity from hydropower.
Electricity from reservoirs can be produced exactly when it is needed.

abschnitte.text: Water that flows downhill has energy. Dammed water high up in a reservoir has **potential energy**, which turns into movement energy as it rushes down. This energy drives a **turbine**, which turns like a wheel. A connected **generator** turns the turning movement into electrical energy.

For very large heads of water in the Alps, the **Pelton turbine** is suitable, in which jets of water hit bucket-shaped cups. In river power stations with a small head and a lot of water, the **Kaplan turbine** is often used, which looks like a ship’s propeller. In between is the Francis turbine for medium heads. The turbines are named after their inventors.

A **run-of-river power station** stands on a river and uses the flowing water continuously, without a large reservoir. A **storage power station** collects water from snow and glaciers in a reservoir in the mountains. This means electricity can be produced when it is needed, for example on cold winter evenings. **Pumped storage power stations** pump water back up when there is surplus electricity, and so store energy like a gigantic battery.

Switzerland gets about 60 percent of its electricity from hydropower. In the record year 2024 it was about 48 terawatt hours. The mountain cantons of **Valais** and the **Grisons** supply the most electricity. The Grande Dixence dam in Valais, at 285 metres, is the highest gravity dam in the world.

Hydropower is **renewable** and produces hardly any CO2 when running. But reservoirs flood valleys, and power stations change rivers, which harms fish and other animals. That is why the law requires a **residual flow** that must stay in the stream, and fish ladders are built at river power stations. With climate change, glaciers are melting, which will change the amounts of water in future.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that something has because it is high up.
A bladed wheel that is turned by flowing water.
A machine that turns a turning movement into electricity.
A billion kilowatt hours, a huge amount of electricity.
Water that must stay in the stream below a water intake.

gewusst: More than 2000 years ago, people already used water wheels to grind grain.
The cantons receive a fee for the use of their water, called the water rate.
The Nant de Drance pumped storage power station in Valais lies almost entirely in caverns inside the mountain.

teile.einleitung: An algorithm is an exact step-by-step set of instructions for solving a task. A recipe or building instructions work in a very similar way. Computers need algorithms so that they know exactly what to do.
wichtigste: An algorithm is a set of instructions made of clear and exact steps.
A recipe is very similar to an algorithm.
If a step is missing from a set of instructions, it often does not work.
A computer carries out algorithms that are written in a programming language.
The order of the steps is important.
Algorithms can contain decisions and repetitions.
The word goes back to the scholar al-Khwarizmi from the 9th century.

abschnitte.text: An **algorithm** is a set of instructions that tells you step by step how to solve a task. Every step must be clear and exact so that it cannot be misunderstood. In addition, the algorithm must finish at some point and lead to a result. An example: “Take 2 steps, then 3 more steps”; at the end you have taken 5 steps.

A **recipe** tells you which ingredients you need and what you have to do one after another. Building instructions for bricks show how to build a model step by step. Brushing your teeth is a small algorithm too: first you put toothpaste on the brush, then you brush all your teeth, then you rinse. If a step is missing or the **order** is wrong, it often does not work.

Most algorithms are made of three building blocks. A **sequence** is a series of steps that are carried out one after another. A **branch** is a decision, such as “If it is raining, take an umbrella, otherwise do not.” A **loop** repeats steps, for example “Stir until the dough is smooth.”

A computer is very fast, but it only understands exact commands. That is why algorithms are written in a **programming language**; this makes a program, and the computer carries it out. Satnavs use algorithms to work out the shortest route, search engines sort results, and games use them to control their characters. Children in Switzerland often learn their first algorithms with learning robots or with the programming environment **Scratch**.

The word algorithm goes back to the scholar **al-Khwarizmi**, who lived in Baghdad in the 9th century and wrote an important book on arithmetic. More than 2000 years ago, the Greek mathematician Euclid already described an algorithm for finding the greatest common divisor of two numbers. In the 19th century, the Englishwoman **Ada Lovelace** wrote an algorithm for a planned calculating machine and is therefore regarded as the first programmer. Today algorithms are the basis of the whole of computer science.

begriffe.erklaerung: An exact step-by-step set of instructions for solving a task.
The part of an algorithm that repeats steps several times.
A point at which different steps follow depending on a condition.
An algorithm written down in a language that the computer understands.

gewusst: Directions to school are an algorithm too.
There are dozens of different algorithms for sorting numbers by size, and some are much faster than others.
A Rubik’s Cube can be solved with fixed algorithms that you can learn by heart.

teile.einleitung: A hydroelectric power station is a facility that produces electricity from the force of flowing or falling water. They are found on rivers in the lowlands and high up in the mountains at large reservoirs.
wichtigste: A hydroelectric power station produces electricity from flowing or falling water.
The water flows onto a turbine and turns it.
Run-of-river power stations stand on rivers.
Storage lakes in the mountains hold water ready until electricity is needed.
The water reaches the power station in the valley through thick pipes inside the mountain.
The water in Alpine reservoirs comes mainly from melted snow and glaciers.
Fish ladders help fish to swim past the power station.

abschnitte.text: The water flows with great force onto the blades of a **turbine** and makes it turn. The turbine is connected by a shaft to a **generator**. In the generator, magnets turn next to coils of wire, and this produces electricity. Through transformers and lines, the electricity reaches the grid and finally our homes.

A **run-of-river power station** stands right on a river, for example on the Rhine or the Aare. A weir holds the water back a little so that it flows through the turbines with a bit of a drop. It produces electricity day and night, usually more in summer, because the rivers carry more water then. So that fish can continue their journey, a **fish ladder** made of small pools is built next to it.

In the Alps, a **dam** collects water from melted snow and glaciers in a storage lake. Through a tunnel and a steep **penstock** made of thick pipes, the water shoots down to the power station in the valley. Because the lake holds water ready, electricity can be produced exactly when it is needed. This is very important for Switzerland, especially in winter.

A **pumped storage power station** has an upper and a lower lake. When there is too much electricity, it pumps water up, and when electricity is needed, it lets the water flow back through the turbines. In this way it acts like a gigantic battery. Well-known Swiss examples are Nant de Drance in Valais and Linth-Limmern in the canton of Glarus.

In the past, the water of a stream turned a large wheel that drove a **water mill** or a saw. At the end of the 19th century, people began to produce electricity with hydropower. One of the first large river power stations in Europe started operating in 1898 at Rheinfelden on the Rhine. The largest hydroelectric power station in the world today is the Three Gorges Dam in China.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wall that blocks a valley and holds back water to form a lake.
A thick pipe in which water flows at high pressure to the turbine.
A staircase of small pools that fish use to get round a power station.
A structure across a river that holds back the water.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are hundreds of hydroelectric power stations, from small plants on streams to huge power stations in the Alps.
Some dams can be visited, and you can even walk through passages inside them.
When pumping water up, a pumped storage power station uses a little more electricity than it later supplies again, but it is still very useful.

teile.einleitung: Image resolution tells you how many picture points, the pixels, a digital image is made of. The more pixels a picture has, the more detail it can show. When printing, how densely the dots lie on the paper also becomes important.
wichtigste: A digital image consists of many tiny picture points, the pixels.
A Full HD image has 1920 × 1080 pixels, which is 2 073 600 picture points.
4K UHD has 3840 × 2160 pixels, four times as many as Full HD.
One megapixel is a million picture points.
The abbreviation dpi means dots per inch.
For a good photo print, 300 dpi is the usual guideline.
More resolution means more detail, but also a bigger file.

abschnitte.text: A **pixel** is the smallest picture point of a digital image and has exactly one colour. The word comes from the English picture element. Many thousands or millions of pixels next to one another make a picture, similar to a mosaic. If you zoom right into a photo, you can see the individual squares.

**Resolution** is often written as width times height in pixels. A Full HD image of 1920 × 1080 pixels has 2 073 600 pixels altogether. The 4K UHD format has 3840 × 2160 pixels and so exactly four times as many. A photo of 4000 × 3000 pixels has 12 million pixels, that is 12 **megapixels**.

For cameras and mobile phones, resolution is usually given in megapixels. Modern smartphones have cameras with often 12 to more than 100 megapixels. But more megapixels do not automatically mean better photos, because the lens and the size of the sensor also matter. Screens also have a fixed resolution, and the more densely the pixels are packed, the sharper the display looks.

When printing, what counts is how many dots fit into one inch, which is 2.54 centimetres. This figure is called **dpi**, the abbreviation for dots per inch. For a good-quality photo print, 300 dpi is the guideline. An image 1200 pixels wide therefore becomes 4 inches wide at 300 dpi, which is about 10 centimetres.

More pixels mean more detail, but also a bigger file. A large photo therefore needs more storage space and loads more slowly on the internet. Formats such as **JPEG** make the file smaller by compression, but small details are lost in the process. For websites and messages, pictures are therefore often reduced to a lower resolution.

If you greatly enlarge a picture with few pixels, it becomes blurred or pixelated. This is because the program cannot simply conjure up missing details; it has to estimate the new pixels. New methods using artificial intelligence try to scale up such pictures cleverly. Even so: if you want to print large later, it is best to take the photo at high resolution in the first place.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest picture point of a digital image.
A million pixels.
Dots per inch, that is how many dots fit into 2.54 centimetres.
Making a file smaller so that it needs less storage.

gewusst: A 4K screen has more than 8 million pixels, each of which can change its colour individually.
On many screens, each pixel consists of three tiny points of light in red, green and blue.

teile.einleitung: A toaster is an electrical kitchen appliance that toasts slices of bread crisp and brown in a few minutes. Glowing heating wires produce the heat, and when the toast is ready it pops up.
wichtigste: A toaster toasts slices of bread with heat.
The heat comes from heating wires that glow orange-red.
With the dial you set how brown the bread will be.
When the toast is ready, it pops up automatically.
Crumbs collect in a crumb tray at the bottom of the appliance.
If you toast for too long, you get black, burnt toast.
You must never put a fork into a toaster that is switched on.

abschnitte.text: Inside a toaster, thin **heating wires** are stretched, usually made of a mixture of nickel and chromium. When electricity flows through them, they become so hot that they glow **orange-red**. The heat radiates onto the bread and toasts its surface. Sugar and protein in the bread combine to form brown, fragrant substances, much as in a crust.

With a lever you push the bread down and so switch the toaster on. The **dial** decides how long it toasts, and therefore how light or dark the toast will be. When the time is up, a spring releases the lever and the slices **pop up**. Many appliances also have buttons for defrosting, reheating or cancelling.

In the past, people toasted bread over an open fire, on forks or grills. Electric toasters existed from the end of the 19th century, when more and more homes got electricity. Around 1920 the American Charles Strite invented the **pop-up toaster**, in which the bread jumps up by itself. Since then the toaster has been a standard item in many kitchens.

If a piece of bread gets stuck, you first pull out the **plug** and wait until the appliance has cooled down. Reaching into a toaster that is switched on with a fork or knife is dangerous, because you could get an **electric shock**. You should empty the **crumb tray** regularly, because otherwise old crumbs can burn and smoke. Also, you should never put the toaster under curtains or wall cupboards.

The most popular is soft **sliced bread**, which is sold already cut into slices of the same size. Toasted bread is eaten with butter, jam, honey or cheese. There are also sandwich toasters, which press together two filled slices of bread and toast them. A normal toaster needs only about two to three minutes per round.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wire that becomes hot when electricity flows through it.
A tray at the bottom of the toaster that can be pulled out and where crumbs land.
A toaster in which the finished toast jumps up by itself.
A dangerous flow of electricity through the body.

gewusst: Bread already cut into slices has only existed since the end of the 1920s; before that, people had to slice it themselves.
The smell of toast comes from the same browning reaction as with fried meat or roasted coffee beans.
A toaster turns almost all of its electricity into heat.

teile.einleitung: A screenshot is a picture of exactly what a screen is showing at a particular moment. In German it is called a “Bildschirmfoto” (screen photo). You take it with a key or a combination of keys and get a perfectly normal image file.
wichtigste: A screenshot captures what can be seen on the screen at that moment.
In German it is called a “Bildschirmfoto”.
On many Windows computers, the Print key takes a screenshot.
On a mobile phone, a screenshot usually ends up in the photo gallery.
A screenshot is an image file that you can share like a photo.
You may only send on screenshots of private chats with permission.
If you record the screen like a film, this is called a screen recording.

abschnitte.text: A **screenshot** saves an exact copy of the screen as a picture. Unlike a photo taken with a camera, it is pin-sharp and has no reflections. It is produced directly in the device, without a camera being needed. The English word **screenshot** is also very commonly used in German.

On many Windows computers you press the **Print key**, often labelled Print or PrtSc. With the combination Windows key, Shift and S, you can choose a section. On a Mac it works with Command, Shift and 3 for the whole screen or 4 for a section. The picture then ends up on the clipboard or as a file on the desktop or in the pictures folder.

On a mobile phone you usually press two buttons at the same time, such as the side button and a volume button. The screen flashes briefly, and the picture appears in the **photo gallery**. Some devices can also capture long web pages in a single picture. Afterwards you can crop the picture, draw on it or send it.

A screenshot helps to show an **error message** when you ask someone for help. You can use it to save timetables, tickets or directions so that you can look at them even without the internet. Teachers use screenshots for instructions and worksheets. They can also be important for keeping evidence, for example of insults on the internet.

You must not simply send a screenshot of a private chat to other people; you may only do so with **permission**. Otherwise you violate the privacy of the person who wrote to you. Pictures of other people must not be spread without their consent either. Remember that a screenshot shows what was visible on your screen, perhaps including personal messages or addresses.

A **screen recording** records the screen like a film. With it, you can show how a program or a game works. Many learning videos on the internet are made this way. Here too: only record and share other people’s content and other people with permission.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture of what is on the screen; in German a “Bildschirmfoto”.
An invisible store in which something you have copied is kept for a short time.
A video of everything that happens on the screen.
The right for private things to stay private.

gewusst: The Print key dates from the time when it really did send the contents of the screen straight to a printer.
Some apps, for example for banking, prevent screenshots for security reasons.

teile.einleitung: In self-driving, or autonomous, vehicles, the vehicle steers, brakes and accelerates by itself, without a person having to drive. Cameras, sensors and computers take the place of the driver’s eyes and brain. In some cities of the world, robotaxis are already on the road today; in Switzerland there are mainly trials.
wichtigste: A self-driving car is a car that drives by itself.
It sees the road with cameras and sensors.
A digital map helps it to find the way.
It must always recognise people on the road and stop at red traffic lights.
Thick fog can make things difficult for the cameras.
From 2016, a self-driving PostBus shuttle ran in Sion as a trial bus.
On test drives, there is often still an attendant on board for safety.

abschnitte.text: An **autonomous vehicle** drives on its own, without anyone steering or braking. Experts distinguish six **levels of automation**, from 0 to 5. At level 0 the human does everything; at level 5 no driver is needed at all. Many of today’s cars already have helpers, such as lane-keeping assistance or cruise control that keeps the distance. But only a few vehicles drive entirely without a human.

A self-driving car uses many **sensors**. Cameras recognise traffic lights, signs, road markings and people. **Radar** measures the distance and speed of other vehicles, even in the rain. **Lidar** scans the surroundings with laser beams and creates a 3D picture. A very precise digital map and GPS help to find the way.

A powerful computer in the car analyses all the data at lightning speed. With **artificial intelligence**, it recognises whether there is a bike, a dog or a child ahead. Then it decides whether the car brakes, swerves or carries on. At a red traffic light it stops, just like a human. The most important thing is that it always recognises people on the road safely.

From 2016, a self-driving **PostBus shuttle** ran through the old town of **Sion** in Valais as a trial bus. It was one of the first of its kind on public roads. On such test drives there is usually an **attendant** on board who can step in in an emergency. Since 2025, new rules in Switzerland have allowed, for example, a motorway pilot under certain conditions. Further trials with self-driving buses are running in various places.

Thick **fog**, heavy rain or snow can make things difficult for cameras and sensors. Unexpected situations, such as a police officer directing traffic by hand, are also tricky. There is also the question of who is responsible in an accident. But self-driving cars could prevent many accidents, because they are never tired or distracted. People who cannot drive themselves would become more mobile.

begriffe.erklaerung: Independent, without a person having to steer.
A component that senses the surroundings, such as a camera.
A sensor that creates a 3D picture of the surroundings with laser beams.
A taxi that drives entirely without a driver.

gewusst: A self-driving car collects so much data that its computer has to carry out millions of calculations every second.
In some cities in the USA and China, you can already order robotaxis with no driver at all.
The shuttle in Sion went only as fast as a bike, so that it could stop safely.

teile.einleitung: The instruction set is the list of all the machine instructions that a processor understands and can carry out. It is, so to speak, the mother tongue of a processor. Well-known instruction sets are called x86, ARM and RISC-V.
wichtigste: An instruction set decides which basic instructions a processor can carry out.
Roughly, a distinction is made between RISC, with few simple instructions, and CISC, with many complex instructions.
RISC stands for Reduced Instruction Set Computer.
The x86 architecture belongs to CISC and goes back to the Intel 8086 of 1978.
The vast majority of smartphones contain the ARM architecture.
RISC-V was created in 2010 at the University of California, Berkeley, and can be used openly and without licence fees.
The opcode is the part of a machine instruction that sets the operation.

abschnitte.text: A processor can only do very simple tasks, such as adding two numbers, loading a value from memory or jumping to another place in the program. The list of all these basic instructions is called the **instruction set**, or instruction set architecture. Every program, whether a game or a browser, is in the end translated into such **machine instructions**. Programs for one instruction set do not simply run on a processor with a different instruction set. That is why apps often come in different versions.

Every machine instruction consists of zeros and ones. One part of it, the **opcode**, says what is to be done, for example “add”. The other parts, the **operands**, say what is to be used in the calculation, such as which storage places. So that people can read such instructions, they are written in **assembly language** with short words such as ADD or MOV. A program called an assembler then translates these words into the processor’s numbers.

With **CISC**, Complex Instruction Set Computer, there are many instructions, some of them very powerful. With **RISC**, Reduced Instruction Set Computer, there are fewer and simpler instructions, which run very fast. Many RISC processors are a **load-store architecture**: only load and store instructions access the main memory, and calculations are done only in the registers inside the processor. Today the boundaries are blurring, because modern x86 processors split their complex instructions internally into simpler steps.

The **x86** family began in 1978 with the Intel 8086 and is still found today in most Windows PCs. The company AMD extended it to 64 bits; this version is called x86-64. The **ARM** architecture originally comes from England and is particularly energy-saving, which is why it is found in almost all smartphones and tablets. Since 2020, Apple has also used its own ARM chips in its Mac computers.

**RISC-V** was developed in 2010 at the University of California in Berkeley. Unlike x86 or ARM, any company and any university may use RISC-V without licence fees. That is why it is popular in research and teaching and for small chips in devices. At ETH Zurich too, processors with RISC-V are being developed and researched.

begriffe.erklaerung: The calculating unit of a computer, which carries out the instructions.
The part of an instruction that says what is to be done.
Tiny, very fast storage places directly in the processor.
A way of writing machine instructions with short words instead of numbers.

gewusst: The name x86 comes from the fact that the early Intel processors in this family had numbers ending in 86, for example 8086 and 80286.
A modern x86 processor still understands many instructions of the 8086, which is more than 45 years old.
ARM chips are found not only in mobile phones, but also in many games consoles, smartwatches and cars.

teile.einleitung: A submarine is a vessel that can dive under water and travel there. In German it is called a “U-Boot”, where the U stands for “Unterseeboot” (undersea boat). Submarines are used for research, rescue, tourism and by the military, and the Swiss explorers Auguste and Jacques Piccard, father and son, made history with diving vessels.
wichtigste: In the German word U-Boot, the U stands for Unterseeboot, meaning undersea boat.
To dive, a submarine fills tanks with water.
To surface, it forces the water out again with compressed air.
With the periscope, you can look over the surface of the water from a submerged submarine.
Under water, submarines find their way using sound.
Because the water presses very hard at depth, a submarine needs very thick walls.
In 1964 tourists at the Expo in Lausanne travelled through Lake Geneva in a submarine.

abschnitte.text: A submarine has large tanks, the **ballast tanks**. When they are flooded with water, the boat becomes heavier and sinks. To surface, **compressed air** is blown into the tanks, the water is forced out, and the boat becomes lighter and rises. With small fins, the diving planes, the boat is steered up or down while it is moving.

Under water it is dark after just a few metres, and you can hardly see anything. That is why submarines find their way using sound, with **sonar**: it sends out sound waves and listens for their echo, rather like a bat. Just below the surface, a **periscope** can be raised, a long tube with mirrors through which you can look over the water. The air inside is constantly cleaned and refreshed with oxygen so that the crew can breathe.

With every 10 metres of water depth, the pressure rises by about 1 bar, which is as much as the weight of all the air above us. At a depth of 1000 metres, the water therefore presses about a hundred times harder than the air at the surface. That is why a submarine needs a very strong **pressure hull** with thick walls of steel or titanium. In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived almost 11 000 metres deep into the Mariana Trench, the deepest place in the oceans, in the diving vessel **Trieste**.

As early as 1775, the American David Bushnell built a small wooden diving vessel, the “Turtle”, which was driven by muscle power. In the novel “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea” by **Jules Verne**, Captain Nemo travels through the oceans in the submarine Nautilus. In both world wars, navies used many submarines. In 1954 the American USS Nautilus was launched, the first nuclear-powered submarine, which could stay under water for months.

For the national exhibition **Expo 64** in Lausanne, Jacques Piccard built the tourist submarine **Mésoscaphe Auguste Piccard**, named after his father. It took visitors on dives into the depths of Lake Geneva. During the Expo, more than 30 000 people travelled in it. Today the Mésoscaphe is on display at the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tank in the submarine that is filled with water to dive and with air to surface.
A viewing tube with mirrors, used to look over the water from a submerged submarine.
A locating device that finds obstacles using sound waves and their echo.
The strong shell of the submarine that withstands the water pressure.

gewusst: Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench; his father Auguste Piccard had earlier risen into the stratosphere in a balloon.
The Mésoscaphe is regarded as the world’s first tourist submarine.
Jules Verne described his submarine Nautilus before such submarines really existed.

teile.einleitung: Thomas Alva Edison was an American inventor and businessman who lived from 1847 to 1931. He improved the light bulb, invented the phonograph and built one of the first power stations. With more than 1000 patents, he is regarded as one of the most successful inventors in history.
wichtigste: The young Edison worked as a telegraph operator before he became known as an inventor.
In 1877 he invented the phonograph, with which sounds could be recorded and played back.
In 1879 he improved the light bulb so that it shone for many hours.
From 1880 he used carbonised bamboo fibres as a particularly long-lasting filament.
In 1882 he started up one of the first public power stations on Pearl Street in New York.
Because of his laboratory in Menlo Park, he was called “the Wizard of Menlo Park”.
Edison held more than 1000 US patents.

abschnitte.text: Thomas Alva Edison was born in 1847 in Milan in the US state of Ohio. He went to school only for a short time; his mother taught him at home, and he read a great deal. As a teenager he was already selling newspapers on the train and experimenting with chemicals. Later he worked as a **telegraph operator**, sending messages with the Morse telegraph, and began to improve these devices.

In 1876 Edison set up a large research laboratory in **Menlo Park** in the state of New Jersey. Many experts worked there together on inventions, which was something completely new at the time. That is why Edison is regarded as the inventor of the modern research department. Because so many new things came out of Menlo Park, he was called “the Wizard of Menlo Park”.

In 1877 Edison invented the **phonograph**, the first device that could record sounds and play them back. The sound waves were scratched as grooves into a cylinder covered with tinfoil. The first words recorded were a nursery rhyme. Later his laboratory developed the **kinetoscope**, a box in which one person at a time could watch short moving films through a peephole.

Other inventors had already built light bulbs, but their bulbs burnt out quickly. Edison and his team tested thousands of materials and in 1879 found a filament that lasted many hours; from 1880 they used **carbonised bamboo fibres**. For lamps to shine in homes, electricity was needed, so in 1882 Edison started up one of the first public **power stations** on Pearl Street in New York. He relied on direct current and argued with George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla, who promoted alternating current, which finally won out.

Edison died in 1931 in West Orange in New Jersey. He held more than 1000 US patents, more than almost anyone else. His companies gave rise, among others, to the **General Electric** group, which still exists today. His famous saying is that genius is 1 percent inspiration and 99 percent perspiration, in other words mainly hard work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A legal right that allows an inventor to be the only one to use their invention.
Someone who sends messages with the telegraph using Morse code.
The first device for recording and playing back sounds.
A thin wire or thread inside the glass bulb that is made to glow by electricity.

gewusst: Edison was hard of hearing from his youth.
To find the right filament, Edison’s team tested thousands of different materials before they found bamboo.
His research laboratory from Menlo Park was later taken apart and rebuilt in a museum in Michigan.

teile.einleitung: Materials testing examines how strong, hard, tough or free of faults a material is. This is how experts make sure that bridges, aircraft, bikes or screws can withstand their loads.
wichtigste: Materials testing finds out properties of materials such as strength, hardness and toughness.
In a tensile test, a sample is pulled until it breaks.
The tensile strength Rm is the highest stress in relation to the original cross-section.
In the Vickers test, a four-sided diamond pyramid is pressed into the material.
Unlike Brinell and Vickers, the Rockwell test measures the permanent depth of indentation.
The Charpy impact test checks toughness under a sudden blow.
The Wöhler curve shows how many load cycles a part can withstand before it breaks.

abschnitte.text: Before a material goes into a part, people want to know how much it can take. They test, for example, its **strength**, that is how hard you can pull before it tears. **Hardness** shows how well it resists being dented, and toughness whether it splinters when struck. In **destructive tests** the sample is broken; in non-destructive tests the part stays whole.

In a **tensile test**, a bar is clamped into a machine and pulled slowly until it breaks. The **tensile strength** Rm is the highest force divided by the original cross-section. A round sample 10 millimetres in diameter that breaks at 31.4 kilonewtons has a tensile strength of about 400 newtons per square millimetre. If a 50-millimetre measuring length stretches by 0.1 millimetres, the **strain** is 0.2 percent.

In hardness testing, a very hard object is pressed into the material and the dent is measured. The **Brinell** method uses a ball, the **Vickers** method a four-sided diamond pyramid, and in each case the size of the impression is measured. The **Rockwell** method, on the other hand, measures the permanent depth of indentation. In this way steels, aluminium or plastics can be compared well with one another.

In the **Charpy impact test**, a heavy pendulum smashes through a notched sample. This shows how tough a material is under a sudden blow, for instance in the cold. But many parts do not break because of one single large force, but because of constant back-and-forth movement. The **Wöhler curve**, named after the railway engineer August Wöhler, shows how many load cycles a part can withstand before it breaks.

With **ultrasound** or X-rays, you can look inside parts and find cracks. In **magnetic particle testing**, fine iron powder shows surface cracks in ferromagnetic materials such as steel. In this way, for example, railway wheels, aircraft parts and welds are checked regularly. In Switzerland, **Empa** in Dübendorf is a well-known research institute for materials testing.

begriffe.erklaerung: The highest stress that a material can withstand when pulled.
The resistance of a material to another object pressing into it.
The ability to absorb energy without breaking in a brittle way.
Slow weakening caused by many repeated loads.
How much a sample stretches in relation to its length.

gewusst: A diamond is so hard that in the Vickers test it makes a dent even in hardened steel.
In the 19th century, August Wöhler studied why railway axles suddenly broke after a long time.
Some steels become as brittle as glass in great cold; the Charpy impact test shows this.

teile.einleitung: A statement is a single command in a computer program, for example print("Hoi"). The computer carries out the statements one after another, like the steps in a recipe. Large programs are made up of many small statements.
wichtigste: A single command in a program is called a statement.
Statements are carried out in order from top to bottom.
In Python, the sign = assigns a value to a variable.
With x = 3, then x = 7, then print(x), 7 is printed, because the old value is overwritten.
With x = 5, y = x, x = 2, y stays equal to 5.
print(7 / 2) prints 3.5 in Python.
print(17 % 5) prints 2, which is the remainder of the division.

abschnitte.text: A program is a list of **statements**. Each statement tells the computer exactly what to do. In Python you usually write one statement per line. print("Hoi"), for example, is a statement that writes the word Hoi, Swiss German for hello, on the screen. The computer works through the lines in the **order** in which they are written.

A very important statement is the **assignment**. In Python the sign = is used for it. With x = 3, the value 3 is stored in the **variable** x. A variable is like a box with a name label. If you then write x = 7, the old value is replaced, and print(x) shows 7.

With x = 5, then y = x, then x = 2, a copy of the value 5 is stored in y. If you then change x, y still stays 5. With a = 2, b = 3, a = b, b = a, a first becomes 3, and then b gets the new value of a, so also 3. That is why print(a, b) gives the output 3 3. With a = 4 and b = a * 3, b is equal to 12, and print(b-a), which subtracts a from b, shows 8.

Python can also calculate with statements. The slash / divides exactly, which is why print(7 / 2) prints the **decimal number** 3.5. Python writes a point instead of a comma, as is usual in English. The percent sign % calculates the **remainder** of a division. 17 divided by 5 is 3 remainder 2, so print(17 % 5) prints the number 2.

Besides simple commands, there are statements that control the flow. A **conditional statement** with if only carries something out when a condition is met. A **loop** with for or while repeats statements several times. With such building blocks you can write almost any program. Learning robots and Scratch also work on this principle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single command in a program.
A named storage place that holds a value.
A statement that gives a variable a value, in Python with =.
A statement that repeats other statements.

gewusst: The = in Python does not mean “is equal to” as in mathematics, but “store”.
To swap two values, in many languages you need a third helper variable, otherwise both end up the same.
Python writes decimal numbers with a point, as is usual in English.

teile.einleitung: A binary tree is a way of organising data in computer science that looks like an upside-down tree. Each node may have at most two children, a left one and a right one. Binary trees help computers to find and sort data very quickly.
wichtigste: In a binary tree, each node has at most 2 child nodes.
The top node is called the root; nodes without children are called leaves.
A binary tree with 4 completely filled levels has 15 nodes.
In a binary search tree, smaller keys are in the left subtree.
An inorder traversal gives the keys of a search tree sorted in ascending order.
A binary tree with 1000 nodes needs at least 10 levels.
The AVL tree is named after Adelson-Velsky and Landis.

abschnitte.text: A **binary tree** is a data structure made of **nodes** that are connected by lines. Right at the top is the **root**, and unlike in nature, the tree grows downwards. Each node has at most two children, a left one and a right one, hence the word “binary”, meaning in two parts. Nodes without children are called leaves. You can imagine it like a family tree, except that each person has at most two descendants.

A tree has several **levels**: on the first there is only the root, on the second up to 2 nodes, on the third up to 4. With each level, the possible number of nodes doubles. A tree with 4 completely filled levels therefore has 1 plus 2 plus 4 plus 8, which is 15 nodes. With 10 levels, up to 1023 nodes fit in. That is why a tree with 1000 nodes needs at least 10 levels.

In a **binary search tree**, there is a fixed order: smaller keys are in the left subtree, larger ones in the right. If you are looking for a number, you compare it with the root and then go only left or only right. In this way about half of the tree is ruled out at each step, similar to the game “guess the number”. In a well-built tree with 1000 numbers, you need only about 10 comparisons. But if the tree is lopsided and looks like a long chain, the search may in the worst case have to go through all the nodes.

There are different orders for visiting all the nodes. In a **preorder** traversal, you visit the root first, then the left and then the right subtree. In an **inorder** traversal, you go left first, then to the root, then right. In a search tree, this gives you all the keys sorted in ascending order. In a postorder traversal, the root comes right at the end.

So that a search tree does not become lopsided, there are **self-balancing trees**. The best known is the AVL tree, which the Soviet mathematicians Georgy Adelson-Velsky and Evgenii Landis presented in 1962. After every insertion, it rearranges itself so that the left and right stay roughly the same height. Binary trees are also found in databases, in programs for compressing files and in decision trees, where each question has only two answers.

begriffe.erklaerung: An element in the tree that contains data.
The top node, where the tree begins.
A node without children, right at the bottom of the tree.
A node together with all the nodes hanging below it.

gewusst: A completely filled binary tree with only 30 levels would already have more than a billion nodes.
The draw for a knockout tournament is also a binary tree, with the winner at the root.
Computer scientists almost always draw trees with the root at the top.

teile.einleitung: An assembly language is a programming language that is very close to the machine language of the processor. Instead of long columns of numbers, you write short abbreviations such as MOV or ADD. A program called an assembler then translates these abbreviations into machine code.
wichtigste: An assembly language is a low-level language with abbreviations for machine instructions.
The readable abbreviations such as MOV or ADD are called mnemonics.
The x86 instruction MOV copies a value into a destination.
JMP jumps unconditionally to another address; PUSH puts a value on the stack.
A label is a symbolic name for an address.
Assembly programs are tied to a particular instruction set and can hardly be transferred.
A disassembler translates machine code back into assembly notation.

abschnitte.text: A processor only understands **machine code**, that is numbers made of zeros and ones. For people this is very hard to read. In an **assembly language**, you therefore write a short abbreviation for every machine instruction. Almost every line corresponds to exactly one instruction of the processor. A program called an **assembler** then translates the text into machine code.

The abbreviations are called **mnemonics**, which means something like memory aids. On processors of the x86 family, which are found in many PCs, MOV copies a value into a destination. ADD adds two values. JMP always jumps, that is without a condition, to another place in the program. With PUSH you put a value on the **stack**, a special area of memory.

A processor has a few very fast storage places called **registers**. Many assembly instructions work directly with these registers. So that you do not have to remember memory addresses, there are **labels**. A label is a symbolic name for an address, for example “start” or “loop”. The assembler later works out the right address from it.

Assembly programs can be very fast and very small. But they are laborious to write and hard to read. Also, every assembly program is tied to a particular **instruction set**. A program for x86 therefore does not simply run on an ARM processor, the kind found in most mobile phones. Today people usually program in high-level languages such as Python or C.

Assembly language is still used where every byte and every microsecond counts. Examples are small **microcontrollers**, start-up programs of computers and especially fast parts of programs. Security experts also need assembly language. With a **disassembler** they translate machine code back into assembly notation, for example to examine malware. In the past, many computer games were also written in assembly language.

begriffe.erklaerung: The instructions as numbers that the processor understands directly.
A readable abbreviation for a machine instruction, such as MOV.
A very fast, small storage place in the processor.
All the instructions that a particular processor understands.
A tool that translates machine code back into assembly language.

gewusst: The word assembler comes from the English “to assemble”, meaning to put together.
Both the translating program and the language itself are often simply called assembler.
The software for the Moon landing in 1969 was written largely in assembly language.

teile.einleitung: Reinforcement learning is a field of artificial intelligence in which a program learns by trying things out. For good decisions it gets a reward, for bad ones none or a penalty. This is how computers learnt to play games such as Go better than any human.
wichtigste: In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by trial and error.
After each action, the environment reports back the new state and a reward.
The rule by which the agent chooses an action is called a strategy or policy.
The agent has to weigh up trying things out against using what it knows; this is called exploration and exploitation.
The environment is usually described as a Markov decision process.
Q-learning learns the expected total value of every action in every state.
In 2017 AlphaGo Zero learnt Go purely by playing games against itself.

abschnitte.text: In reinforcement learning there is an **agent** and an **environment**. The agent is the learning program, for example a game character or a robot. It chooses an action, and the environment reports back the new state and a **reward**. The aim is to collect as much reward as possible in the long run. This is reminiscent of a dog that gets a treat for a successful trick.

The rule by which the agent acts in a situation is called a **strategy** or policy. Later rewards often count a little less than immediate ones; a discount factor is used for this. If an agent gets a reward of 10 three times in a row and the factor is 0.9, this gives 10 plus 9 plus 8.1, which is 27.1. Mathematically, the environment is usually described as a **Markov decision process**. In it, what happens next depends only on the current state and the chosen action.

An agent always faces a choice: should it take an action that has proved itself, or try something new? This dilemma is called **exploration and exploitation**. With the epsilon-greedy strategy, the agent chooses at random with a small probability, and otherwise the best known action. In this way it discovers new possibilities without completely forgetting what it has learnt. People know this too: in a restaurant, do you order your favourite dish or try something new?

A well-known method is **Q-learning**, which was presented by Christopher Watkins in 1989. The agent learns a value for every state and every action, which says how much reward it can expect in total. After each step, this value is improved a little. Combined with large **neural networks**, programs learnt in this way, from about 2013, to play old video games directly from the screen.

In 2016 the program AlphaGo by the company DeepMind beat the Go master Lee Sedol. A year later **AlphaGo Zero** learnt the game purely by playing against itself, with no human games at all, and became even stronger. Reinforcement learning also helps robots to walk and grasp. With chatbots, **RLHF** is used, reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rate answers, and the language model learns from this to give more helpful answers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The program that acts and learns as it does so.
A number that says how good an action was.
The rule for which action the agent chooses in which situation.
The current situation the agent is in.

gewusst: Go has so many possible positions that people believed for a long time that computers would not beat top players for decades.
The idea of reinforcement learning comes partly from psychology, where scientists studied how animals learn through reward.
An agent sometimes finds surprising tricks that the programmers themselves would never have thought of.

teile.einleitung: A bit is the smallest unit of information in computer science. It can have only two states: 0 or 1, off or on. Everything a computer stores, that is texts, pictures, music and games, is in the end made of countless bits.
wichtigste: The word bit stands for “binary digit”.
A bit has exactly two possible values: 0 or 1.
With 3 bits you can make 8 different combinations.
8 bits make 1 byte.
Internet speeds are given in bits per second.
80 megabits per second are equal to 10 megabytes per second.
Computers work with bits because current on or off is very easy to tell apart.

abschnitte.text: A **bit** is the smallest unit of information. The name is short for the English **binary digit**. A bit can only have the value 0 or 1, like a light switch that is off or on. So with one bit you can answer a yes-or-no question. For more information, you simply need more bits.

With every extra bit, the number of possibilities doubles. With 1 bit there are 2 combinations, with 2 bits already 4, namely 00, 01, 10 and 11. With 3 bits there are 2 times 2 times 2, which is **8 combinations**. With 8 bits you can already represent 256 different values. Counting with only 0 and 1 like this is called the **binary system**.

Eight bits together are called a **byte**. One byte is enough, for example, to store a single letter. Larger amounts have prefixes: kilo for a thousand, mega for a million and giga for a billion. Storage space is usually given in bytes, but internet speed in bits per second. That is why you have to be careful: 80 megabits per second divided by 8 is exactly 10 megabytes per second.

In a computer, a bit is represented by an electrical state, for example voltage present or not. On a hard drive, tiny magnetic areas store the bits. On a CD, they are small pits that a laser scans. A picture on a mobile phone consists of millions of picture points, and each colour is described with several bits. In this way many zeros and ones become a colourful photo.

The American mathematician **Claude Shannon** used the term bit in 1948 in a famous paper about information. He wrote that his colleague John W. Tukey had suggested the word. Shannon is regarded as the founder of **information theory**. But the idea of calculating with only two digits had already been described by the scholar Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz around 1700. Today scientists are researching quantum computers, which work with so-called qubits.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest unit of information; it is either 0 or 1.
A group of 8 bits.
A number system that knows only the digits 0 and 1.
A measure of how many millions of bits are sent per second.

gewusst: The English word “bit” also means “a little”, which suits the smallest unit well.
With only 20 yes-or-no questions, you can find one out of more than a million possibilities.
Half a byte, that is 4 bits, is sometimes jokingly called a “nibble”.

teile.einleitung: Image editing means changing photos and other pictures on a computer, tablet or mobile phone. You can crop them, brighten them, rotate them, adjust colours or add text and stickers. Professionals use programs such as Adobe Photoshop for this; for everyday use, apps on a mobile phone are often enough.
wichtigste: When cropping, you cut away distracting edges of a photo.
If a photo is too dark, you turn up the brightness.
You can rotate or flip a photo; when flipping, left and right swap over.
Red-eye correction removes glowing red eyes in flash photos.
With the Undo command, you reverse the last step.
It is best to save an edited photo as a copy so that the original is kept.
Many apps let you add text and stickers to a photo.

abschnitte.text: **Image editing** means changing a digital picture with a program. The colours and the arrangement of the pixels are recalculated. You can correct mistakes or design a picture creatively. In the past, photos were edited in the darkroom with chemicals; today it takes just a few clicks.

When **cropping**, you remove edges so that what matters is in the centre. If a picture is upside down, you rotate it, and when flipping, left and right swap sides. With **brightness** and contrast, you make dark photos lighter and dull pictures more vivid. Red-eye correction makes red eyes in flash photos dark again.

With **filters**, you can make a photo look, for example, black and white or like an old picture. With saturation, you set how strongly the colours glow. Professional programs work with **layers**, which lie on top of each other like transparent sheets. This lets you add text, stickers or other pictures without destroying the photo underneath.

The best-known professional program is **Adobe Photoshop**, which came out in 1990. A free alternative is the program GIMP. On mobile phones, the photo galleries often have their own editing tools built in. There are also many apps with filters, frames and stickers.

The **Undo** command reverses the last step; on many computers you can do this with the key combination Ctrl and Z. It is best to save an edited picture as a copy so that the original is kept. That way you can always start again later. It is also worth giving files sensible names.

With image editing and artificial intelligence, photos can be changed so that they look real even though they are not. In advertising, people are often made slimmer or more flawless than they really are. That is why it is worth not believing pictures on the internet blindly. Anyone who edits and shares photos of other people also needs their **permission**.

begriffe.erklaerung: To cut away the edges of a picture to keep only part of it.
A function that changes the look of a whole picture at once.
A kind of transparent sheet in an image program on which you can work separately.
The unchanged first version of a file.

gewusst: As early as the 19th century, photos were changed by scratching, painting over or combining negatives.
The word “photoshop” has become an expression for changing photos in both English and German.

teile.einleitung: The sampling rate tells you how many times per second a sound or another signal is measured when it is turned into digital numbers. It is given in hertz. It affects how good a digital recording sounds and how big the file becomes.
wichtigste: The sampling rate tells you how many measurements are recorded per second.
It is given in hertz; one hertz means one measurement per second.
Music on an audio CD is stored at 44.1 kHz.
For sound with video and DVD, 48 kHz is usual.
Classic digital telephony works at 8 kHz.
If the sampling rate is too low, disturbances called aliasing appear.
If you double the sampling rate, the file size roughly doubles.

abschnitte.text: A sound is a vibration of the air that changes continuously. But a computer can only store numbers. That is why a device measures the vibration at very short, regular intervals and writes down each measurement as a number. How many such measurements are made per second is called the **sampling rate**. The unit is the **hertz**, abbreviated Hz, and 1 kHz is 1000 measurements per second.

A microphone turns the sound waves into an electrical signal. Then an **analogue-to-digital converter** measures this signal at regular intervals and turns it into numbers. Besides the sampling rate, it also matters how precise each single measurement is; this is called the resolution or bit depth. When playing back, a digital-to-analogue converter turns the numbers back into a signal for loudspeakers or headphones. You can imagine it like a flip book: many single pictures together make a smooth movement.

People hear sounds from about 20 Hz to about 20 000 Hz. The **sampling theorem** says that you have to measure more than twice as often as the highest frequency in the signal. So to capture sounds up to 20 000 Hz properly, you need more than 40 000 measurements per second. This rule is named after the researchers Harry Nyquist and Claude Shannon. If you measure too rarely, **aliasing** occurs, and false sounds appear that were not in the original at all.

The audio CD stores music at 44.1 kHz, that is 44 100 measurements per second per channel. For films, DVDs and many videos, 48 kHz is usual. Recording studios often record at 96 kHz or more, so as to have something in reserve when editing. Classic digital telephony, for example ISDN, managed with 8 kHz, because speech needs fewer high sounds. That is why voices on the phone sound a bit duller than in real life.

The more measurements you store per second, the more space the file needs. If you double the **sampling rate**, the file size roughly doubles. One minute of music in CD quality needs about 10 megabytes without compression. Formats such as MP3 make the file much smaller by leaving out parts that you can hardly hear. When choosing the sampling rate, you therefore always look for a good compromise between sound and storage space.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit for “how many times per second”.
A component that measures a signal and turns it into numbers.
Interfering noises that occur when measurements are taken too rarely.
How fast something vibrates; for sounds it decides the pitch.

gewusst: The value of 44.1 kHz for the CD has to do with old video recorders, which were once used to store digital sound recordings.
A video camera also samples: it records, for example, 25 or 30 pictures per second.
Dogs and bats hear much higher sounds than people; for them you would need a higher sampling rate.

teile.einleitung: A clock-face timetable is a timetable in which trains and buses leave at regular intervals, always at the same minute. In 1982 Switzerland was one of the first countries to introduce a nationwide clock-face timetable. Since then, many departure times have been easy to remember.
wichtigste: In a clock-face timetable, trains run regularly, always at the same minute.
Switzerland introduced the nationwide clock-face timetable in 1982.
The idea came from a group of young experts who called themselves the “Spinnerclub” (crackpots’ club).
A hub is a station where trains meet so that people can change.
Bern is an important full hub in the Swiss clock-face timetable.
PostBus was also brought into the timetable pattern.
For travellers, the departure times are easy to remember.

abschnitte.text: In a **clock-face timetable**, a train leaves, for example, every hour at the same minute, such as at 7.04, 8.04 and 9.04. With a **half-hourly service**, a train comes every 30 minutes: after 7.04 the next one leaves at 7.34. In big cities, S-Bahn trains often even run every quarter of an hour. This means you do not have to look at the timetable every time.

At the beginning of the 1970s, a group of young engineers and transport experts developed the idea of a nationwide clock-face timetable. Because many people thought their plans were crazy at the time, they called themselves the **Spinnerclub**, which means something like crackpots’ club. They showed that regular connections would get more people to travel by train. Their idea was taken up by SBB.

On 23 May 1982 the nationwide **clock-face timetable** came into force in Switzerland. Most lines got at least an hourly service. Private railways and **PostBus** were also brought into the pattern so that the connections in the villages would fit. As a result, many lines got far more connections than before.

The **hubs** are especially clever. In stations such as Bern, Zurich or Basel, many trains arrive shortly before the full or half hour and leave again shortly afterwards. In a **full hub** such as Bern, trains from all directions meet in this way, and you can change easily. For this to work, the journey times between the hubs have to fit exactly.

With the **Rail 2000** project, which voters approved in 1987, the clock-face timetable was expanded further. New lines such as the new line between Mattstetten and Rothrist shortened journey times so that the hubs would work. Since 2004, trains have run every half hour on many main lines. Today other countries such as Austria and Germany take the Swiss clock-face timetable as a model.

begriffe.erklaerung: A regular gap in time at which trains or buses run.
A station where trains meet at the same time so that people can change.
A link where you can change from one train to the next.
A big expansion project of the Swiss railways for faster and more frequent connections.

gewusst: The Swiss railways are among the most punctual in the world, which is very important for connections to work in the clock-face timetable.
With Rail 2000, the journey time between Zurich and Bern was cut to just under an hour so that both hubs fit together.

teile.einleitung: The Advanced Encryption Standard, AES for short, is one of the most important encryption methods in the world. It protects data on wifi, in online banking, in messenger apps and on encrypted hard drives. Without the right key, encrypted text looks like a jumble of characters.
wichtigste: AES is a symmetric block cipher, so the sender and the recipient need the same key.
The algorithm was originally called Rijndael and was chosen as AES in 2000.
AES encrypts data in blocks of 128 bits.
Keys of 128, 192 or 256 bits are allowed, but not of 512 bits.
With a 128-bit key, AES goes through 10 rounds.
AES replaced the older DES standard, whose key was only 56 bits long.
When used correctly, AES is still regarded as very secure today.

abschnitte.text: AES is a method for changing data so that only someone with the right **key** can read it again. It is a **symmetric** method: the same key is used for encrypting and decrypting. AES works as a **block cipher** and processes the data in pieces of 128 bits each, which is 16 bytes. Longer texts are split into many such blocks.

The old DES standard had keys only 56 bits long and could be cracked with powerful computers at the end of the 1990s. That is why in 1997 the US agency **NIST** announced an open competition for a successor. Researchers from all over the world submitted proposals, which were examined publicly. In 2000 the **Rijndael** algorithm by the two Belgian cryptologists Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen won. Since 2001 it has officially been the AES.

AES processes each block in several **rounds**: 10 rounds with 128-bit keys, 12 with 192 bits and 14 with 256 bits. In each round the bytes are mixed up in fixed steps. In the **SubBytes** step, each byte is replaced using a fixed table, the S-box. Then rows are shifted (ShiftRows), columns are mixed (MixColumns) and part of the key is added (AddRoundKey). After all the rounds, nothing of the original text can be recognised.

How the individual blocks are linked with one another is decided by the **mode of operation**. The simplest mode, ECB, is regarded as insecure, because identical plaintext blocks always give identical encrypted blocks, so that patterns remain visible. Modern modes prevent this by linking the blocks with each other or with random values. The **GCM** mode encrypts the data and at the same time checks whether it has been changed on the way. It is often used, for example, for secure internet connections with HTTPS.

AES protects the wifi at home when the router works with WPA2 or WPA3. AES is also involved in online banking, in many messenger apps and in encrypting smartphones and laptops. Many modern processors have special instructions with which they can run AES particularly fast. The biggest weakness is usually not AES itself, but a badly chosen or leaked **password**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A secret sequence of numbers used to encrypt and decrypt data.
A method that encrypts data in pieces of the same size.
The smallest unit of information; it is either 0 or 1.
The readable message before it is encrypted.

gewusst: A 128-bit key has so many possibilities that all the computers in the world together would not have enough time to try them all.
The name Rijndael is made up of the surnames of the two inventors, Rijmen and Daemen.
AES is freely available; anyone may use it without paying licence fees.

teile.einleitung: USB is short for “Universal Serial Bus” and is the name of a worldwide standard for connecting devices. With USB cables you transfer data and charge mobile phones, headphones or tablets. Almost every child knows the small plug, and with USB-C there is now one connector for almost everything.
wichtigste: USB stands for Universal Serial Bus.
The first version, USB 1.0, appeared in 1996.
“Serial” means that the bits are sent one after another.
A USB cable carries not only data but also electricity for charging.
You can plug in a USB-C plug either way round.
In the EU, USB-C has been required as the charging port for new smartphones since the end of 2024.
A USB hub shares one port between several.

abschnitte.text: **USB** is a shared set of rules for what plugs look like and how devices talk to each other over a cable. Before USB, computers had many different ports for the mouse, keyboard, printer and joystick. USB replaced all these ports with a single **standard**. The word “universal” means that it is meant for all kinds of devices.

The name contains the word **serial**: the data is sent bit by bit, one after another, through a few wires, but extremely fast. Alongside them, other wires carry electricity, which powers devices or charges batteries. Thanks to **plug and play**, a device usually works straight after you plug it in, without complicated setting up. If you need more ports, a **USB hub** can share one port between several.

The first version, **USB 1.0**, appeared in 1996, developed by several computer companies, including Intel and Microsoft. In 2000 USB 2.0 followed, which could transfer up to 480 megabits per second. With USB 3.0 it became about ten times faster again; you can often recognise such ports by their blue insides. Today USB4 reaches speeds at which you can copy a whole feature film in a few seconds.

The flat, rectangular **USB-A** plug is still found on many computers, but it only fits one way round. For mobile phones there was for a long time the small Micro-USB plug. The newer **USB-C** plug is small and oval and can be plugged in either way round. Through USB-C you can transfer data, pictures and sound and even charge laptops.

In the past, almost every mobile phone needed its own charger, which caused a lot of electronic waste.
