That is why, since the end of 2024, the European Union has required new smartphones, tablets and headphones to have a **USB-C** charging port. This way one charger can be used for many devices. Devices sold in Switzerland therefore almost always have USB-C too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A shared rule that all manufacturers follow.
The smallest unit of information in a computer, a 0 or a 1.
Plug in and use straight away, without complicated setting up.
A splitter that shares one USB port between several.

gewusst: With the old USB-A plug, many people often try twice before it fits the right way round.
A USB stick is really a small memory chip with a built-in USB connector.
Today, with a single USB-C cable you can charge, transfer data and connect a screen all at the same time.

teile.einleitung: A binary code is a way of representing information with only two symbols, usually 0 and 1. Computers store and process everything like this: texts, pictures, music and videos. This suits the technology perfectly, because an electric circuit knows the two states off and on.
wichtigste: Binary code uses only the two symbols 0 and 1.
The smallest unit of information is called a bit and can be 0 or 1.
Eight bits together make one byte.
In binary code, 1 usually stands for on and 0 for off.
The number system with only 0 and 1 is called the binary system.
Computers store texts, pictures and music as zeros and ones.
The on-off symbol on many devices came from a 1 and a 0.

abschnitte.text: A light switch can only be off or on, and this is exactly what **binary code** uses. The 1 usually stands for on, with current flowing, and the 0 for off. In a computer there are billions of tiny switches, the **transistors**, which do exactly that. Because two states are easy to tell apart, computers work fast and reliably.

The smallest unit of information is called a **bit**, from the English binary digit. A bit can have exactly two values, 0 or 1. Eight bits make one **byte**, and a byte can represent 256 different values. Larger amounts are measured in kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes and terabytes.

In the **binary system**, each place is worth double the place to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. The number 5 is written as 101, that is 4 plus 0 plus 1. The number 10 is 1010 in binary. The scholar Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz described this system in detail in a famous essay in 1703.

So that a computer can store letters, every character gets a number, for example in the **ASCII code** or in today’s usual Unicode. Capital A has the number 65 in ASCII, which is 1000001 in binary. For pictures, the computer stores numbers for red, green and blue for each pixel. Music is broken down into many tiny measurements, which are also stored as zeros and ones.

A **QR code** consists of black and white squares and so is a kind of binary code. Barcodes at the supermarket till also work with light and dark. The on-off symbol on many devices came from a 1 and a 0. Even the punched cards of early calculating machines knew only hole or no hole.

The idea of sending messages with only two symbols is older than the computer. **Morse code** from the 19th century uses short and long signals. Smoke or light signals also work on the principle of on or off. Binary code perfected this idea and is today the language of all digital devices.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smallest unit of information; it is 0 or 1.
A group of 8 bits.
A number system that knows only the digits 0 and 1.
A tiny electronic switch in a computer chip.

gewusst: With only 8 bits you can represent 256 different values, from 0 to 255.
A single mobile phone photo often consists of several million bytes, that is dozens of millions of zeros and ones.

teile.einleitung: In image recognition, a computer learns to recognise objects, people, animals or text in pictures. It is used in smartphones, cars, hospitals and apps that identify plants. This was made possible above all by artificial intelligence and huge collections of example pictures.
wichtigste: In image recognition, a computer recognises objects, people or text in pictures.
A digital image consists of many small picture points, the pixels.
An AI needs many labelled example pictures to recognise cats, for example.
Convolutional neural networks, CNN for short, are used particularly often.
The image database ImageNet, with more than 14 million pictures, greatly advanced image recognition.
Text recognition, OCR for short, turns printed text in photos into editable text.
Face recognition can unlock a smartphone using the camera.

abschnitte.text: For people it is easy to see a cat in a photo. But for a computer, a picture is just a huge amount of numbers. Every digital image consists of many small picture points, the **pixels**, and each pixel has number values for red, green and blue. In **image recognition**, a program learns to work out from these numbers what can be seen in the picture. A mobile phone photo with 12 megapixels has about 12 million such points.

Modern image recognition uses **machine learning**. An AI is shown thousands of pictures labelled “cat” and others without a cat. Over time it learns by itself which features, such as pointed ears and whiskers, belong to a cat. **Convolutional neural networks**, CNN for short, which examine a picture layer by layer, are particularly well suited. The first layers recognise simple edges, later layers whole shapes such as eyes or wheels.

The image database **ImageNet** was built up from 2009 and contains more than 14 million labelled pictures. From 2010 there was a yearly competition in which programs had to sort pictures into categories. In 2012 a neural network called AlexNet won by a wide margin. Since then image recognition has improved rapidly, and today programs recognise some things as reliably as people.

With **face recognition**, a smartphone can be unlocked using the camera. **Text recognition**, also called OCR, turns a photo of a printed page into editable text. Many cars read traffic signs with a camera and show the speed limit. Apps identify plants, mushrooms or birds from a photo. In hospitals, image recognition helps to analyse X-rays and other scans.

Some websites show tests in which you have to click on all the pictures with traffic lights or bikes. These tests are called **CAPTCHA** and are meant to tell humans apart from automatic programs. But image recognition can also get things wrong, for example in poor light or from unusual angles. In addition, face recognition in public places raises questions about the protection of privacy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single picture point of a digital image.
A computer program that learns roughly in the way that nerve cells in the brain do.
Text recognition that turns printed text in pictures into real text.
Examples with which an AI learns.

gewusst: For ImageNet, thousands of people labelled the pictures by hand over the internet.
An AI can be completely misled by tiny changes to a picture that are invisible to humans.
The answers to some picture tests on the internet have also been used in part to train programs.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Plasma Center is a research institute at EPFL, the federal institute of technology in Lausanne, which researches nuclear fusion. There, experts study how extremely hot gas, a so-called plasma, can be held in place with magnets. The aim is one day to produce energy the way the Sun does.
wichtigste: The Swiss Plasma Center is at EPFL in Lausanne.
Until 2015 it was called the Centre de Recherches en Physique des Plasmas (CRPP).
The predecessor institute has been part of EPFL since 1973.
The TCV tokamak has been in operation since 1992.
The special strength of the TCV is that it can create a great many different plasma shapes.
In 2022 researchers, together with Google DeepMind, managed to control the plasma in the TCV magnetically using artificial intelligence.
Superconducting cables for fusion magnets are tested in the SULTAN facility at the PSI in Villigen.

abschnitte.text: In the Sun, light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones and release huge amounts of energy as they do so. This process is called **nuclear fusion**. On Earth, it needs temperatures of more than 100 million degrees. At such heat, gas turns into a **plasma**, in which electrons and atomic nuclei move about freely.

A plasma this hot must not touch any wall, so it is held in a ring-shaped vessel by strong magnetic fields. Such a machine is called a **tokamak**. Since 1992 the Swiss Plasma Center has run the **TCV**, the Tokamak à configuration variable. Its strength is that it can create a great many different plasma shapes, which makes it special worldwide.

At the TCV, for example, the **snowflake divertor** was studied, a special magnetic field shape that looks like a snowflake. A divertor carries hot particles away from the plasma and so protects the walls. In 2022 researchers from the Swiss Plasma Center, together with **Google DeepMind**, managed to control the plasma magnetically using **artificial intelligence**. The program learnt to adjust the magnetic coils so that the plasma took on the desired shape.

Large fusion machines need very strong magnets made of **superconductors**, which conduct electricity without resistance when they are strongly cooled. For this, the Swiss Plasma Center runs the **SULTAN** test facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in Aargau. There, superconducting cables are tested under extreme conditions. Cables for the international experimental reactor ITER in France were also tested here.

The institute used to be called the **Centre de Recherches en Physique des Plasmas**, CRPP for short, and has been part of EPFL since 1973. Since 2015 it has had the name Swiss Plasma Center. It is the most important centre for fusion research in Switzerland and works closely with research groups all over Europe. Many young physicists are also trained there.

begriffe.erklaerung: An extremely hot gas in which electrons and atomic nuclei are separated.
The fusing of atomic nuclei, which releases a lot of energy.
A ring-shaped machine that holds plasma in place with magnetic fields.
A material that, when cooled, conducts electricity with no resistance at all.

gewusst: The plasma in a tokamak is many times hotter than the inside of the Sun.
The word tokamak comes from Russian, because this design was invented in the Soviet Union.

teile.einleitung: A jet engine is an aircraft engine that sucks in air, burns it with fuel and pushes it out backwards as a hot jet. This pushes the aircraft forwards. Almost all large passenger aircraft and fighter jets fly with such engines today.
wichtigste: The thrust of a jet engine is based on the principle of recoil.
In 1930 Frank Whittle applied for a patent for a turbojet engine in Great Britain.
In 1939 the Heinkel He 178 was the first aircraft to fly with a turbine jet engine.
A turbofan sends a large part of the air past the hot core.
Accelerating a lot of air a little is more economical than accelerating a little air a lot.
A ramjet has no compressor and only works at high speed.
An afterburner gives fighter aircraft more thrust but uses much more fuel.

abschnitte.text: If you let go of a blown-up balloon, the air shoots out at the back and the balloon flies forwards. A jet engine works in exactly the same way, using the **principle of recoil**. The more air per second is accelerated backwards and the faster it comes out, the greater the **thrust**. If an engine accelerates, for example, 50 kilograms of air per second from 250 to 650 metres per second, this gives roughly 20 kilonewtons of thrust.

At the front, the **intake** sucks in the air. The **compressor** squeezes it together strongly with many bladed wheels. In the **combustion chamber**, kerosene is injected and burnt, which makes the gases very hot so that they expand. They drive a turbine, which in turn spins the compressor, and then flow out backwards through the nozzle.

Modern airliners have **turbofan engines** with a huge fan at the front. Most of the air flows past the hot core and produces most of the thrust. The **bypass ratio** tells you how much air flows past the core compared with the air that goes through the core. The higher it is, the more economical and quieter the engine.

In 1930 the Briton **Frank Whittle** applied for a patent for a turbojet engine. In Germany, Hans von Ohain developed his own engine independently. With it, on 27 August 1939, the **Heinkel He 178** became the first aircraft in the world to fly with turbine jet propulsion. After the Second World War, jet engines quickly took over in aviation.

A **ramjet** has no mechanical compressor. The air is squeezed together only by the high flying speed, so it only works once the aircraft is already very fast. Fighter aircraft often have an **afterburner**, which burns extra fuel behind the turbine. This gives much more thrust at take-off or in supersonic flight, but costs a great deal more fuel.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which an engine pushes an aircraft forwards.
A part with bladed wheels that squeezes the air that has been sucked in.
A bladed wheel that is driven by flowing gas.
How much air flows past the engine core compared with the air that goes through the core.

gewusst: In modern passenger jets, often ten times more air flows past the core than through it.
The combustion chamber of an engine is hotter than the metals of the turbine blades can actually withstand, so they are cooled with air.

teile.einleitung: A tunnel is an underground route through a mountain, under a river or under a city. Switzerland is a land of tunnels, because without them the Alps would be much harder to cross.
wichtigste: A tunnel is an artificial route through a mountain or underground.
Tunnels are built because they make the route shorter and safer.
The Gotthard road tunnel is about 17 kilometres long.
When the first Gotthard railway tunnel was built, the rock was blasted with dynamite.
Today huge tunnel boring machines with a rotating head bore through the rock.
Saint Barbara is regarded as the protector of tunnel builders.
When driving in a tunnel, your lights must be switched on.

abschnitte.text: A tunnel makes a route **shorter**, because you do not have to drive over a mountain or a pass. It is also open in winter, when snow and avalanches close the pass roads. Under cities, tunnels make room for underground railways, roads and pipes and cables. There are also tunnels under rivers and seas, such as the **Channel Tunnel** between France and England.

In **drill and blast** tunnelling, holes are drilled in the rock, filled with explosives and blasted bit by bit. The first Gotthard railway tunnel was built this way using dynamite, which was still new at the time. Today a **tunnel boring machine** is often used, which eats its way through the rock with a rotating head. Afterwards the walls are secured with concrete so that nothing collapses.

The first **Gotthard railway tunnel** is about 15 kilometres long and was opened in 1882. The Gotthard road tunnel, about 17 kilometres long, followed in 1980. The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** was opened in 2016 and, at about 57 kilometres, is the longest railway tunnel in the world. The Lötschberg Base Tunnel in the Bernese Oberland and Valais is also one of the great structures of the New Rail Link through the Alps.

Tunnel building used to be very dangerous; many workers died while the first Gotthard tunnel was being built. Heat, dust, inrushes of water and falling rocks made the work hard. That is why miners honour **Saint Barbara** as their patron saint, and there is often a statue of her at the tunnel entrance. Her feast day is 4 December.

When driving in a tunnel, you must switch on your **lights** and keep enough distance. Emergency exits, emergency call points and fire extinguishers are placed at regular intervals and clearly signposted. Large fans provide fresh air: this is the **ventilation**. If there is a fire, you should leave the car where it is and walk to the nearest emergency exit.

begriffe.erklaerung: A skilled worker who works in tunnel building.
Tunnel building in which the rock is blasted bit by bit.
The moment when the two sides of a tunnel meet.
A tunnel deep down at the foot of the mountains, so that trains hardly have to climb.

gewusst: Animals build tunnels too, such as the mole, which digs long passages underground.
Deep inside the Gotthard Base Tunnel, the rock is more than 40 °C hot.
Swiss railways run through hundreds of tunnels, many of them in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: A heat engine turns heat into movement, that is into mechanical work. Steam engines, car engines and the turbines in power stations are all heat engines.
wichtigste: A heat engine gets work from a flow of heat from a hot reservoir to a cold one.
According to the second law of thermodynamics, it always has to give off part of the heat to colder surroundings.
A machine that turned heat completely into work would be a perpetual motion machine of the second kind and is impossible.
The work is the heat taken in minus the waste heat given off.
Steam power stations work according to the Rankine cycle.
In a Stirling engine, the heat comes from outside and the working gas stays sealed in.
In 1865 Rudolf Clausius introduced the term entropy.

abschnitte.text: A **heat engine** takes in heat from a hot source, such as fire, steam or burning fuel. It turns part of this into work, for example the turning of a shaft. It gives off the rest as **waste heat** to colder surroundings. Examples are the steam engine, the car engine, the jet engine and the steam turbine.

The work gained is the heat taken in minus the waste heat given off. If a machine takes in 1000 joules of heat per cycle and gives off 650 joules, it does 350 joules of work. Its **efficiency** is then 35 percent. Car engines often reach only about 25 to 40 percent, modern combined-cycle gas and steam power stations about 60 percent.

The **second law of thermodynamics** says that heat flows by itself only from hot to cold. That is why every heat engine always has to give off part of the heat to colder surroundings. A machine that turned heat from only one reservoir completely into work would be a **perpetual motion machine of the second kind** and cannot be built. In 1824 the Frenchman Sadi Carnot showed that the efficiency can be higher the greater the difference in temperature.

In the **steam engine**, hot steam drives a piston; James Watt improved it decisively in the 18th century. In the **Stirling engine**, the heat comes from outside and the working gas always stays sealed in. Steam power stations work according to the **Rankine cycle**, in which water is turned into steam, drives a turbine and becomes liquid again in the condenser. Internal combustion engines produce the heat directly in the cylinder.

Nuclear power stations are also thermal power stations, because they use nuclear fission to produce steam for a turbine. At the **Gösgen** and **Leibstadt** power stations you can see large cooling towers. They give off the waste heat from the condenser into the air; the white clouds above them are water vapour. Other power stations are cooled with river water and therefore do not need a tall cooling tower.

begriffe.erklaerung: The share of energy that is turned into useful work.
Heat that a machine gives off unused to its surroundings.
The part of physics that studies heat, energy and work.
A measure of how spread out energy is, and therefore how hard it is to use.
In a power station, the part where steam is cooled and turns back into water.

gewusst: The steam engine was the driving force of the industrial revolution and powered factories, locomotives and ships.
Robert Stirling patented his hot air engine as early as 1816.
Your body also converts energy, but it is not a heat engine, because it uses chemical energy directly.

teile.einleitung: Streaming means that music or videos are played over the internet while the data is still loading. So you do not have to wait until a whole file has been downloaded. Music services, video platforms and livestreams all work on this principle.
wichtigste: With streaming you play music or videos while the data is still loading.
A buffer loads a few seconds in advance so that playback does not stutter.
Videos are compressed so that less data has to be sent.
The bitrate tells you how much data is sent per second.
With slow internet, the picture quality adjusts automatically and becomes blurrier.
A livestream broadcasts an event in real time.
With a download, a file is saved permanently; with streaming it usually is not.

abschnitte.text: The English word **stream** means a current or a brook. With streaming, the data flows without a break from the server to the device, like a brook. The video or song starts after a few seconds, even though far from everything has arrived yet. Unlike with a **download**, the file normally does not stay saved on the device afterwards.

So that it does not keep juddering, the device always loads a few seconds ahead into a temporary store, the **buffer**. If the internet slows down for a moment, the buffer is used up first. The **bitrate** tells you how much data is sent per second. A video in high resolution needs a much higher bitrate than a song.

An uncompressed video would be huge and could hardly be sent. That is why it is **compressed**: a program leaves out information that you would hardly notice, for example parts of the picture that do not change from one frame to the next. With **adaptive streaming**, several quality levels are ready. If the connection is slow, the player automatically switches to a blurrier version so that the video keeps playing.

Big providers do not store their videos in just one place. They use **content delivery networks**, which are networks of many servers all over the world. A video then comes from a server that is as close as possible to the viewers. This makes the transfer faster and takes pressure off the internet.

In a **livestream**, an event is broadcast in real time, such as a football match, a concert or a computer game. Swiss television also offers its programmes for streaming on platforms such as Play SRF. Because streaming uses a lot of data, it is worth using wifi when you are out rather than mobile data. Data centres and data transfer also use electricity, so streaming sparingly is good for the environment too.

begriffe.erklaerung: A temporary store that loads data in advance.
The amount of data that is sent per second.
To make data smaller so that it takes up less space.
A computer on the internet that provides data for other devices.

gewusst: Video streaming makes up a large part of all the data traffic on the internet.
In a livestream the picture often arrives a few seconds later than it really happens.

teile.einleitung: Big data is the English term for enormous amounts of data that are too big or too fast for normal programs. Such data is produced by search engines, social networks, sensors, weather stations and research facilities. With special tools you can find patterns in it, but there are risks too.
wichtigste: Big data is amounts of data that are too big, too fast or too varied for conventional methods.
Big data is often described with the features volume, velocity and variety, often with veracity added.
Velocity means the high speed at which data is produced and processed.
In 2004 Google presented the programming model MapReduce.
The Hadoop framework is named after the toy elephant of Doug Cutting’s son.
A data lake stores large amounts of raw data in its original format.
In huge data sets you can easily find chance connections with no real meaning.

abschnitte.text: Every day an unimaginable amount of data is produced in the world, for example through searches, photos, videos, payments and measuring devices. When amounts of data become so big that a single computer can no longer handle them, people speak of **big data**. This is often described with the three Vs: **volume** for the amount, **velocity** for the speed and variety for the diversity. Veracity, meaning the trustworthiness and quality of the data, is often named as a fourth V. Such amounts are measured in petabytes or even zettabytes; one zettabyte is 10 to the power of 21 bytes.

Instead of using one supercomputer, the work is spread across hundreds or thousands of normal computers. For this, Google presented the programming model **MapReduce** in 2004. The free program **Hadoop** put this idea into practice and is named after the yellow toy elephant of the son of the developer Doug Cutting. Hadoop includes the distributed file system HDFS. The later program Apache Spark is often faster, because it keeps interim results in the working memory instead of on the hard drive.

Big companies run huge **data centres** with thousands of servers. A central store that collects raw data in its original format is called a **data lake**. Only when it is needed is the data prepared and analysed. Data centres need a lot of electricity and cooling, which is why some are in cold regions or use their waste heat for heating.

At **CERN** near Geneva, the Large Hadron Collider particle accelerator produces enormous amounts of data, which are analysed on computers spread across many countries. MeteoSwiss uses huge amounts of measurements and computer models for weather forecasts. Transport companies analyse data to plan timetables and how full vehicles will be. Hospitals and researchers also work with large collections of data, for instance to understand diseases better.

Big data can help to predict traffic jams, save energy or detect diseases earlier. But anyone who searches huge amounts of data for any connections at all will find many **chance correlations** with no real meaning. In addition, much data contains personal information about people. That is why in Switzerland the Federal Act on Data Protection, which has applied in a new version since September 2023, regulates how companies may handle personal data.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large building full of computers that store and process data.
A collecting store for raw data in its original format.
A connection between two things, which does not always mean cause and effect.
Rules that protect people’s personal data.

gewusst: A zettabyte is a one with 21 zeros of bytes.
Because you almost always find some chance patterns in huge amounts of data, researchers have to check results carefully.
Hadoop’s mascot is still a yellow elephant today.

teile.einleitung: In alphabetical order, words and names are arranged according to the order of the letters in the alphabet. This way you can quickly find what you are looking for in dictionaries, class lists and telephone directories. Computers also sort alphabetically all the time.
wichtigste: Without Ä, Ö and Ü, the German alphabet has 26 letters.
You compare the first letter first; for example, Ben comes before Lea and Mia.
If the first letters are the same, the second one decides: “Haus” comes before “Hund”.
If these are the same too, you look at the third: “Rabe” comes before “Rad” and “Rose”.
With Bern, Lucerne and Zurich, Zurich comes last.
The series “Ast”, “Ball”, “Dach” is correctly sorted in alphabetical order.
Computers sort words using number codes for each letter.

abschnitte.text: The **alphabet** is the fixed order of the letters. In German, without Ä, Ö and Ü, it has 26 letters, from A to Z, just like the English alphabet. Directly before F comes E, directly after M comes N. The word “alphabet” comes from the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta. If you know the alphabet well, you can sort quickly.

You always compare the **first letter** first. That is why Ben comes before Lea and Mia, and the German words “Ast” (branch), “Ball” (ball), “Dach” (roof) are correctly sorted. If the first letters are the same, you look at the second: with “Haus” (house) and “Hund” (dog), the a before the u decides, so “Haus” comes first. With “Rabe” (raven), “Rad” (wheel) and “Rose” (rose), the first two letters of “Rabe” and “Rad” are the same, so the third decides: b comes before d. If one word is the beginning of another, the shorter one comes first, so “Ball” comes before “Ballon” (balloon).

For Ä, Ö and Ü there are two rules. In dictionaries they are usually treated like A, O and U, so “Bär” (bear) comes next to “Bar” (bar). In lists of names they are sometimes written as ae, oe and ue. With Swiss place names such as **Zürich** or **Glarus**, simply the first letter counts, which is why Zurich comes after Bern and Lucerne. Capital and small letters usually do not matter for people when sorting.

A computer does not know any letters, only numbers. Every character has a **number code**, for example in the Unicode standard. The computer compares the codes character by character. Capital letters often come before all small letters, which is why programs sometimes sort in unexpected ways. For fast sorting there are special **sorting algorithms**, such as bubble sort or quicksort.

You find alphabetically sorted lists everywhere: in the **dictionary**, in the index of a non-fiction book, in class lists and in the contact list on your phone. Because you know the order, you do not have to read through everything. You can open it in the middle and say straight away whether you need to search further towards the front or the back. In computer science this fast method is called **binary search**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fixed order of all the letters of a writing system.
The letters Ä, Ö and Ü.
A set of instructions that a computer uses to put things in the right order.
You halve a sorted list again and again until you find what you are looking for.

gewusst: In a thick dictionary, you can find any word with binary search in about 20 steps.
Not all languages have the same alphabet: the Swedish alphabet ends with Å, Ä and Ö.
Many computers would sort “Zebra” before “apfel” (apple), because capital letters have smaller codes.

teile.einleitung: A hydrofoil is a boat with small wings under the hull that lift it out of the water when it travels fast. Because almost only the wings are then in the water, it can go much faster than an ordinary boat.
wichtigste: A hydrofoil has wings under the hull in the water.
At high speed the hull lifts out of the water.
The underwater wings work in a similar way to aircraft wings.
Because the water slows the hull down less, the boat is very fast.
In waves it rocks less, because the hull is above the waves.
When it slows down, the hull sinks back into the water.
In German it is called a “Tragflügelboot”.

abschnitte.text: Under the hull there are narrow **foils**, which are fixed to struts. They are shaped like the wings of an aircraft. When water flows quickly over them, **lift** is produced, which pushes the boat upwards. Because water is much denser than air, quite small wings are enough for this.

A normal boat has to push the water aside with its whole hull, which takes a lot of force. With a hydrofoil at full speed, only a small part reaches into the water, so the **water resistance** is much smaller. In this way it saves fuel and reaches high speeds. When it slows down, the lift is no longer enough and the hull **sinks back** into the water.

Because the hull floats above the waves, the boat rocks less than an ordinary ship. That is why the journey is often more pleasant for passengers. In very rough seas, however, hydrofoils cannot travel well. Also, the wings are easily damaged by driftwood and other obstacles in the water.

As early as around 1906, the Italian **Enrico Forlanini** tested a hydrofoil on Lake Maggiore. Alexander Graham Bell, the inventor of the telephone, later also built a fast hydrofoil. From the 1950s, hydrofoils ran in scheduled services, for example on lakes in Italy and on rivers in the Soviet Union. To this day, such **fast ferries** connect islands with the mainland in some places.

In water sports the principle is very popular today and is called **foiling**. Racing yachts, for example in the America's Cup, float above the water on foils. Boards for kitesurfing, windsurfing or wing foiling also often have a wing on a long fin. On Swiss lakes you see more and more people gliding silently above the water like this.

begriffe.erklaerung: A force that pushes a wing upwards in a flow.
The main body of a boat.
The word for both the underwater wing and the boat that uses it.
A water sport in which you glide above the water on a foil.

gewusst: Modern racing yachts with foils can go faster than the wind that drives them.
The word hydrofoil is made up of Greek hydro for water and English foil for wing.
Some electric surfboards with foils run without any wind or waves at all.

teile.einleitung: A telegram was a short, fast message that was sent from town to town over telegraph lines. Long before there were mobile phones and emails, this was the fastest way to send someone an important message.
wichtigste: A telegram was a short message that was sent electrically over lines.
You handed it in at the post office counter and paid per word.
That is why people wrote as briefly as possible and left out small words.
Instead of a full stop, the English word STOP was often used.
At the destination, a telegram messenger delivered the message to the house.
People liked to send greetings telegrams for weddings and birthdays.
Today text messages on mobile phones have mostly replaced the telegram.

abschnitte.text: The telegram is based on the **telegraph**, a device that sends messages over wires using electrical pulses. The American Samuel Morse developed an alphabet of short and long signals for it, **Morse code**. In 1844 Morse sent a famous message from Washington to Baltimore. Soon telegraph lines stretched across whole countries, and from 1866 a cable that worked permanently lay across the Atlantic.

Anyone who wanted to send a telegram went to the **post office counter** and filled in a form. A clerk then sent the text over the line to the telegraph office at the destination. Later, **teleprinters** took over this work; these were machines that looked like typewriters and sent the text automatically. At the destination, the message was printed or stuck onto paper and put into an envelope.

The last part of the journey was covered by a **telegram messenger**, often on foot or by bike. He brought the message straight to the recipient’s home, sometimes just a few hours after it had been sent. A telegram messenger ringing the bell was therefore always something special. Because telegrams often contained very important news, people opened them with great excitement.

A telegram cost money per word, so people kept it as short as possible. Articles and polite phrases were usually left out, and instead of a punctuation mark people wrote **STOP**. A typical telegram might read “ARRIVING MONDAY TRAIN STOP PLEASE COLLECT”. This very brief language is still called **telegram style** today.

For weddings, births or special birthdays, people liked to send beautifully designed **greetings telegrams**. With the telephone, the fax, email and finally the mobile phone, telegrams became rarer and rarer. In many countries the service was therefore stopped or greatly reduced. Today **text messages** and chat apps do the job of delivering a message in seconds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that sends messages over a line using electrical pulses.
A script of short and long signals, called dots and dashes.
Very brief language without unnecessary words.
A machine that sends typed text over a line to another machine.

gewusst: The word telegram comes from Greek and means roughly “something written into the distance”.
Punctuation marks often cost extra, so the word STOP was cheaper than a full stop.
The SOS distress signal used by ships was also sent by radio in Morse code.

teile.einleitung: A heat pump is a heating system that takes heat from its surroundings, for example from the air, the ground or water. Using a little electricity, it pumps this heat up to a higher temperature, a bit like a fridge, only the other way round.
wichtigste: A heat pump takes heat from air, ground or water.
Technically it is closely related to the fridge.
It needs electricity to run.
Inside, a refrigerant circulates that evaporates even at low temperatures.
A compressor squeezes the gaseous refrigerant and makes it hotter.
The seasonal performance factor shows how much heat it delivers per kilowatt hour of electricity.
Because it does not burn heating oil, it is regarded as more climate-friendly than an oil heating system.

abschnitte.text: Even cold winter air still contains heat that can be used. An **air-to-water heat pump** takes this heat from the outside air and passes it to the water in the heating system. A **ground heat probe** is a deep borehole, often 100 to 300 metres deep, in which pipes take heat from underground. Other heat pumps use groundwater, lakes or rivers.

In a heat pump, a **refrigerant** flows round in a loop and evaporates even at low temperatures. As it does so, it takes in heat from the surroundings. A **compressor** squeezes the gas, which makes it much hotter, similar to the way a bike pump gets warm when you pump. The hot gas gives its heat to the heating water, becomes liquid again, and the cycle starts all over again.

A **fridge** works on the same principle. It pumps heat from the inside to the outside, which is why its back is warm. A heat pump does it the other way round and pumps heat from outside into the house. Some devices can even switch over in summer and cool the house.

The **seasonal performance factor** tells you how much heat a heat pump delivers per kilowatt hour of electricity over the whole year. A figure of 4 means that one kilowatt hour of electricity gives four kilowatt hours of heat. Ground heat probes usually achieve better values than air heat pumps, because in winter the ground is warmer than the air. A heat pump works best with underfloor heating, which only needs moderately warm water.

As early as 1938, a heat pump heated **Zurich’s town hall** with heat from the River Limmat. Today most new buildings in Switzerland are heated with heat pumps, and many old oil and gas heating systems are being replaced. Because Swiss electricity comes largely from hydropower, the climate balance is especially good. The federal government and the cantons often support the switch with grants.

begriffe.erklaerung: A liquid that evaporates even at low temperatures and carries heat.
A pump that squeezes a gas and so heats it up.
A deep borehole with pipes that takes heat from the ground.
How much heat is produced per kilowatt hour of electricity over the year.

gewusst: An air heat pump can still get heat from the air even at minus 15 degrees.
A heat pump delivers more heat energy than it uses in electricity, because the rest comes from the surroundings.
The hum of an air heat pump comes from the fan that draws air through the device.

teile.einleitung: Binary search is a very fast algorithm for finding a value in a sorted list. Instead of going through everything from front to back, it looks in the middle and halves the search area at each step. In this way it finds a value even among a million entries with at most 20 comparisons.
wichtigste: Binary search only works in a sorted list.
At each step it compares the value it is looking for with the middle element of the search area.
After each comparison, about half of the list is left.
With 1000 entries it needs at most 10 comparisons, with a million at most 20.
If the list becomes twice as long, it needs at most one more comparison.
If the search area becomes empty, the value is not in the list.

abschnitte.text: Imagine someone thinks of a number between 1 and 100 and only says higher or lower. The smartest thing is to guess 50 first, then 25 or 75 depending on the answer, and so on. This is exactly how **binary search** works. It halves the search area at every step, which is why it is also called the **bisection method**.

The list must first be **sorted**, for example in ascending order. The algorithm compares the value it is looking for with the middle element. If the value is smaller, it searches on in the front half; if it is larger, in the back half. If it is equal, it has been found, and if the search area becomes empty, the value is not there.

We are looking for 7 in the list 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 29. The middle element is 15, and because 7 is smaller, only 3, 7, 11 are left. There the middle is 7, so the number has been found after 2 comparisons. A **linear search** from the front would also have needed only 2 steps here, but with large lists binary search is enormously faster.

Because the area halves each time, the number of comparisons grows only very slowly. With 1000 entries, at most 10 comparisons are enough, because 2 to the power of 10 is 1024. With a million entries it is at most 20. If the list becomes twice as long, only **one comparison** is added; experts say that the running time is **logarithmic**.

Anyone who looks something up in a printed dictionary or telephone directory does something similar. You open it roughly in the middle and decide whether the word is further forward or further back. Databases, search engines and programs use binary search all the time. When looking for bugs in program code, the idea of narrowing the problem down by halving also helps.

Binary search only works if the data is **sorted**. An unordered list has to be sorted first, and that takes time. If sorting is not worth it, the simple linear search is used. Although the idea is simple, small mistakes with the boundaries of the search area easily creep in when programming it.

begriffe.erklaerung: An exact set of instructions for solving a task.
The entries are in a fixed order, for instance by size.
You check all the entries one after another from the front.
The work grows only very slowly, even though the amount of data grows a lot.

gewusst: With only 33 comparisons, binary search could find a name in a sorted list of all the people on Earth.
The number-guessing game with higher and lower is a playful binary search.

teile.einleitung: A username is the name you use to log in to a game, an app or a website. Other people often see it, so it should not give anything away about you. Together with a secret password, it opens your own account.
wichtigste: A username is a name for logging in.
Unlike the password, the username is not secret, but the password is.
A good username does not contain your full name, your age or where you live.
A made-up name such as “Starfox” is safer than your real name.
Your parents should help you to think up your username.
You must never use a friend’s username to pretend to be them.
A small profile picture often appears next to the username.

abschnitte.text: A **username** is the name by which a computer, an app or a game recognises you. In games it is sometimes also called a nickname. Each username usually appears only once in a service, so that there is no confusion. To log in you also need a **password**. The username says who you are; the password proves it.

The username is often visible to others, for example in a ranking or in a chat. The password, on the other hand, is **secret** and belongs only to you. You should not tell it to anyone, not even your best friend. Some services use your email address to log in instead of a username. You should not show that publicly either.

A good username gives nothing personal away about you. It does not contain your full name, your year of birth or where you live. A name such as “Noah_Thun”, for example, shows where someone lives, and a year gives away your **age**. Made-up names using animals, colours or things you like are better, such as “Starfox”. Ask your parents for advice when you are thinking one up.

Next to the username, many apps show a small picture, the **profile picture** or avatar. Here too, a drawn picture or a game character is safer than a real photo of you. In the profile you can often give further details, but you do not have to fill them in. The less strangers know about you, the better you are protected. In the settings you can often decide who may see your profile.

You must never use another person’s username or account to pretend to be them. That is unfair, can hurt others and may even be against the law. If someone has used your account, tell your parents straight away and change the password together with them. If you get unpleasant messages, you can report or block other users. In Switzerland, children and young people can also get help from Pro Juventute on the number 147.

begriffe.erklaerung: Your personal area in an app or on a website.
A secret word with which you prove that the account belongs to you.
A picture or figure that represents you on the internet.
To get access to an account with a username and password.

gewusst: With many services you cannot change your username later, so it is worth choosing it well.
Big services have so many members that popular usernames are quickly taken.
In technical language, logging in with a username and password is also called a “login”.

teile.einleitung: Swissmetro was a bold Swiss transport project: trains were to race through Switzerland in tubes deep underground at several hundred kilometres per hour. From Bern to Zurich would have taken only about 12 minutes. Swissmetro was never built, but the idea lives on to this day.
wichtigste: Swissmetro was meant to be a maglev train in underground tubes with thin air.
The engineer Rodolphe Nieth launched the project in 1974.
The air in the tubes was to be reduced to about 10 percent of normal air pressure.
A main line was planned from Geneva via Lausanne, Bern and Zurich to St Gallen.
In 1992 Swissmetro AG was founded, and in 1998 an application for a licence for the Geneva to Lausanne line followed.
In 2009 Swissmetro AG was wound up.
The successor project Swissmetro-NG is developing the idea further.

abschnitte.text: Swissmetro was meant to connect the big Swiss cities so quickly that they would become almost like one single big city. The vehicles were not to roll on wheels but to float above the track as a **maglev train**. Speeds of about 400 to 500 kilometres per hour were planned. A journey from Bern to Zurich would then have taken only about 12 minutes, and a journey from Geneva to St Gallen less than an hour.

At high speed, **air resistance** is the biggest obstacle: it slows you down and uses a lot of energy. That is why the vehicles were to run in tunnel tubes in which the air is thinned to about 10 percent of normal air pressure, similar to the air at great flying heights. The tubes were to lie deep underground so that they would not cut through the landscape. Magnetic forces would have carried, guided and driven the vehicles.

The French-speaking Swiss engineer **Rodolphe Nieth** launched the idea in 1974. Experts, among others from EPFL in Lausanne, developed the concept further, and in 1992 **Swissmetro AG** was founded. In 1998 the promoters submitted an application for a licence for a first pilot line from Geneva to Lausanne. Because of the enormous costs and a lack of investors, however, it was never built, and in 2009 the company was wound up.

With **Swissmetro-NG** there is a successor project that is developing the idea further with new technology. Similar ideas are being studied around the world under the name **Hyperloop**, in which capsules are to travel through tubes that are almost empty of air. In Switzerland, researchers are testing on test tracks how such systems could work. Whether such a train will ever be built for passengers is still open.

begriffe.erklaerung: A train that is carried by magnets and floats above the track without wheels.
How strongly the air presses on everything; in thin air it is lower.
The force with which the air slows down a fast vehicle.
Permission from the state, for example to build and run a railway line.

gewusst: The Swissmetro idea came about almost 40 years before the term Hyperloop became known around the world.
With Swissmetro, the journey from Bern to Zurich would have been shorter than many people’s journey to work.
The tubes were to lie so deep that nothing would have been noticed at the surface.

teile.einleitung: An internal combustion engine is a machine that burns fuel such as petrol or diesel inside itself and turns this into movement. For more than 100 years it has powered cars, lorries, motorbikes, ships and lawnmowers. Because it produces exhaust gases, people are now looking for cleaner ways of powering vehicles.
wichtigste: In an internal combustion engine, a mixture of fuel and air burns in a closed cylinder.
In 1876 Nikolaus August Otto developed the four-stroke engine with compression; the Otto engine is named after him.
The four strokes are called intake, compression, power and exhaust.
The crankshaft turns the up-and-down movement of the pistons into a turning movement.
In a diesel engine, the fuel ignites because of the heat of the highly compressed air.
In 1886 Carl Benz applied for the patent for his motor car; in 1888 Bertha Benz drove it from Mannheim to Pforzheim.
Burning petrol produces carbon dioxide, which strengthens the greenhouse effect.

abschnitte.text: Inside the engine there are **cylinders**, in which **pistons** move up and down. A mixture of fuel and air is squeezed together in them and burnt. The hot gases expand explosively and push the piston down. The **crankshaft** turns this up-and-down movement into a turning movement, which finally drives the wheels.

Most car engines are **four-stroke engines**. In the first stroke, the piston sucks in air and fuel. In the second stroke, the mixture is compressed, that is squeezed together. In the third stroke it is ignited and pushes the piston down, and in the fourth stroke the exhaust gases are pushed out.

In the **Otto engine**, the petrol engine, a spark plug ignites the mixture with an electric spark. In a **diesel engine**, the air is compressed so strongly that it becomes very hot. When diesel is then injected, it ignites by itself. Rudolf Diesel developed this engine in the 1890s; it is used mainly in lorries, buses and ships.

As early as 1807, **François Isaac de Rivaz** from Valais received a patent for a vehicle with an internal combustion engine that ran on gas. In 1876 **Nikolaus August Otto** built the four-stroke engine with compression. In 1886 Carl Benz applied for the patent for his motor car, which is regarded as the first modern automobile. In 1888 **Bertha Benz** drove with her sons from Mannheim to Pforzheim without her husband knowing, and proved that the car was fit for everyday use.

Burning fuel produces **carbon dioxide** and other exhaust gases such as nitrogen oxides and soot. Carbon dioxide strengthens the greenhouse effect and so contributes to climate change. Catalytic converters and particle filters make the exhaust gases cleaner, but they cannot prevent the carbon dioxide. That is why more and more electric cars are being built today.

Internal combustion engines are found in cars, motorbikes, lorries, tractors, construction machines and ships. Lawnmowers, chainsaws and emergency generators also often have a small engine. Aircraft mostly use **jet engines**, which also burn fuel. In Switzerland, however, almost all trains run on electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: A moving part in the cylinder that is pushed down by the hot gases.
A tube in the engine in which the fuel burns.
A shaft that turns the up-and-down movement of the pistons into a rotation.
A part that lights the mixture in a petrol engine with a spark.
To squeeze a gas into a smaller space.

gewusst: On the way, Bertha Benz had to buy petrol at a chemist’s, because there were no petrol stations yet.
The power of engines is often still given in horsepower.
A car engine can turn several thousand times per minute.

teile.einleitung: A traffic control system is a system on motorways that controls speed and lanes with changing displays. It measures the traffic all the time and so helps to prevent traffic jams and accidents.
wichtigste: A traffic control system controls the traffic with changing displays.
When traffic is heavy, it lowers the speed limit.
This makes the traffic flow more evenly, and jams form later.
Sensors such as induction loops in the road count the vehicles.
A phantom traffic jam forms without an accident, just through braking in heavy traffic.
In Switzerland, the hard shoulder is sometimes opened as a driving lane at peak times.
FEDRO’s Swiss traffic management centre is in Emmenbrücke.

abschnitte.text: Above the motorway hang gantries with **variable message signs**, which can show different signs. For example, they set 80 or 100 km/h, warn of traffic jams or close a lane with a red cross. A computer decides what is shown. The displays count like normal traffic signs and must be obeyed.

In the road surface there are **induction loops**, loops of wire that notice when a car drives over them. There are also radar devices, cameras and sensors for fog, rain and ice. From the data, the system works out how dense and fast the traffic is. When it gets crowded, it lowers the speed so that everyone drives **evenly**.

A **phantom traffic jam** forms without an accident or roadworks, just because someone brakes in heavy traffic. The driver behind brakes a little harder, the next one harder still, until everything stops. If everyone drives a little more slowly and evenly, this happens less often. That is why the aim of the system is called **harmonising** the traffic flow.

A **section control system** regulates speed and warnings on a particular stretch of motorway. A **network control system**, on the other hand, diverts traffic onto alternative routes using variable direction signs. At some slip roads, traffic lights control how many vehicles per minute may join the motorway; this is called **ramp metering**. This keeps the motorway flowing for longer.

The national roads belong to the federal government and are looked after by the **Federal Roads Office FEDRO** (ASTRA in German). Its Swiss traffic management centre is in **Emmenbrücke** in the canton of Lucerne and monitors the traffic round the clock. On very busy stretches there is **hard shoulder running**, PUN for short in German, where the hard shoulder is opened as a driving lane at peak times. When you are a passenger in a car, you can watch how the displays change depending on the traffic.

begriffe.erklaerung: A loop of wire in the road that detects vehicles driving over it.
A jam out of nowhere, caused only by braking in heavy traffic.
Everyone drives at a similar speed so that the traffic flows smoothly.
The strip on the far right for breakdowns and emergencies.
The Federal Roads Office (ASTRA in German), responsible for the Swiss motorways.

gewusst: A small reduction in speed can get more cars through per hour than free-flowing traffic, because there is less braking.
A phantom traffic jam can spread backwards as a wave over many kilometres, even though everyone is driving forwards.
On stretches with hard shoulder running, there are emergency lay-bys for vehicles that break down.

teile.einleitung: A particle accelerator is a machine that brings tiny electrically charged particles such as electrons or protons up to very high speeds. Researchers make these particles collide to find out what the world is made of at its very core. The largest particle accelerator in the world is at CERN in Geneva.
wichtigste: Particle accelerators speed up charged particles with electric fields and steer them with magnets.
Rolf Widerøe built the first linear accelerator in 1928 and later worked at Brown Boveri in Baden.
Ernest Lawrence invented the cyclotron around 1930 and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1939.
In 1932 Cockcroft and Walton split lithium nuclei for the first time with artificially accelerated protons.
In a synchrotron, the strength of the magnetic field is increased along with the particle energy, so that the path stays the same size.
The Large Hadron Collider at CERN is a ring about 27 kilometres long.
In many hospitals, accelerators are used for radiotherapy of tumours.

abschnitte.text: A **particle accelerator** gives charged particles a push again and again with electric fields until they are almost as fast as light. Magnets steer the particles along their path and bundle them into a fine beam. The particles fly in tubes from which almost all the air has been pumped out, so that they do not collide with air particles. Their energy is measured in **electronvolts**; one electronvolt is about 1.6 times 10 to the power of minus 19 joules.

In a **linear accelerator**, the particles fly along a straight line and get faster bit by bit. In a **cyclotron**, they circle in a magnetic field on a spiral path outwards. In a **synchrotron**, they stay on a ring with a fixed radius, because the magnetic fields are strengthened in step with the energy. Electrons lose a lot of energy through synchrotron radiation when going round in a circle, because they are much lighter than protons.

The Norwegian **Rolf Widerøe** built the first linear accelerator in 1928 and later worked at Brown Boveri in Baden in Aargau. The American **Ernest Lawrence** invented the cyclotron around 1930 and received the Nobel Prize in Physics for it in 1939. In 1932, John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton in England achieved the first nuclear transformation with artificially accelerated protons: they split lithium nuclei. Since then the machines have become bigger and more powerful.

**CERN** near Geneva was founded in 1954 and is one of the largest research centres in the world. Its **Large Hadron Collider**, LHC for short, lies in a ring tunnel about 27 kilometres long, about 100 metres underground, beneath Switzerland and France. There, two proton beams travelling in opposite directions crash head-on into each other, because this makes much more energy available for new particles than with a target that is standing still. In 2012 researchers at the LHC detected the long-sought Higgs particle.

In many hospitals there are small linear accelerators that produce beams for the **radiotherapy** of tumours. At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen in the canton of Aargau, tumours are also treated with protons. The Swiss Light Source is there too; its powerful light makes tiny structures of materials and viruses visible. Accelerators also help to test materials and produce medical substances.

begriffe.erklaerung: A positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.
A very small unit of energy for particles, abbreviated eV.
A ring-shaped accelerator whose magnetic fields grow along with the energy.
An accelerator in which two particle beams crash into each other head-on.
A space from which almost all the air has been removed.

gewusst: The protons in the LHC go round the 27-kilometre ring more than 11 000 times per second.
At CERN in 1989, Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web so that researchers could exchange information.
The LHC magnets are cooled to about minus 271 degrees Celsius, colder than outer space.

teile.einleitung: Taylorism is a method of planning work in factories as precisely as possible and breaking it down into small, simple steps. It goes back to the American engineer Frederick Winslow Taylor, who studied work with a stopwatch around 1900. His ideas changed industry worldwide, but they were also strongly criticised.
wichtigste: In 1911 Frederick Winslow Taylor published his main work, The Principles of Scientific Management.
A key feature of Taylorism is the separation of planning work from carrying out work.
Taylor studied the individual work steps with a stopwatch in time studies.
His experiments on loading pig iron at the Bethlehem Steel works are well known.
He suggested performance-related pay with a bonus for completing the set amount of work.
Frank and Lillian Gilbreth added precise motion studies to Taylor’s time studies.
Taylorism is criticised above all for monotonous work and the loss of craft skills.

abschnitte.text: **Frederick Winslow Taylor** lived from 1856 to 1915 in the USA. In a steelworks he worked his way up from ordinary labourer to engineer. While doing so, he noticed that many jobs were done without planning and at different speeds. He wanted to find out the best way to carry out every task and called this **scientific management**.

Taylor broke every job down into small steps and measured with a **stopwatch** how long each step took. Such **time studies** showed him which movements were unnecessary. At the **Bethlehem Steel** works he studied how workers loaded heavy bars of pig iron. With fixed breaks and precise instructions, they managed many times the amount they had before.

One principle of Taylorism is the separation of **planning** work from **carrying out** work. Engineers and supervisors decide how a job is to be done and how long it should take. The workers then only carry out the set movements. Anyone who completed the set amount of work was to be rewarded with **performance-related pay** and a bonus.

Taylor’s book **The Principles of Scientific Management** appeared in 1911 and was translated into many languages. The married couple Frank and Lillian Gilbreth added precise **motion studies** to his time studies, filming the movements of the hands. From 1913 Henry Ford combined these ideas with the **assembly line** in car production. In Germany, the association **REFA** was founded in 1924 to standardise time studies and the design of work.

Many people criticised the fact that work became very **monotonous**, because you made the same movement all day long. The craftsmen’s expertise and skill were lost, and the pressure on the workers increased. Charlie Chaplin’s film Modern Times from 1936 makes fun of this kind of work. Today many companies rely more on teamwork and varied tasks, but time measurement and precise planning are still common in industry.

begriffe.erklaerung: Measuring exactly how long a work step takes.
A conveyor belt on which a product moves from one workstation to the next.
Pay that depends on how much someone gets done.
Sameness, when you do the same thing over and over again.

gewusst: Taylor was also a good sportsman and, together with a partner, won the US doubles championship in tennis in 1881.
The Gilbreths had twelve children, and their family life was later told in the book and film Cheaper by the Dozen.

teile.einleitung: Telephony means sending speech over long distances, so that people can talk to each other even though they are far apart. It developed out of the telegraph of the 19th century. Today we make calls over landlines, mobile networks and the internet.
wichtigste: Before the telephone, messages were sent by telegraph, often in Morse code.
Samuel Morse developed the alphabet of dots and dashes that is named after him.
In 1861 the German teacher Philipp Reis presented a device that transmitted sounds electrically.
In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell received the patent for the telephone in the USA.
In 1973 Martin Cooper made the first public call on a portable mobile phone.
In Switzerland the mobile phone is traditionally called a “Natel”.
SMS stands for Short Message Service.

abschnitte.text: Before people could make telephone calls, there was the electric **telegraph**. It sent messages as short and long electrical pulses through wires. For this, **Samuel Morse** developed an alphabet of dots and dashes, **Morse code**. The best-known signal is SOS: three short, three long, three short.

In 1861 the German teacher **Philipp Reis** presented a device that could transmit sounds electrically and called it a “Telephon”. In 1876 **Alexander Graham Bell** received the patent for the telephone in the USA. Other inventors such as Elisha Gray were also working on similar devices at that time. Soon telephone networks sprang up in many cities; in Switzerland the first was in Zurich in 1880.

With a **landline**, the telephone is connected to the network by cable. At first, operators in exchanges connected the calls by hand. Later, automatic exchanges took over this job, and people dialled the number themselves with a rotary dial. Today landline calls in Switzerland mostly run digitally over the internet; this is called **Voice over IP**.

On 3 April 1973, **Martin Cooper** made the first public call on a portable mobile phone in New York. The device weighed about a kilogram. In Switzerland the mobile network was called **Natel**, which stands for Nationales Autotelefon (national car telephone), and many people still call a mobile phone that today. Mobile networks became faster and faster, from 2G through 3G and 4G to 5G.

From the 1990s, the GSM mobile network also let people send short text messages. **SMS** stands for Short Message Service; an SMS could be at most 160 characters long. Today many people send messages through apps that use the internet. Video calls, in which you can see each other, are also completely normal today.

Telephony connects people all over the world in seconds. It is important for families, companies and above all for **emergency calls**. For calls between continents, undersea cables and satellites are used. In Switzerland several companies run their own mobile networks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that sends messages as electrical pulses over wires.
A code of short and long signals for letters and numbers.
A telephone network in which the telephone is connected by a cable.
Making calls without a cable, using radio waves and masts.
A short text message that you send with a mobile phone.

gewusst: Martin Cooper’s first mobile phone was as big as a brick and had a battery for about half an hour of talking.
The abbreviation Natel comes from the time when mobile phones were mainly built into cars.
An SMS could be at most 160 characters long.

teile.einleitung: A ticket machine is a machine at which you buy tickets for the train, bus or tram. In Switzerland, such machines stand at stations and at many stops. Inside, a small computer works out prices, checks money and prints the ticket.
wichtigste: At a ticket machine you buy tickets, which in Switzerland are called “Billette”.
Modern machines have a touchscreen on which you tap your destination.
First you enter where you want to go.
You can often pay with coins or a card.
If you put in too much money, you get change back.
In Switzerland, children travel free by train until their 6th birthday.
Children from the age of 6 usually pay half price.

abschnitte.text: A **ticket machine** sells tickets without anyone having to stand at a counter. In Switzerland a ticket is called a “Billett”, in Germany a “Fahrkarte” or “Fahrschein”. The red SBB machines stand at many stations, and there are also machines run by the local transport companies at bus and tram stops. They work round the clock.

Inside the machine there is a small **computer** with a screen, a printer and a money checker. On the **touchscreen**, you first enter where you want to go. Then you choose, for example, the class, whether you are travelling there and back and whether you have a Half Fare travelcard. The computer works out the price from a database of fares and prints the ticket.

At many machines you can pay with coins, sometimes with notes, and with a card. A sensor checks whether the coins are genuine and what they are worth. If you put in too much, the machine gives you **change**. If a ticket costs 4 francs, for example, and you put in 5 francs, you get 1 franc back.

In Switzerland, children travel free by train until their 6th birthday when accompanied. From the age of 6, children usually pay **half price**, until their 16th birthday. With the Junior travelcard or the Grandchild travelcard, children can travel cheaply with their parents or grandparents. At the machine you choose the right reduction for this.

Today many people prefer to buy their ticket in an app such as the **SBB Mobile** app. There are also offers there where you simply check in and the app works out the price at the end. But the machine remains important for people without a smartphone or without internet. The important thing is that you must buy the ticket before travelling, otherwise you risk a fine.

In the past, tickets were bought almost only at the counter, where railway staff handed out small cardboard tickets. Over time, mechanical machines for simple journeys appeared. Later came machines with buttons and finally with a touchscreen. With them you can now buy tickets to anywhere in Switzerland and even day passes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss word for a ticket.
A screen that you operate with your finger.
A pass with which you travel at half price in Switzerland.
The money you get back if you have paid too much.

gewusst: The word “Billett” comes from French and originally means a small slip of paper.
A ticket machine has to know thousands of different routes and prices and is therefore regularly updated over the network.

teile.einleitung: A composite material is a material made up of two or more different substances. Together they have better properties than each substance on its own; for example, they are both light and very strong at the same time. Reinforced concrete, plywood and the carbon fibre in racing bikes are well-known examples.
wichtigste: A composite material combines the advantages of different materials.
In fibre composites, the matrix holds the fibres together.
GFRP stands for glass-fibre-reinforced plastic.
Fibre composite parts are anisotropic, so their strength depends on the direction of the load.
Plywood is a layered composite of wood layers glued crosswise.
A sandwich structure consists of two stiff outer layers and a light core.
Fibre composites with a thermoset matrix are hard to recycle, because the matrix does not melt again.

abschnitte.text: In a **composite material**, different materials are combined so that they complement each other. Often there is a load-bearing part, such as fibres, and a substance that holds everything together, the **matrix**. Thousands of years ago, people already mixed straw into clay bricks so that they would crack less. Nature knows composites too: wood consists of strong fibres in a binding substance, and bones combine hard minerals with tough protein fibres.

In **fibre composites**, strong fibres of glass, carbon or aramid are embedded in a plastic. In **particle composites**, small grains are embedded; hard metal, for example, consists of tungsten carbide grains in a cobalt binder. **Layered composites** consist of layers glued on top of one another, like plywood made of veneers glued crosswise. A sandwich structure has two thin, stiff outer layers with a light core of foam or honeycomb in between.

Fibre composites are very strong in the direction of the fibres but much weaker across them; they are called **anisotropic**. That is why the fibres are laid exactly in the directions in which the forces act. The stiffness in the direction of the fibres can be estimated with the **rule of mixtures**: with 60 percent fibres at 230 gigapascals and 40 percent matrix at 3 gigapascals, you get about 139 gigapascals. In reinforced concrete, the combination only works because steel and concrete expand almost equally when they get warm.

Carbon-fibre-reinforced plastic, **CFRP** for short, is found in racing bikes, Formula 1 cars, tennis rackets and modern aircraft. Glass-fibre-reinforced plastic, **GFRP** for short, is used for boats, wind turbine blades and skis. The Swiss solar aircraft Solar Impulse was made mostly of carbon fibre, so that it was very light despite its huge wings. Many bike helmets and snowboards are also built from composite materials.

Many fibre composites have a matrix made of a **thermoset**, a plastic that becomes firmly cross-linked when it hardens. Afterwards it cannot be melted again, so fibres and matrix are hard to separate. Worn-out wind turbine blades are therefore a growing waste problem. Researchers are developing new processes and plastics that make such materials easier to recycle.

begriffe.erklaerung: The substance in a composite material that embeds the fibres or particles and holds them together.
Having different strength or stiffness depending on the direction.
Glass-fibre-reinforced plastic.
Carbon-fibre-reinforced plastic, very light and strong.
A build-up of two strong outer layers and a light core.

gewusst: Wood and bone are natural composite materials.
A carbon-fibre racing bike frame can weigh less than one kilogram.
Even in ancient civilisations, people reinforced clay bricks with straw so that they would not crack.

teile.einleitung: Agile software development is a way of working in which programs are built in small steps and improved again and again. Instead of planning everything precisely at the start, the team works closely with the customers. It is based on the Agile Manifesto of 2001.
wichtigste: The Agile Manifesto was written in 2001 in Snowbird in the US state of Utah.
It names four values, which are added to by 12 principles.
Working software is more important than comprehensive documentation.
The opposite of agile development is the waterfall model, with phases that strictly follow one another.
Well-known agile methods are Scrum, Kanban and Extreme Programming.
Kanban shows the work on a board and limits the number of tasks running at the same time.
Requirements are often written as a user story from the users’ point of view.

abschnitte.text: “Agile” means nimble or quick on your feet. In agile software development, a program is not finished all at once but in short **iterations**. After each step there is a working version that can be tried out. The feedback goes into the next step. In this way the team can react quickly to new wishes or problems.

In the past, people often worked according to the **waterfall model**. In it, the phases strictly follow one another: planning, design, programming, testing and delivery. Only at the very end does the customer see the result. If a mistake in the planning is noticed then, it is expensive to correct. Agile methods aim to avoid exactly this problem.

In February 2001, 17 software developers met at a ski resort in **Snowbird**, Utah. There they wrote the **Agile Manifesto**. It names four values, for example: working software is more important than comprehensive documentation. Also, working together with the customer is more important than negotiating contracts. The values are added to by 12 principles.

The most widespread agile method is **Scrum**. In it, a team works in periods of usually two to four weeks, called sprints, and has a short meeting every day. In **Kanban**, the work is made visible on a board with columns such as “To do”, “In progress” and “Done”. **Extreme Programming**, shaped by Kent Beck, relies among other things on pair programming, in which two people work at one computer.

Requirements are often written as a **user story**, for example “As a customer, I want to track my order so that I know when it will arrive.” This way it always stays clear who a feature is useful for. Today many companies in Switzerland work in an agile way, not only in IT. School projects can also be planned in an agile way, with small stages and regular reviews.

begriffe.erklaerung: A short work step after which there is a new interim result.
A fixed period of time in Scrum, usually two to four weeks.
A short description of a requirement from the users’ point of view.
A board with columns on which tasks move along as cards.

gewusst: Kanban originally comes from Toyota’s car factory in Japan.
In pair programming, the two people regularly take turns at the keyboard.
The Agile Manifesto fits on a single page.

teile.einleitung: A command is an instruction to do something particular, for example “Go!” or “Jump!”. People give each other commands, and computers and robots also work with commands. Because machines do not think for themselves, commands for them have to be completely exact.
wichtigste: A command says what someone or something should do.
In language, a command is usually in the imperative form, for example “Go!” or “Come!”.
A robot only carries out commands that it knows.
Commands for machines have to be completely exact, because machines do not think for themselves.
Several commands one after another make a program.
On a computer, the “Save” command keeps your work safe.

abschnitte.text: When the teacher says, “Stand up, take your exercise book, sit down,” those are three commands. In grammar, this form is called the **imperative**. A command often ends with an exclamation mark, such as “Go!” or “Jump!”. With the word “please”, a command becomes a polite request. People understand even inexact commands, because they can think along and ask questions.

A robot knows only a certain number of commands, for example “forward”, “backward”, “turn left” and “turn right”. If you give it an unknown command, it does not understand it and either does nothing or reports an error. With “backward” it moves back without turning round. With “turn left” it faces left without moving away. Because a robot **does not think for itself**, every command must be exactly right.

When you put several commands into a fixed order, you get a **program**. The command “Clap twice, then stamp once” means three movements one after another. Programming languages such as **Scratch** show commands as coloured blocks that you fit together. If something has to be repeated often, you use a loop instead of writing the same command again and again. In Swiss schools, children often learn to plan commands with small floor robots in the subject media and computer science.

On the computer you also give commands all the time, usually with the mouse, keyboard or your finger. The **Save** command keeps your work safe, while “Copy” and “Paste” duplicate text or pictures. Many commands have keyboard shortcuts, for example Ctrl and S for saving. Experts also type some commands as text into a special window, the command line. Deep inside, the processor carries out millions of tiny machine instructions per second.

In video games, every button triggers a command, such as “Jump!” for the character. In board games, the rules are a kind of list of commands. Voice assistants on mobile phones also react to spoken commands such as “Set an alarm.” A good game for practising is “playing robots”: one child gives commands, and the other carries them out exactly, without thinking for themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form of a word used to tell someone to do something, for example “Run!”.
A series of commands in a fixed order.
A command that repeats other commands several times.
A combination of keys that quickly triggers a command.

gewusst: A modern processor can carry out billions of simple instructions per second.
Even one single wrong command can make a whole program fail to work.
Many voice assistants first listen for a wake word before they accept a command.

teile.einleitung: Werner von Siemens was a German inventor and businessman who played a decisive part in shaping the age of electrical engineering. He invented telegraphs, discovered the dynamo-electric principle and built the world’s first electric tram. His company still exists today.
wichtigste: Werner von Siemens lived from 1816 to 1892 and came from near Hanover.
As a young man he received his technical training in the Prussian army.
