In 1847, together with Johann Georg Halske, he founded the Telegraphen-Bauanstalt von Siemens & Halske, a telegraph-building works, in Berlin.
In 1866 he discovered the dynamo-electric principle, which made powerful generators without permanent magnets possible.
In 1879 he showed the first electric railway at the Berlin trade exhibition.
In 1881 the world’s first electric tram ran in Berlin-Lichterfelde.
The unit of electrical conductance is called the siemens in his honour.

abschnitte.text: Werner Siemens was born on 13 December 1816 in Lenthe near Hanover. He grew up in a large farming family with many brothers and sisters. Because the family had no money for university, he joined the **Prussian army**. There, at an artillery and engineering school, he learnt mathematics, physics and chemistry. Only in 1888 was he raised to the nobility and allowed to call himself “von Siemens”.

Siemens improved the **pointer telegraph**, with which messages could be sent over wires. To build it, in 1847 he founded the **Telegraphen-Bauanstalt von Siemens & Halske** in Berlin together with the mechanic Johann Georg Halske. The small workshop quickly grew into a large company. By 1870 the company had built the **Indo-European Telegraph Line**, which connected London with Calcutta in India.

In 1866 Siemens made his most important discovery: the **dynamo-electric principle**. With it, a generator can use its own electricity to strengthen its electromagnets. This means that weak permanent magnets are no longer needed. Only this made powerful **generators** possible, which produce a lot of electricity. This principle was the starting signal for the modern electricity supply.

At the Berlin trade exhibition in 1879, Siemens presented a small **electric railway** on which visitors could ride. In 1881 the world’s first electric **tram** ran in regular service in Berlin-Lichterfelde. In 1880 an electric **lift** made by Siemens carried people upwards for the first time, in Mannheim. These inventions changed transport in the cities.

Werner von Siemens died on 6 December 1892 in Berlin. His company became today’s **Siemens AG**, one of the largest technology groups in the world, with its headquarters in Munich. The unit of electrical **conductance** is called the siemens and has the symbol S. Siemens also has sites in Switzerland today, for example in Zug.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that sends messages over wires with electrical signals.
A machine that turns movement into electric current.
The generator strengthens its magnets with its own electricity.
Shows how well a material lets electricity through. Unit: siemens.

gewusst: Werner von Siemens never studied at a university; he learnt engineering in the army.
The first electric railway of 1879 was so small that the passengers sat one behind the other as if on a bench.
The telegraph line from London to Calcutta was more than 10 000 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: SwissFEL is an X-ray laser at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen in the canton of Aargau. It produces extremely short and bright flashes of X-ray light. With them, researchers can watch how atoms and molecules move in tiny fractions of a second.
wichtigste: SwissFEL is a free-electron X-ray laser at the Paul Scherrer Institute.
The facility is about 740 metres long in total.
SwissFEL was inaugurated in 2016.
The electrons are accelerated to an energy of about 5.8 GeV.
In an undulator, a row of magnets with alternating poles, the electrons give off X-ray light.
The X-ray pulses last only a few femtoseconds.
The Aramis beamline delivers hard X-rays.
SwissFEL can produce up to 100 X-ray pulses per second.

abschnitte.text: A **free-electron laser**, FEL for short, does not produce light with crystals or gases like other lasers. Instead, **electrons** are accelerated to almost the speed of light. Then they are sent through a long row of magnets, where they give off extremely bright X-ray light. SwissFEL is one of the largest research facilities in Switzerland.

First, in a building about 740 metres long, electrons are brought to an energy of about 5.8 GeV in a **linear accelerator**. Then they fly through the **undulator**, an arrangement of magnets with alternating poles. There they are steered back and forth like a slalom skier and give off X-ray light as they go. The light amplifies itself, so that a very bright, laser-like flash is produced.

The X-ray pulses last only a few **femtoseconds**. A femtosecond is a millionth of a billionth of a second. In this time, even light travels only a fraction of the thickness of a hair. SwissFEL can produce up to 100 such pulses per second.

SwissFEL has two beamlines. **Aramis** delivers hard X-rays, which can make very fine structures such as the arrangement of atoms visible. **Athos** delivers softer X-rays, which are suitable, for example, for studying magnetic materials and chemical reactions. Researchers from all over the world work at the experiment stations.

With the short flashes, you can take snapshots, rather like with a high-speed camera. If you put many pictures in a row, you get a kind of **molecular film** that shows how a chemical reaction takes place. In this way scientists can study, for example, how plants use light for photosynthesis or how medicines attach to proteins. There are only a few similar facilities in the world, for example the European XFEL in Hamburg.

begriffe.erklaerung: A row of magnets that forces electrons onto a wavy path.
A quadrillionth of a second, so unimaginably short.
A straight facility in which particles are made faster and faster.
Invisible, very high-energy light that can pass into materials.

gewusst: The abbreviation FEL stands for free-electron laser.
An X-ray pulse from SwissFEL is so short that, compared with one second, it is about as long as one second compared with several million years.

teile.einleitung: Wind energy is the energy contained in moving air. People have used it for thousands of years for sailing ships and windmills; today it is used mainly to produce electricity with wind turbines. Wind energy is renewable, because the wind never runs out.
wichtigste: Wind turbines use the movement energy of the wind.
Most modern large wind turbines have 3 rotor blades.
If the wind speed doubles, there is about 8 times as much power in the wind.
In a very strong storm, wind turbines are switched off to prevent damage.
In Switzerland, wind farms are often on the Jura heights and passes, because the wind blows more strongly and steadily there.
Well-known Swiss wind farms are on Mont-Crosin, on the Gütsch near Andermatt and at the Nufenen Pass.
In 2024 wind energy supplied less than 1 percent of Switzerland’s electricity.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the wind come from?
abschnitte.text: Wind is created because the Sun heats the Earth unevenly. Warm air rises and cold air flows in to replace it. In this way differences in **air pressure** even out. So wind energy is really transformed solar energy. That is why it counts as one of the **renewable energies**, just like hydropower and solar energy.

The wind turns the rotor blades of a wind turbine. The turning drives a **generator**, which produces electricity. So the turbine uses the **movement energy** of the air. The power depends greatly on the wind speed: if the wind blows twice as fast, there is about 8 times as much power in it. That is why people look for places where the wind blows strongly and regularly.

Thousands of years ago, people already used the wind with **sailing ships**. Later they built **windmills** to grind grain or pump water. The many windmills in the Netherlands are famous. At the end of the 19th century, the first wind turbines that produced electricity were built. Since the 1990s, wind turbines have become bigger and more powerful.

In Switzerland, wind energy still plays a small role: in 2024 it supplied less than 1 percent of the electricity. The largest wind farm is on **Mont-Crosin** in the Bernese Jura. Other turbines turn on the **Gütsch** above Andermatt, on the Gotthard Pass and at the **Nufenen Pass** at more than 2400 metres. There is often a lot of wind especially in winter, when solar panels supply little electricity.

Wind turbines produce no exhaust gases and no CO2 when running. But they only supply electricity when the wind blows, so the amount varies. Some people feel that large turbines spoil the **landscape** or make noise. The rotors can also be dangerous for birds and bats. That is why every new site is examined carefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy from sources that do not get used up, such as wind, sun and water.
The energy something has because it is moving.
Several wind turbines standing together in one place.
Wind farms that stand out at sea.

gewusst: The wind farm at the Nufenen Pass is one of the highest wind farms in Europe.
At sea the wind blows much more steadily, which is why in countries such as Denmark many wind farms stand off the coast.
Because there is about 8 times as much power in the wind at double the speed, even a slightly windier site is very worthwhile.

teile.einleitung: Electricity consumption tells you how much electrical energy appliances, households or a whole country need. It is usually measured in kilowatt hours. If you know which appliances use a lot of electricity, you can save energy and money.
wichtigste: On the electricity bill, consumption is given in kilowatt hours (kWh).
In 2024 Switzerland used about 57 terawatt hours of electricity (final consumption).
Electricity consumption in Switzerland is highest in winter.
An appliance with 2000 watts that runs for 3 hours uses 6 kWh.
The energy label shows how economical an appliance is with energy.
Even appliances that seem to be switched off still use electricity on standby.
LED lamps use less electricity than light bulbs, because they turn more energy into light and less into heat.

abschnitte.text: The **power** of an appliance is given in watts; a kettle, for example, has 2000 watts. How much energy is used also depends on how long the appliance runs. You multiply power by time: 2000 watts for 3 hours gives 6000 watt hours, which is 6 **kilowatt hours**. If a kilowatt hour costs 30 centimes, these 6 kWh cost 1.80 francs altogether.

In 2024 Switzerland used about 57 **terawatt hours** of electricity, which is 57 billion kilowatt hours. About a third of this is used by households, and the rest mainly by industry, trade, services and transport, for example the railways. Most electricity is needed in **winter**, because it is dark for longer and many heat pumps are heating. At the same time, hydropower and solar panels supply less in winter, so Switzerland then imports electricity.

Fridges, washing machines and televisions carry a coloured **energy label**. It uses letters and colours from green to red to show how economical an appliance is. Green classes mean low consumption, red classes mean high consumption. When buying, an economical appliance is worth it, because it uses less electricity over many years.

Appliances that heat or cool use a lot of electricity, such as the oven, the tumble dryer, the fridge or an electric water heater. An **LED lamp** needs only a fraction of the electricity of an old light bulb for the same brightness. This is because a light bulb turns most of its energy into heat instead of light. The **standby consumption** of televisions, games consoles or chargers also adds up over the year.

Switching appliances off completely or using an extension lead with a switch saves standby electricity. When cooking, a lid on the pan helps, and it is best to heat water in a kettle. Switching off the light in empty rooms is an easy contribution. If you use less electricity, you save money and protect the **environment**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit of energy: 1000 watts for one hour.
How much energy an appliance needs per second, measured in watts.
A ready state in which the appliance seems to be off but still uses electricity.
A sticker that shows how economical an appliance is.

gewusst: One terawatt hour is a billion kilowatt hours.
With one kilowatt hour, a 10-watt LED lamp can shine for about 100 hours.

teile.einleitung: Web accessibility means that all people can use websites and apps, including people with a disability. This includes blind and partially sighted, deaf or physically impaired people. In the end, everyone benefits from a well-made, accessible website.
wichtigste: The aim of web accessibility is that all people can use websites.
A screen reader is a program that reads out what is on the screen.
The internationally used guidelines for accessible web content are called WCAG.
Enough colour contrast helps people with poor sight to read the text.
A website should also be usable without a mouse, with the keyboard alone.
Information should not be shown by colour alone, because some people cannot tell colours apart.
In Switzerland, the Disability Discrimination Act requires federal websites to be accessible.

abschnitte.text: A **barrier** is an obstacle. On the internet, this can be, for example, a picture without a description, which a blind person cannot recognise. Or a video without subtitles, which a deaf person cannot understand. **Web accessibility** aims to avoid such obstacles. All people should be able to find information, fill in forms and use services.

Blind people use a **screen reader**. This is a program that reads out the content of the screen or shows it in braille on a braille display. For this to work, pictures need an **alternative text** that describes what can be seen in them. People with poor sight often enlarge the text a lot. Anyone who can hardly move their hands controls the computer, for example, with their voice or with the keyboard alone.

There needs to be enough **colour contrast** between text and background so that people with poor sight can read too. Information should not be shown with colour alone. A red box for an error is not enough, because some people cannot tell red and green apart. It is better to add a text or a symbol as well. Videos need **subtitles** so that deaf people can understand them.

The most important guidelines are called **WCAG**, which stands for Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. They are published by the World Wide Web Consortium, which also sets other standards for the web. In Switzerland, the **Disability Discrimination Act** requires federal websites to be accessible. Many cantons, municipalities and companies also follow this. In Zurich, the foundation “Zugang für alle” (Access for all) campaigns for an accessible internet.

Accessibility does not only help people with a disability. Subtitles are also useful on a noisy train or when you are not allowed to switch the sound on. Good contrast helps in sunlight on a mobile phone. Clear language and simple operation help older people and children. That is why **accessibility** should be thought about from the very start when building any website.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program that reads out what is on the screen.
A short description of a picture for people who cannot see it.
The difference in brightness between text and background.
International guidelines for accessible web content.

gewusst: Experienced blind people often have their screen reader read texts so fast that other people can hardly understand a word.
About one man in twelve finds it hard to tell certain colours such as red and green apart.
Search engines also benefit from alternative texts, because otherwise they cannot understand pictures.

teile.einleitung: A motion detector is a small electronic sensor that notices when something moves nearby. Then, for example, it automatically switches on the light or sets off an alarm. You probably know it from the stairwell or the front door of a building.
wichtigste: A motion detector on a lamp switches the light on as soon as someone comes.
Many motion detectors sense the warmth of bodies, that is invisible infrared radiation.
When nobody is there any more, the light goes off again after a set time.
Motion detectors save electricity, because the light only shines when it is needed.
Animals such as a cat can also set off a motion detector in the garden.
In alarm systems, motion detectors report burglars.

abschnitte.text: A **motion detector** is a **sensor**, that is a feeler that measures something in its surroundings. It often sits in a small white housing with a round, milky dome on the wall or ceiling. When it detects movement, it sends a signal to a lamp, a door or an alarm system. This way nobody has to search for the light switch in the dark.

Most motion detectors are **passive infrared detectors**, PIR detectors for short. Every warm body, including yours, gives off invisible **infrared radiation**. The sensor notices when this heat radiation changes in its field of view, for example because someone walks past. The milky dome is a special lens that divides the field of view into many small zones. Other detectors send out radar or ultrasound waves and measure their echo, rather like a bat.

Motion detectors are often found in the **stairwell**, in cellars, garages, toilets and at front doors. Automatic sliding doors in shops and stations also open thanks to such sensors. In school buildings and offices, they switch on the lights in corridors and toilets. Outside, they light up garden paths so that you do not trip at night.

On many motion detectors you can set how long the light should stay on and how dark it must be before it reacts. If you sit completely still, for example on the toilet, the sensor no longer notices any movement and the light goes out. Then it helps to wave your arm briefly. Because the detector senses warmth, a cat, a fox or a passing car can also set it off. Good devices can therefore have their **sensitivity** adjusted.

In an **alarm system**, motion detectors watch over rooms when nobody is at home. If they notice movement, they set off an alarm or send a message to a mobile phone. For pets there are special detectors that ignore small animals. In museums too, such sensors protect valuable exhibits.

A light that is on all night uses a lot of unnecessary energy. With a motion detector, the lamp only shines when someone is really there. This protects the environment and lowers the electricity bill. Together with economical LED lamps, this is a simple step towards more **energy efficiency**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that measures something in the environment, such as warmth, light or movement.
Invisible heat radiation that every warm body gives off.
A passive infrared detector that recognises changes in heat radiation.
A system that raises the alarm in case of a break-in or danger.

gewusst: A PIR detector does not send anything out itself; it only watches passively, which is why it is called passive.
Motion detectors react better when you walk across in front of them than when you walk straight towards them.

teile.einleitung: A tram is an electrically powered rail vehicle that runs right through the streets of a town. In Switzerland people usually just say “Tram”. In Zurich, Basel, Bern and Geneva, trams are a firm part of the townscape.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the tram is usually called “Tram”.
A tram takes its electricity from a line above the street through a pantograph.
Because it runs on rails, a tram cannot swerve around obstacles.
A tram warns people in the street with a bell.
The trams in Zurich are blue and white, the BVB trams in Basel are green.
The first tram in Zurich was pulled by horses and was called the “Rösslitram”.
Trams have right of way, even on zebra crossings.

abschnitte.text: A **tram** runs on rails set into the street and often shares the street with cars, bikes and pedestrians. It can carry many more people than a bus and needs no fuel to do so. Modern trams have a low floor, so you can easily get on even with a pushchair or wheelchair. Because they run on electricity, they are quiet and give off no exhaust fumes in town.

Above the streets hangs an **overhead line**, a wire that carries electric current. An arm on the roof, the **pantograph**, presses against this wire from below and so collects the electricity. The current flows through the electric motors and back through the rails. In Switzerland, the city trams in Zurich, Basel, Bern and Geneva run on **metre gauge**, which means the rails are one metre apart.

A tram cannot swerve and, because of its great weight, needs a long distance to brake. That is why it warns with a bright **bell** when someone is standing on the rails. In Swiss road traffic the tram has right of way, even on zebra crossings. When cycling, you have to be careful that your wheel does not get caught in the grooves of the rails, and cross rails as close to a right angle as possible.

The first trams were pulled by horses; in Zurich it was called the **Rösslitram** and ran from 1882. In 1881 Werner von Siemens opened the world’s first electric tramway near Berlin. Soon the horses were replaced by electric motors in Swiss towns too, in Zurich from 1894. Many Swiss towns removed their tram networks in the 20th century, but Zurich, Basel, Bern and Geneva kept them and are expanding them again today.

The blue and white trams of the Zurich transport company, VBZ, form the largest tram network in Switzerland. In Basel, the green trams of the **BVB** and the yellow trams of the BLT run, and some lines even go as far as Germany and France. Bern has red trams run by Bernmobil, and in Geneva the trams of the TPG run. Newer lines such as the Glattalbahn and the Limmattalbahn now also connect suburbs with the city.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rail vehicle that runs through the streets; in Switzerland this is the usual word.
A wire above the street from which the tram gets its electricity.
An arm on the roof that collects electricity from the overhead line.
Rails that are one metre apart.

gewusst: With the Basel tram you can cross the national border as far as Weil am Rhein in Germany.
One long tram can carry as many people at once as several buses together.
The word “tram” comes from English and originally meant a rail or a wagon in mines.

teile.einleitung: Computability is a field of theoretical computer science and mathematics. It asks which tasks can be solved at all with an exact set of calculating instructions, an algorithm. The surprising answer is: there are problems that no computer in the world can ever solve, however fast it is.
wichtigste: A function is called computable if an algorithm gives the right result for every input after a finite number of steps.
In 1931, with his incompleteness theorem, Kurt Gödel showed that every consistent, sufficiently strong formal system contains true statements that it cannot prove.
In 1936 Alonzo Church and Alan Turing answered David Hilbert’s decision problem in the negative.
A set is decidable if an algorithm always stops and says whether an element belongs to it.
LOOP programs compute exactly the primitive recursive functions; with WHILE loops they become Turing-complete.
The Ackermann function is computable, but not primitive recursive.
The busy beaver function is a well-known example of a function that is not computable.

abschnitte.text: A task is **computable** if it can be solved with an **algorithm**, that is with a clear step-by-step set of instructions. The instructions must be finished after a finite number of steps for every input. Adding two numbers, for example, is computable. How long the calculation takes does not matter, as long as it ends at some point.

Between about 1900 and 1928, the German mathematician **David Hilbert** hoped that every mathematical question could be decided mechanically. His **decision problem** asked for a method that says for every logical statement whether it holds. In 1936 Alonzo Church and Alan Turing showed, independently of each other, that such a method cannot exist. Hilbert’s tenth problem about Diophantine equations, that is equations with whole numbers, is also undecidable. Yuri Matiyasevich finally proved this in 1970.

In 1931 the Austrian logician **Kurt Gödel** published his famous **incompleteness theorem**. It shows that every consistent and sufficiently strong system of rules in mathematics contains true statements that it cannot prove. This made it clear that mathematics can never be entirely complete. This result was a shock for many researchers and an important foundation for the later theory of computability.

Computer scientists study simple model languages in order to understand computability. **LOOP programs** may only repeat loops a number of times that is fixed in advance. They therefore always stop and compute exactly the **primitive recursive functions**. If you add WHILE loops, which run as long as a condition holds, the programs become Turing-complete. The **Ackermann function** grows so extremely fast that it is computable, but not primitive recursive.

The best-known unsolvable problem is the **halting problem**: no program can predict for every other program whether it will stop at some point. The **busy beaver function** is also not computable. It asks how many steps a small Turing machine can make at most before it stops. The mathematician Tibor Radó presented it in 1962, and its values grow faster than any computable function.

Computability shows the limits of every computer, including the supercomputers of tomorrow. It explains, for example, why no program can automatically find all the errors in other programs. Anyone who checks software must therefore work with tests and clever methods. The theory is also the basis of **complexity theory**, which asks how quickly solvable tasks can be solved.

begriffe.erklaerung: An exact step-by-step set of instructions that solves a task.
A computer can say yes or no for certain to every question and always stops.
The unsolvable question of whether any given program will stop at some point.
A system can compute everything that a Turing machine can compute.

gewusst: Even for a Turing machine with only five states, it took decades to work out the value of the busy beaver function.
Alan Turing proved that the halting problem is unsolvable as early as 1936, before modern computers even existed.

teile.einleitung: A telephone is a device that lets people talk to each other over long distances. In the past it hung on the wall with a cable; today most people carry a mobile phone in their pocket. With a smartphone you can not only make calls but also write messages, take photos and surf the internet.
wichtigste: Alexander Graham Bell applied for a patent for the telephone in 1876.
A telephone turns speech into electrical signals or radio waves, and back again at the other end.
A telephone that you can take anywhere is called a mobile phone, in Switzerland also a “Natel”.
A mobile phone call travels by radio waves to the nearest mast.
Smartphones are usually operated with a finger on the touchscreen.
In the past, you put coins into a payphone to make a call.
In Switzerland you dial 117 for the police, 118 for the fire brigade and 144 for an ambulance.

abschnitte.text: When you speak into a telephone, a **microphone** picks up the vibrations of your voice. They are turned into electrical signals and sent on through cables or as radio waves. At the other person’s end, a small **loudspeaker** turns them back into sounds you can hear. All this happens so quickly that you can talk almost without delay.

In 1876, **Alexander Graham Bell** applied for a patent for the telephone in the USA. Even before that, other inventors such as Philipp Reis in Germany had worked on similar devices. The first telephones had a crank handle, and an **operator** in an exchange had to connect the lines by hand. Later came rotary dials and then buttons.

In the past there were **phone boxes** with payphones on many street corners. You put in coins and could then talk until the money ran out. Later there were also phonecards. Because almost everyone has a mobile phone today, most public telephones in Switzerland have been removed.

A **mobile phone** is a portable telephone without a cable. It sends speech by **radio waves** to the nearest mast, and from there the call travels on through the network. A **smartphone** is a small computer with a touchscreen that you operate with your finger. Since the first iPhone in 2007, smartphones have changed the way people communicate.

In an emergency you can call free of charge even without credit. You can reach the **police** on 117, the fire brigade on 118 and an ambulance on 144. Rega, the air rescue service, has the number 1414, and 112 is the European emergency number. The number 147 is for children and young people who have worries and would like to talk to someone.

Only give your mobile number to people you know and trust. Do not answer calls from unknown numbers that seem strange to you, and tell an adult about them. Learn the most important **emergency numbers** by heart. And put your phone aside when eating, studying and before going to sleep.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part that turns sound into electrical signals.
Invisible waves with which information is sent through the air.
A screen that you operate by touching it with your finger.
A telephone number that you can call free of charge when in danger to get help.

gewusst: The word telephone comes from Greek and means something like “distant voice”.
In Switzerland people often call a mobile phone a “Natel”; this was originally the name of the mobile network.
The emergency numbers work even when the mobile phone has no credit left.

teile.einleitung: A seesaw is a long board that rests on a pivot in the middle. In the playground, two children sit at the ends and take turns going up and down. Along the way, the seesaw shows how a lever works.
wichtigste: A seesaw is a board with a pivot in the middle.
In physics, a seesaw is a lever, one of the simple machines.
Two children of the same weight balance when they sit the same distance from the pivot.
If a heavy child and a light child both sit right at the ends, the heavy child goes down.
To make it work, the heavy child moves closer to the pivot.
A balance scale works on the same principle as a seesaw.
On many seesaws, a rubber buffer or an old tyre softens the bump at the bottom.

abschnitte.text: A seesaw consists of a strong board or beam. In the middle it rests on a **pivot**, around which it can move up and down. At both ends there are seats and handles. When a child pushes off from the ground, their side goes up and the other side goes down. This creates the typical up and down.

A seesaw is a **lever**, one of the oldest simple machines. How hard one side presses down depends on the weight and on the distance from the pivot. Two children of the same weight are in **balance** when they sit the same distance from the pivot. Then the seesaw stays still and level. You can remember: weight times distance must be the same on both sides.

If a heavy child and a light child both sit right at the ends, the heavy child goes down and stays there. But if the heavy child moves closer to the pivot, their side becomes “lighter”. If a child is, for example, twice as heavy, they only need to sit half as far from the pivot. In this way a child can even seesaw with an adult. This principle is called the **law of the lever**.

We come across the law of the lever everywhere. A **balance scale** works exactly like a seesaw: there must be the same weight on both sides for the beam to be level. Scissors, pliers, crowbars and bottle openers are levers too. With a long lever you can move a lot with little force. More than 2000 years ago, the Greek scholar **Archimedes** already described this law.

When a seesaw hits the ground hard, it can hurt your back and bottom. That is why many playground seesaws have a **rubber buffer** or an old tyre buried in the ground. It is also important to hold on tight and not to get off suddenly. Otherwise the other child bumps down roughly on the ground. There are also spring seesaws, which stand on a strong spring and give way gently.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point around which the seesaw turns.
A beam that turns around a point and can multiply force.
Both sides press equally hard, and the seesaw stays still.
A scale with a beam that has two pans hanging from its ends.

gewusst: Archimedes is said to have claimed that with a long enough lever and a fixed point he could even move the Earth.
A child can seesaw with an adult if the adult sits close enough to the pivot.
Your forearm also works like a lever, with the elbow as the pivot.

teile.einleitung: A barcode is a pattern of dark bars and light gaps in which a number is hidden. A scanner can read this number in a fraction of a second. Almost every product in a shop carries a barcode, so that the till knows straight away what it is and how much it costs.
wichtigste: The EAN barcode on most products has 13 digits.
The last digit is a check digit, which is used to spot reading errors.
Companies with numbers from Switzerland have barcodes that begin with 760 to 769.
Books carry a barcode with the ISBN, which begins with 978 or 979.
Dark bars reflect less light than light gaps, so the scanner can tell them apart.
Norman Joseph Woodland and Bernard Silver patented the idea in 1952.
A barcode is one-dimensional, a QR code is two-dimensional.

abschnitte.text: A barcode contains a coded number that clearly identifies the product. The best-known form is the **EAN code** with 13 digits, which are also printed below the bars. The first digits show in which country the company received its number; for Switzerland and Liechtenstein these are 760 to 769. Then come numbers for the company and the product, and right at the end is the **check digit**.

abschnitte.titel: How does the scanner read it?
abschnitte.text: A **scanner** lights up the barcode with a beam of light or records it with a camera. The dark bars swallow a lot of light, while the light gaps reflect it. From the pattern of wide and narrow bars, the device works out the number. Using the check digit, the computer checks immediately whether it has been read correctly.

At the till, the computer looks up the price and the name of the product for that number. This way the shop can also keep exact track of how many packs are still in stock. But you also find barcodes on parcels, library books, train tickets or luggage tags at the airport. On books, the barcode contains the **ISBN**, which begins with 978 or 979.

The idea comes from the Americans **Norman Joseph Woodland** and **Bernard Silver**, who were granted a patent for it in 1952. Woodland is said to have had the idea while drawing Morse code in the sand with his fingers and stretching the dots and dashes downwards. In 1974, a product was scanned at a till for the first time, in a supermarket in the USA. It was a packet of chewing gum.

A normal barcode is read in one direction only, from left to right, so it is **one-dimensional**. A **QR code**, on the other hand, is made of small squares and stores information in two directions. That is why much more fits into a QR code, for example an internet address or a whole text. In Switzerland, the QR code is used, for example, on the QR bill for paying.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for an article number with 13 digits that is used worldwide.
A calculated last digit that is used to detect reading errors.
A number that clearly identifies every book.
A reading device that recognises barcodes using light.

gewusst: The packet of chewing gum that was the first to be scanned in 1974 is now in a museum in the USA.
The country number in the barcode only shows where the company is registered, not where the product was made.

teile.einleitung: An age rating shows the age from which a game, a film or an app is suitable. In Europe there is the PEGI system for video games, with the levels 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18. Age ratings are meant to protect children from content that could frighten or overwhelm them.
wichtigste: An age rating shows the age from which a game is suitable.
Age ratings exist to protect children.
The lowest PEGI level is PEGI 3; the highest, PEGI 18, is for adults only.
A game with PEGI 7 is suitable for a 7-year-old child.
An 8-year-old child is still too young for a game with PEGI 12.
The age rating is shown on the packaging and in online shops.
Small symbols also show why a game has a particular level.

abschnitte.text: An **age rating** is a recommendation or rule about the age from which a medium is suitable. There are age ratings for video games, films, series and apps. For this, experts check whether the content contains, for example, violence, fear or swear words. The stronger the content, the higher the age level. Important: the rating says nothing about how difficult a game is.

In Europe, and also in Switzerland, **PEGI** is usually used for video games. The system has existed since 2003. It has five levels: PEGI 3, 7, 12, 16 and 18. A 9-year-old child, for example, still has to wait 3 years before being allowed to play games with PEGI 12. The number is shown clearly on the **packaging** and in online shops.

Next to the number there are small **content descriptors**. A spider stands for content that can be frightening. A fist stands for violence, a speech bubble with symbols for swear words. A symbol with coins shows that you can buy things in the game with real money. This way parents and children can see at a glance what they should look out for.

In Switzerland, parliament has passed a **law on the protection of young people** for films and video games. Under it, shops, cinemas and online providers must check people’s ages. For films there are separate age ratings, which are often similar to those of the **FSK** in Germany. At home, however, it is mainly the parents who decide what their children may play and watch.

Look at the age rating before you play or download something. If a game frightens you or stresses you, you may stop at any time. Talk to your parents about which games are right for you. On consoles, tablets and mobile phones, **parental controls** can be set up. With them, unsuitable games and purchases can be blocked.

begriffe.erklaerung: A European system of age ratings for video games.
Rules that protect children and young people from harmful content.
A small picture that shows why a game has an age level.
A setting with which parents can block content or purchases on a device.

gewusst: PEGI stands for “Pan European Game Information”.
A game with PEGI 3 can still be very difficult; the number only says something about the content.
App stores also have age ratings that work in a similar way to PEGI.

teile.einleitung: An electric circuit is a closed path along which electric current flows from a power source to a device and back again. Only if this circuit is not broken anywhere does a lamp light up or a motor run. There are circuits in every torch, in every battery-powered toy and in every house.
wichtigste: For a lamp to light up on a battery, you need a closed circuit.
If you undo a wire, the circuit is broken and the lamp goes out.
Metals such as copper conduct electricity well.
Materials such as rubber, plastic or glass do not let electricity through; they are called insulators.
If two small bulbs are connected one after the other and one is unscrewed, both go out.
The fuse in the house switches off the electricity if too much current flows.
A yellow warning triangle with a black lightning bolt warns of danger from electricity.

abschnitte.text: A simple circuit has a **power source**, for example a battery. Then there is something that uses the power, such as a small bulb, and wires that connect everything together. Often there is also a **switch**, with which you can open and close the circuit. You can imagine the current like water being pumped round in a loop through pipes.

Current only flows when the circuit is **closed**. If you undo a wire or open the switch, the path is broken and the lamp goes out immediately. A light switch on the wall does exactly that: it opens or closes a circuit. If two wires in a circuit touch each other directly, without a device in between, a dangerous **short circuit** occurs.

Metals such as **copper**, aluminium or iron conduct electricity well, which is why cables are made of copper wire inside. Materials such as rubber, plastic, wood or glass, on the other hand, do not conduct electricity. They are called **insulators**. The plastic coating of a cable protects us from touching the current.

In a **series circuit**, several small bulbs are connected one after the other in a single loop. If you unscrew one, the circuit is broken and all of them go out. In a **parallel circuit**, each bulb has its own path to the battery. If one fails, the others stay lit; this is also how the lights in a flat are connected.

abschnitte.titel: Electricity at home and in nature
abschnitte.text: At home, the **fuse** in the fuse box protects the wiring: if too much current flows, it switches off. Electricity from a socket is much stronger than that from a battery and can be deadly. A yellow warning triangle with a black lightning bolt shows that there is danger from electricity. In nature there are huge electric sparks during a **thunderstorm**, which we see as lightning.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that supplies electricity, for example a battery.
A material through which electricity can flow easily.
A material that does not let electricity through.
When current flows straight back without a device, which can get dangerously hot.

gewusst: With a lemon, a piece of copper and a galvanised nail you can build a small battery.
Our bodies conduct electricity too, so you must never fiddle with sockets or power lines.

teile.einleitung: With video calling, you can see and hear each other even when you are far apart. What used to happen only in science fiction films is now an everyday thing with a mobile phone, tablet or computer.
wichtigste: In a video call you can see each other as well as hear each other’s voice.
The device needs a camera, a microphone and a loudspeaker.
For video calls through an app, you need an internet connection.
If the internet is too slow, the picture judders or freezes.
Many families keep in touch this way with relatives who live far away.
You can mute your own microphone at any time.
You should only make video calls with people you know.

abschnitte.text: In **video calling**, picture and sound are sent at the same time between two or more devices. For this you need a **camera**, a microphone and a screen. Smartphones, tablets and laptops already have all of these built in. When several people talk to each other, it is called a **video conference**.

The camera records many pictures per second, and the microphone records the sound. An app makes this data smaller, which is called **compressing**, and sends it over the internet. At the other end, it is put back together into picture and sound. If the connection is too slow, the picture **judders** or freezes and the sound becomes choppy.

As early as the 1930s there were first trials in Germany with videophones between big cities. In the 1960s the American telephone company AT&T presented a **videophone**, but it was expensive and did not catch on. Only with fast internet and webcams did video calling become possible for everyone from the 2000s. During the coronavirus pandemic from 2020, schools, companies and families used video calls more than ever before.

Many families use it to see grandparents or relatives who live far away, for instance in another country. In companies, **video conferences** often replace long journeys to meetings. Doctors can sort out some questions by video. Deaf people also like using video calls, because they can talk to each other in **sign language**.

Only make video calls with people you really know, and tell your parents if something seems strange to you. Pay attention to what can be seen in the background, for example addresses or private things. With the microphone symbol you can **mute** yourself, and the camera can be switched off too. Good lighting from the front and a quiet place make the conversation more pleasant.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small camera on or in a computer for video calls.
A video conversation with several people at the same time.
To make data smaller so that it can be sent faster.
To switch off your own microphone so that the others cannot hear anything.

gewusst: In old science fiction films, videophones appeared long before they really existed.
On long-distance connections, you sometimes hear the answer with a short delay, because the data travels around the world.
Many apps can blur the background behind a person or replace it with a picture.

teile.einleitung: A tunnel boring machine is a huge machine that eats its way metre by metre through rock or soil with a rotating cutting head. It bores a perfectly round tunnel and secures it right behind itself.
wichtigste: A tunnel boring machine bores with a rotating cutting head.
In hard rock, steel disc cutters break up the rock.
The bored tunnel has a perfectly round cross-section.
Conveyor belts carry the rock out of the tunnel.
Some machines line the tunnel with concrete segments.
Large tunnel boring machines, including their back-up trains, are several hundred metres long.
Four machines called Sissi, Heidi, Gabi I and Gabi II bored the Gotthard Base Tunnel.

abschnitte.text: At the front of the machine, a huge round **cutting head** turns, which can be as big as a house. On it sit many steel **disc cutters**, which are pressed against the rock with enormous force. As the head turns, they roll over the rock and break it into small pieces. Because the head turns, the tunnel has a **perfectly round** cross-section.

Behind the cutting head comes the so-called **back-up train**, a kind of factory on rails. It contains engines, the power supply, ventilation, workshops and even rest rooms. Including the back-up train, large machines are several hundred metres long. The excavated rock is carried out of the tunnel on **conveyor belts**.

In soft ground or crumbly rock, machines with a shield are used, which push themselves forwards under a protective steel tube. They immediately fit ready-made concrete parts in rings, the **segments**. In solid rock, a gripper machine braces itself against the wall with large pads and pushes itself forwards that way. There, the walls are secured with anchors, nets and sprayed concrete.

For the 57-kilometre **Gotthard Base Tunnel**, four tunnel boring machines were used. They were called **Sissi, Heidi, Gabi I and Gabi II** and had a diameter of about nine metres. On **15 October 2010** the main breakthrough was achieved, when the workers met in the eastern tube. The machines were made by the German company Herrenknecht.

Instead of a machine, **drill and blast** tunnelling is also often used, in which the rock is blasted. It is suitable for short tunnels, changing shapes or difficult rock. A tunnel boring machine, on the other hand, is faster for long tunnels and shakes the surroundings less. At the Gotthard, both methods were combined, depending on the rock.

begriffe.erklaerung: A steel wheel on the cutting head that breaks the rock.
A ready-made, curved concrete part for the tunnel wall.
Long equipment behind the cutting head with a conveyor belt, technology and materials.
The moment when two sections of tunnel meet.

gewusst: Tunnel boring machines are traditionally given a woman’s name, often after a godmother.
In good rock, a tunnel boring machine can advance several dozen metres in a day.
Many tunnel boring machines do not stay in the mountain after the work, but are taken apart and used again.

teile.einleitung: An app is a program, usually for a mobile phone or tablet. There are apps for almost everything: for playing, learning, taking photos, for the weather or the timetable. The word comes from the English “application”.
wichtigste: The word app comes from the English word “application”.
New apps are downloaded from an app store.
You open an app with a small picture on the screen, the icon.
An update brings a new version of an app.
Apps that you no longer need can be deleted.
Many apps need an internet connection for everything to work.
The clock app shows the time; the weather app shows what the weather will be like.

abschnitte.text: An **app** is an application program that does a particular job. The word is short for the English “application”. Today it usually means programs for **smartphones** and tablets. Every mobile phone already has some apps installed, for example the clock, the camera or the calendar. You open each app by tapping its **icon**.

New apps are downloaded from an **app store**. On iPhones it is called the App Store, on Android phones Google Play. Apple opened its App Store in 2008, and after that apps became very popular. Many apps are free, others cost money. Some free apps make money from advertising or from purchases inside the app.

Every now and then an app gets an **update**. This brings a new version with improvements, new features or closed security gaps. That is why it is worth installing updates. Apps that you no longer need can simply be deleted. This frees up storage space on the device again.

Many people in Switzerland use apps every day. With the **SBB** app you look up connections and buy tickets. The **MeteoSwiss** app shows what the weather will be like and warns of severe weather. There are also learning apps for languages, maths or geography. Many of these apps need an **internet connection** to load up-to-date data.

Only download apps from the official stores, and ask your parents if you are unsure. Look at the **age rating** and at everything an app is allowed to do. Some apps want access to the camera, microphone or location, which is not always necessary. These **permissions** can be changed in the settings. And always ask first before buying anything in an app!

begriffe.erklaerung: An online shop where you can download apps.
A new, improved version of an app.
A small picture on the screen that you use to open an app.
Allowing an app to use, for example, the camera or the location.

gewusst: When Apple opened its App Store in 2008, there were only about 500 apps in it.
Today the big app stores each have millions of apps.
Programs on a computer or in a web browser are also sometimes called apps.

teile.einleitung: A technological revolution is a period in which new inventions fundamentally change the way people live and work. Examples are printing, the steam engine, electricity and the internet. Such upheavals change not only technology but also the economy, society and everyday life.
wichtigste: Gutenberg’s printing with movable type around 1450 set off a media revolution.
The first industrial revolution began in the late 18th century in Great Britain with the improved steam engine.
The second industrial revolution, from about 1870, was shaped above all by electrification.
The third industrial revolution, from the 1970s, brought automation through electronics and information technology.
In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee developed the World Wide Web at CERN near Geneva.
In 1847 the first railway running entirely on Swiss soil ran between Zurich and Baden.
In the Uster fire of 1832, people afraid for their jobs destroyed a weaving mill.

abschnitte.text: Around 1450, **Johannes Gutenberg** in Mainz invented printing with **movable type**. Before that, books had to be copied out laboriously by hand. Now many identical books could be produced quickly and cheaply. Knowledge spread much faster, and more people learnt to read.

In the late 18th century, **James Watt** in Great Britain improved the **steam engine**. It drove spinning machines, looms and later locomotives and ships. Many people moved from the countryside to the towns to work in factories. The work was often hard, and children too had to toil for long hours.

From about 1870, the second industrial revolution began. **Electrification** brought light bulbs, electric motors and trams. At the same time, the combustion engine, the telephone and the chemical industry appeared. In factories, goods were now produced in large quantities on the assembly line; this is called **mass production**.

From the 1970s, the third industrial revolution followed, with electronics, computers and robots. Machines now worked **automatically**, that is on their own according to programs. In 1989 **Tim Berners-Lee** developed the World Wide Web at CERN near Geneva, which made the internet accessible to everyone. Today people talk about Industry 4.0, in which machines are networked with one another and artificial intelligence is used.

Switzerland was industrialised early, especially in the textile industry. In 1802 the Hard spinning mill in Winterthur started work as the first mechanical spinning mill in Switzerland. On 22 November 1832, home weavers in Uster set fire to the Corrodi und Pfister weaving mill; this **Uster fire** is a well-known example of **machine breaking**. In 1847 the first railway entirely on Swiss soil ran from Zurich to Baden.

Technological revolutions brought more prosperity, better medicine and faster means of transport. At the same time, some people lost their jobs because machines replaced them. Later, laws were passed against child labour and for shorter working hours, in Switzerland for example the **Factory Act** of 1877. Today too, new technologies such as artificial intelligence are changing our jobs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The change from handwork to production with machines in factories.
A machine that produces movement using the power of hot steam.
The destruction of machines by people who feared for their jobs.
Machines carry out work on their own according to a program.
Individual metal letters that are put together for printing.

gewusst: The world’s first website went online at CERN in 1991 and can still be visited today.
The Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn got its name because it could bring fresh pastries from Baden to Zurich.
Even the New Stone Age, when people settled down and started farming, is called a revolution.

teile.einleitung: A library catalogue is a list of all the books and media that a library owns. With it you can find out whether a book is there, where it is shelved and whether it is on loan at the moment. In the past it consisted of index cards; today people usually search on a computer.
wichtigste: A library catalogue lists all the books and media of a library.
You can search in it by title, author and keyword.
The shelf mark on the spine shows where the book is on the shelf.
The catalogue also shows whether a book is on loan at the moment.
In the past, the details were written on index cards in large drawers.
To borrow books, you usually need a library card.

abschnitte.text: A **library catalogue** is like a huge table of contents for a library. For each book it lists the title, author, publisher, year of publication and subject. Audiobooks, DVDs, magazines and e-books are listed there too. Without a catalogue, you would have to search for a long time in large libraries with hundreds of thousands of books.

abschnitte.titel: In the past: the card catalogue
abschnitte.text: Before there were computers, the details of each book were written on an **index card**. These cards were kept in alphabetical order in long wooden drawers, the **card catalogue**. Often there were several catalogues, one by author’s name and one by subject. New books meant new cards, which were written by hand or on a typewriter.

Today most libraries use an electronic catalogue called an **OPAC**, which means online public access catalogue. You type in a title, a name or a keyword and immediately get a list of results. The catalogue also shows whether the book is on the shelf or on loan. Many catalogues can be searched conveniently from home on the internet, and books can be reserved.

On the spine of the book there is a small label with letters and numbers, the **shelf mark**. It is like an address and shows on which shelf and in which place the book stands. In children’s libraries, shelf marks often consist of a subject abbreviation and the first letters of the author’s name. If a book is in the wrong place, it can hardly be found, which is why books are put back after reading or handed in at the desk.

To borrow books, you usually need a **library card**; in many local libraries in Switzerland it is free for children. The book is scanned and booked to your account. When the loan period is over, you bring it back or extend the deadline online. Anyone who is late often has to pay a small fine.

Large academic libraries in Switzerland can be searched together through the **swisscovery** catalogue. The Swiss National Library in Bern collects everything that is published in Switzerland or about Switzerland and lists it in its catalogue. Many municipal and school libraries have their own online catalogues. Librarians are happy to help if you get stuck while searching.

begriffe.erklaerung: A code of letters and numbers that gives the location of a book.
An online catalogue in which anyone can search for media on a computer.
An earlier catalogue made of index cards in drawers.
The time for which you may keep a book.

gewusst: In some large libraries, the old wooden drawers of the card catalogues were sold as furniture after the switch to computers.
The Swiss National Library voluntarily receives a copy of every new book from many Swiss publishers.

teile.einleitung: In engineering, a gear ratio is the ratio by which a gear system changes speed of rotation and force. With gearwheels, chains or belts, a movement can be made faster, or slower but more powerful. Anyone who rides up a hill on a bike with gears is using a gear ratio.
wichtigste: The gear ratio tells you how much a gear system changes the speed of rotation.
If a large gearwheel drives a small one, the small one turns faster.
With a reduction, the output turns more slowly but with more force.
Without friction losses, the power stays the same with a gear ratio.
An idler gear only changes the direction of rotation, not the gear ratio.
With several gear stages, you multiply the individual ratios.
On a bike, steep mountain roads are best ridden with a small gearwheel at the front and a large one at the back.

abschnitte.text: A **gear system** passes a turning movement from one shaft to another, for example with gearwheels. The wheel that drives is called the **input**, and the wheel that passes the movement on is called the **output**. You work out the gear ratio by dividing the teeth of the output by the teeth of the input. So if a wheel with 12 teeth drives one with 36 teeth, the gear ratio is 3.

If a gearwheel with 40 teeth drives one with 20 teeth, the small wheel turns twice for every turn of the big one. So it becomes faster but has less force. The other way round is called a **reduction**: the output turns more slowly, but with more **torque**, that is more turning force. Without friction the power stays the same, because what you gain in speed you lose in force, and the other way round.

On a bike, a chain connects the front **chainring** with the rear gearwheel, the **sprocket**. If the chainring has 48 teeth and the sprocket 16, the back wheel turns three times for every turn of the pedals. For steep mountain roads, you choose a small gearwheel at the front and a large one at the back; then pedalling is easier, but you get less far with each push. On flat stretches you change the other way round in order to ride fast.

If a motor turns at 1500 revolutions per minute and a gear system reduces this in the ratio 3 to 1, the output turns at 500 revolutions per minute. If a gear system has two stages with the ratios 2 and 3, the total ratio is 2 times 3, which is 6. If you put an **idler gear** between two gearwheels, only the direction of rotation changes, not the ratio. This is because two gearwheels that mesh directly always turn in opposite directions.

In a car, the gearbox makes sure that the engine has enough force when starting off and does not turn too fast at high speed. In mechanical clocks and watches, tiny gearwheels change the movement so that the minute hand goes round twelve times faster than the hour hand. Cranes, mixers, drills and wind turbines also contain gear systems. Even in ancient times people used gearwheels, for instance in mills driven by water or animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that passes on a turning movement and changes speed and force as it does so.
How many times something turns per minute.
The turning force of a shaft or a wheel.
A gear ratio in which the output turns more slowly but with more force.
A small gearwheel; on a bike, the gearwheel on the back wheel.

gewusst: In a mechanical wristwatch, gearwheels smaller than a grain of rice mesh with each other.
Racing bikes often have more than 20 different gear combinations.
An idler gear between two gearwheels makes both of them turn in the same direction.

teile.einleitung: A transformer is an electrical device that changes the level of an alternating voltage. Without transformers, electricity could not be transported over long distances and then brought safely into our homes.
wichtigste: A transformer changes the level of an alternating voltage.
It only works with alternating current, not with direct current.
It consists of two coils on a shared iron core.
The input coil is called the primary coil, the output coil the secondary coil.
The ratio of the numbers of turns decides the ratio of the voltages.
If the secondary coil has more turns, the voltage becomes higher.
Transformer stations in neighbourhoods supply 400 and 230 volts for houses.

abschnitte.text: A transformer consists of two coils of wire that sit on a shared **iron core**. The input voltage is applied to the **primary coil**. The changed voltage comes out of the **secondary coil**. The two coils are not directly connected; the energy passes across through the magnetic field in the iron.

Alternating current in the primary coil produces a magnetic field in the iron core that keeps changing. This changing field produces a voltage in the secondary coil; this is called **induction**. Michael Faraday discovered this principle in 1831. Direct current, on the other hand, does not produce a changing field, which is why a transformer does not work with it.

The voltages are in the same ratio as the **numbers of turns** of the coils. If the primary side has 1000 turns and the secondary side only 50, the voltage becomes twenty times smaller, so 230 volts become 11.5 volts. The other way round, to get 12 volts from 230 volts with 460 primary turns, you need exactly 24 secondary turns. If the secondary coil has more turns than the primary coil, the voltage becomes higher.

Power stations produce electricity that flows across the country through **high-voltage lines**, in Switzerland at up to 380000 volts. At high voltage, much less energy is lost along the way. In **substations**, the voltage is lowered step by step. Finally, the transformer stations in the neighbourhood bring the medium voltage down to the 400 and 230 volts that arrive at our sockets.

Small transformers are found in some chargers, model railways and doorbell systems. Large transformers in substations are as big as a lorry and weigh many tonnes. You can often hear them **humming** quietly, because the iron vibrates in time with the alternating current. In Switzerland, the company Brown, Boveri & Cie in Baden built large transformers early on.

begriffe.erklaerung: A voltage whose direction keeps reversing, in Europe 50 times per second.
Producing a voltage with a changing magnetic field.
A single loop of wire in a coil.
The coil to which the input voltage is applied.
A facility where large transformers change the voltage in the power grid.

gewusst: Large transformers are filled with oil, which cools and insulates them.
Good transformers lose only very little energy, often less than one percent.
In Europe, the hum of a transformer usually has a pitch of 100 hertz.

teile.einleitung: Ada Lovelace was a British mathematician who is often called the world’s first computer programmer. As early as 1843, long before there were computers, she wrote down a sequence of steps for a calculating machine that existed only on paper at the time. She also realised that such machines could do much more than just calculate.
wichtigste: Ada Lovelace lived from 1815 to 1852 in England.
She was the daughter of the famous poet Lord Byron.
Through her marriage she became Countess of Lovelace.
She worked with the inventor Charles Babbage and his planned Analytical Engine.
Her program of 1843 was meant to calculate the Bernoulli numbers.
She foresaw that machines could also process music, for example.
The programming language Ada and Ada Lovelace Day are named after her.

abschnitte.text: Ada Lovelace was born in London in 1815 as Augusta Ada Byron. Her father was the poet **Lord Byron**, who left the family shortly after her birth. Her mother, Anne Isabella Milbanke, loved mathematics and made sure that Ada learnt mathematics and science from an early age. At that time this was very unusual for a girl. In 1835 she married William King, who later became Earl of Lovelace, and so Ada became a **countess**.

At the age of 17, Ada met the mathematician and inventor **Charles Babbage**. He was planning a huge mechanical calculating machine, the **Analytical Engine**. This machine was to be controlled with punched cards, much like looms at the time. It already had parts that you find in every computer today, such as a memory and a calculating unit. However, the machine was never fully built.

In 1843 Ada translated an article by the Italian Luigi Menabrea about Babbage’s machine into English. She added her own notes, which were much longer than the original text. In the last note, **Note G**, she described step by step how the machine could calculate the **Bernoulli numbers**. That is why this sequence is regarded as one of the first computer programs in history.

Her idea that calculating machines do not have to work only with numbers was especially far-sighted. She wrote that such a machine could also process symbols and, for example, compose music if sounds were translated into numbers. This is exactly what today’s computers do with music, pictures and texts. Sadly, Ada died of an illness in 1852, at only 36 years of age.

In the 1980s a programming language was named **Ada** after her. Every year, on the second Tuesday in October, **Ada Lovelace Day** is celebrated. On this day, women in science, technology and mathematics are remembered. Today Ada Lovelace is a role model, especially for girls who are interested in computer science.

begriffe.erklaerung: An exact sequence of instructions that a machine carries out step by step.
The mechanical calculating machine planned by Charles Babbage.
A card with holes whose pattern gives a machine commands or data.
A special sequence of numbers in mathematics, named after Jakob Bernoulli from Basel.

gewusst: The Bernoulli numbers are named after the Basel mathematician Jakob Bernoulli, so there is a bit of Switzerland in Ada’s famous program.
Ada Lovelace herself called her way of thinking “poetical science”.
Part of Babbage’s calculating machines was only rebuilt much later and is now in a museum in London.

teile.einleitung: A touchscreen is a screen that you can touch with your finger to operate a device. It shows pictures and takes commands at the same time, which is why almost every smartphone has one today.
wichtigste: A touchscreen is a touch-sensitive screen.
It is an input and output device at the same time.
Most smartphones have a capacitive touchscreen.
A resistive touchscreen reacts to pressure.
Multitouch means that several touches are recognised at the same time.
In 2007 the first iPhone made operating a device with your fingers known around the world.
In Switzerland you come across touchscreens, for example, at SBB ticket machines.

abschnitte.text: The English word means a screen you touch. It is an **input and output device** at the same time, because it shows pictures and recognises touches. Instead of using a mouse and keyboard, you tap, swipe or drag directly on the picture. This is easy and quick to learn, even for small children.

A **capacitive touchscreen** has a transparent, conducting layer under the glass, which holds a weak electric field. When your finger touches the glass, the conductive skin changes this field and the device works out the spot. That is why it usually does not work with ordinary woollen gloves, because wool does not conduct electricity. A **resistive touchscreen** consists of two layers that touch each other under **pressure**, so it also works with a stylus or a glove.

Modern screens recognise several fingers at the same time; this is called **multitouch**. So you can enlarge a photo by pulling two fingers apart. Other **gestures** are swiping to turn pages or turning with two fingers. In 2007 the first **iPhone** made this way of operating a device known around the world.

Apart from smartphones and tablets, you find touchscreens in many places. In Switzerland, people buy train tickets at the **SBB ticket machine** with a tap of the finger. Cash machines, ordering terminals in restaurants, cars and information points in museums use them too. Even fridges and coffee machines sometimes have small touch panels.

The first touchscreens were developed in England as early as the 1960s for air traffic control. In the 1980s and 1990s they were found on machines and in simple pocket computers with a stylus. Only with powerful smartphones did they become an everyday object. Today billions of people operate their devices mainly with their fingers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Reacts to the electrical conductivity of the finger.
Reacts to pressure, because two layers touch each other.
Recognising several touches at the same time.
A particular finger movement, for example swiping or zooming.

gewusst: There are special gloves with conducting threads in the fingertips, so you can use your phone in winter too.
A sausage or a piece of vegetable can also operate a capacitive touchscreen, because they contain water and salts.
Drops of water on the screen can cause unwanted touches.

teile.einleitung: A conditional statement is a command in a program that is carried out only if a particular condition is met. It works like an if-then rule in everyday life: if the traffic light is red, then you stay where you are. Without conditional statements, computers could not make decisions.
wichtigste: A conditional statement carries out commands only if a condition is true.
The “If ...” part is called the condition; the “then ...” part contains the commands.
With “else” you can decide what happens if the condition is false.
When a program takes different paths depending on a condition, this is called branching.
A condition is always either true or false.
With “and”, “or” and “not” you can combine conditions.
In Scratch the block is called “if ... then”; in Python you write “if”.

abschnitte.text: We use if-then rules all the time without thinking about it. If it is raining, you take an umbrella. If it gets dark, an automatic light comes on. In a game, the rule might be: if I show red, you clap; if I show blue, you stamp. A computer works in exactly the same way with a **conditional statement**.

A conditional statement has a **condition** and one or two blocks of commands. If the condition is true, the commands in the then part are carried out. If it is false, the program jumps to the **else part**, if there is one. A robot could have the rule: if it touches a wall, it turns round, otherwise it carries on. So if it does not touch a wall, it carries on.

In the children’s language Scratch there are the blocks “if ... then” and “if ... then ... else”. An example is: if points > 10 then say “Great”, else say “Keep practising”. If the variable points has the value 10, the figure says “Keep practising”, because 10 is not greater than 10. In the programming language Python you write **if**, **else** and, for further cases, “elif”. Spreadsheet programs also have an IF function.

Conditions often come from comparisons such as greater than (>), less than (<) or equal to (=). If x has the value 7, then “x >= 7” is true, because 7 is greater than or equal to 7. With **and**, both parts must be true: “(age > 9) and (age < 13)” is true, for example, for 12. With **or**, it is enough if at least one part is true. The word “not” reverses a value, so “not (5 > 3)” gives false.

The values true and false are called **Boolean values**. They are named after the English mathematician George Boole, who in the 19th century developed a way of calculating with logical statements. His ideas are the basis of all computers today. Every chip consists of countless tiny switches that decide according to such rules. Games, apps and satnavs also make decisions all the time with conditional statements.

begriffe.erklaerung: A statement that can be true or false, for example “points > 10”.
A point in the program where there are different paths depending on a condition.
A truth value that can only be true or false.
A storage place with a name in which a value is stored.
A sign such as >, < or = that is used to compare two values.

gewusst: An automatic sliding door in a shop works with a simple if-then rule: if someone comes, open.
A video game can contain several thousand conditional statements.
George Boole taught himself most of his mathematics.

teile.einleitung: A tokamak is a ring-shaped machine in which researchers are trying to produce energy the way the Sun does: by nuclear fusion. Inside it floats an extremely hot gas, a plasma, trapped by strong magnetic fields.
wichtigste: A tokamak is an experimental machine for nuclear fusion.
The word tokamak comes from Russian.
Andrei Sakharov and Igor Tamm developed the concept in the 1950s.
The plasma has to reach about 150 million °C.
Magnetic fields keep the plasma away from the walls.
When deuterium and tritium fuse, a helium nucleus and a neutron are produced.
In 2023 the British tokamak JET set a record with 69 megajoules of fusion energy.

abschnitte.text: In the Sun, light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones, and a lot of energy is released. This process is called **nuclear fusion**. In a tokamak, the hydrogen types **deuterium** and **tritium** are used. When they fuse, a helium nucleus and a fast neutron are produced, and the neutron carries the energy away.

The name is a Russian abbreviation and means roughly “ring-shaped chamber with magnetic coils”. The chamber has the shape of a doughnut; experts call it a **torus**. Large coils around the outside produce a magnetic field along the ring. An electric current in the plasma itself produces a second one, the **poloidal magnetic field**, and together the field lines wind round the ring like a screw thread.

For the nuclei to fuse, the plasma has to reach about **150 million °C**. That is about ten times hotter than the inside of the Sun. No material can withstand this, so the plasma must not touch the wall. A special part, the **divertor**, carries heat, helium ash and impurities out of the plasma in a controlled way.

The Soviet physicists **Andrei Sakharov** and **Igor Tamm** developed the concept in the 1950s. At the end of the 1960s, Soviet tokamaks achieved such good results that laboratories around the world copied them. The large tokamak **JET** in England ran from 1983 to 2023 and set a record of 69 megajoules in its last experiments. In southern France, the huge research reactor ITER is currently being built, and many countries are taking part.

At **EPFL** in Lausanne, the Swiss Plasma Center runs its own tokamak called TCV. There, scientists study how the shape of the plasma affects its stability. Another design is the **stellarator**, such as Wendelstein 7-X in Germany, in which the twisted magnetic field comes only from coils on the outside. A power station that supplies electricity from fusion all the time does not exist yet.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fusing of light atomic nuclei, which releases energy.
An extremely hot gas in which atoms have broken up into charged particles.
A ring shape like a doughnut or a swimming ring.
A part that carries heat and waste substances out of the plasma.
A fusion machine whose magnetic field comes only from coils on the outside.

gewusst: In a tokamak, the hottest plasma is only a few metres away from superconducting magnets that are cooled to extremely low temperatures.
The plasma in a tokamak usually weighs only a few grams, even though the machine is huge.
Deuterium can be obtained from ordinary water.

teile.einleitung: Sulzer is an industrial company with a long tradition from Winterthur, which started in 1834 as a small iron foundry. In the 19th and 20th centuries it became world-famous for steam engines, huge ship engines and weaving machines. Today Sulzer concentrates mainly on pumps and flow technology.
wichtigste: Sulzer started in 1834 in Winterthur with an iron foundry.
For a long time the company was called Gebrüder Sulzer (Sulzer Brothers).
In the 1880s Sulzer had great international success with steam engines.
In 1881 Sulzer opened its first branch factory in Ludwigshafen in Germany.
Large two-stroke diesel engines made Sulzer world-famous in shipbuilding.
From the 1950s, the projectile weaving machine became an export success.
The large-engine business is carried on today by WinGD (Winterthur Gas & Diesel).
Today Sulzer concentrates mainly on pumps and flow technology (as of 2025).

abschnitte.text: In 1834 the Sulzer family founded an **iron foundry** in **Winterthur**. Johann Jakob Sulzer ran the business together with his sons, which is why the company was called **Gebrüder Sulzer** (Sulzer Brothers) for a long time. At first they cast parts from iron, but soon they were building whole machines. With Sulzer and other firms, Winterthur grew into an important industrial town.

In the 19th century Sulzer made **steam engines**, which powered factories, pumps and ships. Sulzer engines were considered especially economical and reliable. In the 1880s they were sold to many countries. In 1881 Sulzer opened its first branch factory in **Ludwigshafen** in Germany.

At the end of the 19th century Sulzer worked with the inventor Rudolf Diesel and soon built its own **diesel engines**. The huge **two-stroke diesel engines** that power large cargo ships and tankers became famous. Such engines are as big as a house with several storeys. Today this business is carried on in Winterthur by the company **WinGD** (Winterthur Gas & Diesel).

From the 1950s Sulzer built the **projectile weaving machine**. In this machine, a small piece of metal, the projectile, shoots the thread across through the cloth instead of a heavy shuttle. The machine was fast and efficient and was exported to many countries. Sulzer also made heating systems, refrigeration plants and medical products.

From the 1980s Sulzer sold many of its business areas and reorganised itself greatly. Today the company concentrates mainly on **pumps** and **flow technology**, for instance for water supply, chemicals or energy (as of 2025). Its headquarters are still in Winterthur. On the former factory site in the centre of Winterthur there are now flats, schools, offices and cultural venues.

begriffe.erklaerung: A works where liquid iron is poured into moulds.
