A combustion engine that fires once with every turn.
Here a small piece of metal that carries the thread through the weaving machine.
Technology that moves liquids and gases, for example with pumps.

gewusst: As a young engineer, Rudolf Diesel worked for a short time at Sulzer in Winterthur, and Sulzer was later one of the first companies to build his engine under licence.
A large ship’s diesel engine in the Sulzer tradition can have more power than hundreds of car engines together.

teile.einleitung: A signal box is the control centre of the railway, where points and signals are set and secured. It makes sure that every train runs on the right track and that no trains collide. In the past, heavy levers were moved to do this; today computers usually do the job.
wichtigste: A signal box sets and secures points and signals.
In the signal box, the train dispatcher controls the train traffic.
In old mechanical signal boxes, points and signals were moved with levers and wires.
A relay signal box works with many electrical switches called relays.
Modern electronic signal boxes work with computers.
The secured route of a train through a station is called a route.
SBB controls its traffic from large operations centres, one of which is in Olten.

abschnitte.titel: The job of a signal box
abschnitte.text: A train cannot steer; it always follows the rails. Whether it goes left or right is decided by the **points**. Whether it may go or has to stop is shown by the **signals**. The signal box controls both and constantly checks that everything fits together.

For every train, a particular path through the station is set: the **route**. Only when all the points are in the right position and locked can the signal be set to go. This safety technology prevents a signal from showing green while a set of points is in the wrong position. In addition, no second route can be set that crosses or endangers the first one.

The first signal boxes appeared in the 19th century. In a **mechanical signal box** there were long rows of heavy levers. Using **wires** and rods, the signalman moved the points and signals, which were often hundreds of metres away. This was hard physical work, and every larger station needed its own staff.

In the 20th century, electrical signal boxes came in. A **relay signal box** secures the routes with thousands of small electrical switches, the relays. In Switzerland, track-diagram signal boxes were especially common, in which the track layout is reproduced on a control desk. Today more and more **electronic signal boxes** are being built, in which computers take over the safety functions.

In the past, almost every station had its own signal box with staff on site. Today SBB controls its network from four large **operations centres** in Lausanne, Olten, Pollegio and Zurich Airport. There, train dispatchers monitor long stretches of line on many screens. The signal boxes in the stations are operated remotely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where the track divides, used to send a train onto another track.
The set and secured path for a train.
An electrical switch that is operated by electric current.
The person who controls the train traffic in an area.

gewusst: Some old mechanical signal boxes can be visited today as museums.
A single modern signal box can control points and signals over many kilometres of line and in several stations.

teile.einleitung: The Bee-Bot is a small learning robot that looks like a bee. Children give it a series of commands with arrow buttons on its back and then set it off. This way even nursery school children learn what programming means.
wichtigste: The Bee-Bot looks like a bee.
You give it commands with the arrow buttons, and it starts with the GO button.
With a forward command, it moves about 15 centimetres.
An arrow to the right makes it do a quarter turn.
The button with the X clears all the commands.
If you do not clear them, it carries out the old commands again too.
In the classroom, the Bee-Bot usually moves on a mat with squares.

abschnitte.text: The **Bee-Bot** is a small robot in the shape of a bee with yellow and black stripes. It has two big eyes that light up after every step. On its back there are seven **buttons**. Underneath it has wheels with which it moves across the floor. It is sturdily built so that even small children can handle it well.

With the forward and backward arrows, the Bee-Bot moves one step of about 15 centimetres. With the left and right arrows, it turns on the spot by a **quarter turn**, that is by 90 degrees. The pause button makes it wait for a moment. With the **GO** button, it starts all the stored commands. The button with the X clears all the commands from its memory.

First you think about where the Bee-Bot should go. Then you press the commands in order, for example forward, forward, right, forward. Only with GO does it carry out the whole **sequence of commands**. Important: before entering new commands you must clear the old ones with X, otherwise it will carry out the old commands as well. If something does not work, you look for the mistake and improve the program; this is called **debugging**.

In the classroom, the Bee-Bot usually moves on a **mat with squares**. Each square is exactly one step in size. The mats show, for example, letters, numbers, roads or a map. The children get tasks such as “Go to the letter B.” In this way they also practise reading, arithmetic and spatial thinking along the way.

In Switzerland, the subject **media and computer science** is part of Lehrplan 21, the curriculum for German-speaking cantons. That is why Bee-Bots are often used in nursery school and the first school years. The children learn that a robot does exactly what it is told, and nothing more. They learn to break problems down into small steps. There is also a version called Blue-Bot, which can also be controlled with a tablet.

begriffe.erklaerung: A machine that carries out commands on its own.
Several commands that are carried out one after another.
Looking for mistakes in a program and fixing them.
A turn of 90 degrees, that is a quarter of a circle.

gewusst: The Bee-Bot beeps and flashes its eyes when it has carried out a command.
Because each step measures about 15 centimetres, you can easily make Bee-Bot mats yourself.
The Bee-Bot has no eyes for seeing, so it does not notice when something is in its way.

teile.einleitung: A superalloy is a particularly tough metal material that stays strong even at very high temperatures. Most superalloys consist mainly of nickel, mixed with other metals. Without them there would be no modern aircraft engines or gas turbines.
wichtigste: Most superalloys for turbine blades are based on nickel.
Besides nickel, there are also superalloys based on cobalt.
The finely distributed gamma prime phase Ni₃Al is mainly responsible for the high strength at high temperatures.
Creep is the name for the slow, permanent deformation under load at high temperature.
Turbine blades are often cast as a single crystal, because without grain boundaries they deform more slowly.
The blades are usually made by vacuum investment casting.
A ceramic thermal barrier coating made of zirconium oxide and fine cooling channels protect the blades as well.

abschnitte.text: An **alloy** is a mixture of several metals, like bronze, which is made from copper and tin. Superalloys usually consist mostly of **nickel** and also contain chromium, aluminium, cobalt and other elements. There are also superalloys based on **cobalt**. Their special feature is that they stay very strong even close to their melting point.

Normal metals become soft when they are very hot. Under constant load they then stretch very slowly, like chewing gum being pulled apart. This slow, permanent deformation is called **creep**. In an engine, the turbine blades spin very fast in hot gases, so they have to resist creep particularly well.

Under the microscope, you can see tiny little cubes of a compound of nickel and aluminium in a nickel-based superalloy. This **gamma prime phase**, with the formula Ni₃Al, is finely distributed in the metal. It blocks the movements in the crystal lattice that would otherwise deform the metal. This keeps the material strong even in great heat.

Normal metals are made of many small crystal grains, with **grain boundaries** between them. It is precisely at these boundaries that the metal starts to creep in the heat. That is why highly stressed turbine blades are cast as a **single crystal**, that is, from one single continuous crystal. They are made by **vacuum investment casting**, in which the metal flows into a ceramic mould with no air present and solidifies in a controlled way.

The gases in an engine are often hotter than the melting point of the blades. That is why the blades have fine **cooling channels** inside, through which air from the compressor flows. On the outside, a thin ceramic **thermal barrier coating** based on zirconium oxide protects them. Superalloys are used in aircraft engines, in gas turbines in power stations and in rockets.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of a metal with other elements.
Slow, permanent deformation of a material under load in the heat.
A workpiece that consists of one single continuous crystal.
A very precise casting method using ceramic moulds.

gewusst: The first superalloys were developed in the 1940s for the early jet engines.
Without the air cooling inside, some turbine blades would melt during operation.

teile.einleitung: Efficiency tells you how much of the energy put in a machine really turns into useful energy. The rest is usually lost as heat. The higher the efficiency, the less energy is wasted, which is good for your purse and for the environment.
wichtigste: Efficiency is the useful power divided by the power put in.
It is usually given in percent and is always less than 100 percent.
A classic light bulb turns only about 5 percent of its energy into visible light.
Large hydroelectric power stations reach efficiencies of more than 80 percent.
Thermal power stations have a lower efficiency, because heat can only partly be turned into work.
Efficiencies of parts connected one after another are multiplied.
In combined heat and power, the waste heat is used for heating.

abschnitte.text: Every machine converts energy; an electric motor, for example, turns electrical energy into movement. Some energy is always lost along the way, usually as **waste heat** from friction. **Efficiency** is the ratio of useful power to the power put in. It is abbreviated with the Greek letter eta and usually given in percent.

If an engine gives out 45 kilowatts of mechanical power and takes in 150 kilowatts with its fuel, it has an efficiency of 30 percent. If an engine takes in 200 kilowatts and has an efficiency of 35 percent, 130 kilowatts are lost as waste heat. If several parts are connected one after another, their efficiencies are multiplied: a motor with 90 percent and a gearbox with 80 percent give 72 percent together. An efficiency of more than 100 percent is impossible, which is why there can be no **perpetual motion machine**, a machine that runs by itself for ever.

A classic **light bulb** turns only about 5 percent of its electricity into visible light; the rest becomes heat, which is why it gets so hot. An LED lamp is much more efficient and needs only a fraction of the electricity for the same amount of light. Electric motors often reach more than 90 percent, whereas petrol engines in cars usually manage only between 20 and 35 percent. Solar cells on house roofs turn about 20 percent of the sunlight into electricity.

Large **hydroelectric power stations** turn more than 80 percent of the potential energy of the water into electricity, which is a top value. Thermal power stations that use coal, gas or nuclear fuel manage much less, because according to the laws of physics heat can only partly be turned into work. In **combined heat and power**, the waste heat is used to heat houses, so a much larger part of the fuel is used. Because Switzerland gets a large part of its electricity from hydropower, its electricity production is particularly efficient.

For vehicles, people often look at the **well-to-wheel** efficiency, that is from the oil well or power station to the wheel. All the losses are counted: in production, in transport, in charging and in the engine. This makes it possible to compare fairly whether an electric car, a petrol car or a hydrogen car uses energy more economically. High efficiency helps to save energy and give off less CO₂.

begriffe.erklaerung: The share of the energy put in that is usefully converted.
Heat that is produced unused when energy is converted.
How much energy is converted per second, measured in watts.
An imaginary machine that runs for ever without any energy being supplied, but that cannot exist.
Producing electricity and usable heat at the same time in one plant.

gewusst: An old light bulb is really more of a small heater that makes a bit of light on the side.
Large transformers in the power grid reach efficiencies of more than 99 percent.
When cycling, the human body also turns only about a quarter of the energy from food into movement.

teile.einleitung: A socket is the connection point in the wall where you connect electrical appliances to the mains. When you push a plug into it, electricity flows to the appliance. Because a dangerous voltage of 230 volts is present in the socket, you have to be very careful with it.
wichtigste: A normal Swiss socket has three holes for a plug.
A Swiss socket carries a voltage of 230 volts.
You must never push objects such as needles or scissors into a socket.
Child safety covers stop children from pushing things into it.
You should never plug in appliances with wet hands, because water can conduct electricity.
When unplugging, you always hold the plug and never pull on the cable.
Only a qualified electrician may connect new sockets.

abschnitte.text: A socket connects appliances such as lamps, toasters or chargers to the **mains**. Inside the wall, cables run from the fuse box to the socket. When you push a plug in, the **circuit** closes and the appliance gets electricity. An **extension lead** offers several sockets on one cable.

The normal Swiss socket has three holes in a flat hexagonal shape. Two holes are for the wires that bring the electricity in and carry it back. The third is for the **earth wire**, which safely carries the current into the ground if there is a fault. The voltage is 230 **volts** at a frequency of 50 hertz.

Almost every country has its own plug shape. The thick German Schuko plug, for example, does not fit into a normal Swiss socket, and in Great Britain sockets look completely different. That is why you often need a **travel adapter** on holiday. The flat two-pin Europlug, which you find on many mobile phone chargers, does fit into many European sockets, including Swiss ones.

Electricity from a socket can be deadly. So you must never poke metal objects such as needles, scissors or screws into the holes. Many sockets have a **child safety cover**, where small flaps close the holes. Because **water** can conduct electricity, you must never plug in appliances with wet hands or near the bath.

When unplugging, you hold the plug and do not pull on the cable, otherwise the wires inside can break. You should stop using damaged cables or plugs. Only a **qualified electrician** may connect new sockets, for example an electrical installer. A residual current device in the fuse box switches off the electricity in a flash if the current takes a wrong path.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shows how strongly the electric current is driven, measured in volts.
A wire that carries the current away safely if there is a fault.
An in-between plug so that an appliance fits into sockets abroad.
A switch that cuts off the electricity immediately if it could flow through a person.

gewusst: Around the world there are more than a dozen different plug types, named with the letters A to N.
The Swiss plug is type J and is used almost only in Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

teile.einleitung: A washing machine is a household appliance that washes, rinses and spins dirty clothes and laundry automatically. In the past, people had to scrub their laundry by hand for hours; today the machine does it at the press of a button. In Switzerland, many families share a washing machine in the laundry room.
wichtigste: The washing machine washes clothes with water, detergent and movement.
During spinning, the drum turns very fast and gets the water out of the laundry.
Many Swiss blocks of flats have a shared laundry room.
The laundry rota shows who may wash when.
One red sock can turn white laundry pink.
A woollen jumper can shrink a lot if it is washed too hot.
Afterwards the wet laundry is dried in a tumble dryer or on the line.

abschnitte.text: In a washing machine, a stainless steel **drum** with holes turns, and you put the laundry in it. The machine lets water in, heats it up and adds the **detergent**. As the drum turns, the laundry tumbles back and forth again and again, which loosens the dirt. Then the laundry is rinsed several times with clean water.

At the end, the drum turns very fast during **spinning**, often more than 1000 times per minute. The centrifugal force pushes the water outwards through the holes, rather like in a salad spinner. Afterwards the laundry is only damp and dries more quickly. The wet laundry then goes into the **tumble dryer**, which in Switzerland is called a “Tumbler”, or onto the washing line.

In many Swiss blocks of flats, not every flat has its own machine; instead everyone shares a **laundry room** in the basement. The **laundry rota** shows which family may wash on which day. Anyone who misses their washing day or leaves the machine dirty sometimes causes arguments between neighbours. Well-known Swiss makers of washing machines are V-ZUG from Zug and Schulthess.

White and coloured clothes are washed separately, because a single red sock can turn a whole load of white laundry pink. The small symbols on the **care label** show the temperature at which a piece of clothing may be washed. Wool is washed cool and gently, otherwise it felts, and a jumper can shrink so much that it only fits a doll. Before washing, you should empty the trouser pockets so that no tissues or coins end up in the drum.

In the past, people washed laundry in the river, in a washtub or with a washboard, and washing day was hard work. At the beginning of the 20th century, the first electric washing machines appeared, but they only became common in Swiss homes from the 1950s and 1960s. Modern machines use much less water and electricity than older ones. If you wash at 30 or 40 degrees instead of 60 degrees and fill the drum well, you save extra energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The turning container in the washing machine in which the laundry lies.
Turning the drum very fast to get the water out of the laundry.
A machine that dries laundry; in Switzerland it is called a “Tumbler”.
A plan that sets out who may use the shared washing machine when.
A sewn-in label with symbols showing how to wash a piece of clothing.

gewusst: In the past, washing day often took a whole day and was hard physical work.
The Swiss laundry room with its rota is so typical that it often appears in jokes and television programmes.
During spinning, the laundry is subjected to many times the force of gravity.

teile.einleitung: Binary cards are simple cards with dots that let you learn the binary system through play. Each card has twice as many dots as the one before, so 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on. By turning cards face up or face down, you can show any number, just as a computer does with zeros and ones.
wichtigste: Binary cards have 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 dots and so on.
Each card has twice as many dots as the card before it.
A card face up means 1; a card face down means 0.
With the cards 8, 4, 2 and 1, the cards 4 and 1 together show the number 5.
The largest number with the cards 1, 2, 4 and 8 is 15.
The sequence up, down, down, up, that is 1001, means the number 9.

abschnitte.text: **Binary cards** are a learning game, often home-made from paper. On the first card there is 1 dot, on the next 2, then 4, 8 and 16. The number of dots is **doubled** from card to card. The cards are laid out from left to right with the largest number on the left.

To show a number, you turn the right cards face up and add up the visible dots. For 5 you need the cards 4 and 1. If the cards 8 and 2 are face up, you see 10 dots. For 7, with the cards 4, 2 and 1, you need all three cards face up.

If you write a 1 for every card that is face up and a 0 for every card that is face down, you get a **binary number**. With the cards 4, 2 and 1, you write the number 6 as 110. With the cards 8, 4, 2 and 1, 1001 means up, down, down, up, so 8 plus 1 equals 9. This way you can see directly how the **binary system** works.

With the four cards 1, 2, 4 and 8, 15 is the largest number, when all are face up. If you add the 16 card, you can get up to 31. With every new card, the number of possible numbers doubles. With eight cards you can show all the numbers from 0 to 255, which is exactly one **byte**.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the idea come from?
abschnitte.text: Binary cards come from the **CS Unplugged** project, which explains computer science without any computers. It was developed in New Zealand at the University of Canterbury and is used in schools around the world. In Switzerland too, many teachers use such activities in the subject media and computer science. The children themselves play the part of the bits.

You can send each other secret messages with binary cards by numbering the letters: A is 1, B is 2 and so on. Another game: one person says a number, and the group turns up the right cards as fast as possible. You can also count upwards and watch how the 1 card is turned over at every step. This is a playful way to learn how a computer counts.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number that consists only of the digits 0 and 1.
To multiply a number by two.
A place with the value 0 or 1, like a single card.
A learning project that explains computer science without computers.

gewusst: With only ten binary cards you can already count up to 1023.
On the same principle, you can count in binary up to 31 on the fingers of one hand.

teile.einleitung: ASCII is a code that gives a number to every letter, every digit and many punctuation marks. This lets computers store and exchange text as numbers. The code was first published in 1963 and is still the basis of many text formats today.
wichtigste: ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange.
The code was first published in 1963.
ASCII contains 128 characters with the numbers 0 to 127.
The codes 0 to 31 are reserved for control characters.
The capital letter “A” has the code 65, the digit “0” the code 48 and the space the code 32.
Small and capital letters always differ by 32 in the code.
Umlauts such as “ä” are not included in the original ASCII.

abschnitte.text: Computers work only with numbers, or more precisely with zeros and ones. To store text, they need a table that gives each character a number. **ASCII** is such a table and stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange. It was published in the USA in 1963 and revised again in 1968. Each character needs 7 **bits**, which is why there are exactly 128 characters.

The numbers 0 to 31 are **control characters**, which you cannot see, for example for a line break or a tab. The number 32 is the space, then come punctuation marks and the digits 0 to 9 with the codes 48 to 57. The capital letters A to Z have the codes 65 to 90, the small letters a to z the codes 97 to 122. So a small letter and its capital always differ by 32: “A” with 65 becomes “a” with 97. The last number, 127, is the delete character.

Because every character is a number, a program can calculate with text. If it wants to turn a small letter into a capital, it simply subtracts 32. The codes 72 and 105 together make the word “Hi”, because 72 is “H” and 105 is “i”. Sorting in alphabetical order also works by the computer comparing the numbers. So for the computer, a word is really a **sequence of numbers**.

ASCII was made for the English language and so does not know any umlauts such as “ä”, “ö” and “ü” or letters such as “é” and “ç”. For languages such as German and French, extensions with 8 bits and 256 characters were later created. Today people mostly use **Unicode**, which contains more than 100 000 characters from almost all the writing systems in the world, as well as emojis. The UTF-8 encoding is built so that the first 128 characters exactly match the ASCII codes.

Many programming languages, web addresses and file formats still use mainly ASCII characters today. In the past, ASCII was also used for **teleprinters**, which sent messages over lines. You can even draw pictures with ASCII characters; this is called ASCII art. Older smileys such as :-) also consist only of ASCII characters.

begriffe.erklaerung: An agreement that gives each character a particular number.
An invisible character that, for example, causes a line break.
A modern character code for almost all the writing systems in the world and emojis.
The smallest unit of information, either 0 or 1.

gewusst: If you press Ctrl together with certain letters on a computer, you sometimes still produce old ASCII control characters today.
Because web addresses allowed only ASCII for a long time, umlauts in domain names are converted internally into a special sequence of characters.
In the past, whole pictures were put together from letters and punctuation marks alone with ASCII art.

teile.einleitung: The four-stroke engine is an internal combustion engine that works in four steps: intake, compression, power and exhaust. To this day it powers most cars and many motorbikes.
wichtigste: A four-stroke engine works in four strokes: intake, compression, power, exhaust.
One complete cycle takes two turns of the crankshaft.
Only in the power stroke does the engine give work to the crankshaft.
In a petrol engine, the spark plug fires shortly before top dead centre.
In 1876 Nicolaus August Otto built the first working four-stroke engine.
A turbocharger compresses the intake air using energy from the exhaust.
In a two-stroke engine, by contrast, there is a power stroke with every turn of the crankshaft.

abschnitte.text: In the engine, a **piston** moves up and down in a cylinder. A connecting rod links the piston to the **crankshaft**, which turns the up-and-down movement into a rotation. At the top of the cylinder, **valves** open and close, controlled by a camshaft. The highest position of the piston is called top dead centre, the lowest bottom dead centre.

In the first stroke, the piston moves down and sucks in air or a mixture of air and fuel. In the second stroke it moves up and **compresses** the mixture. In the third stroke, the **power stroke**, the mixture burns and pushes the piston down hard. In the fourth stroke, the piston pushes the exhaust gases out through the exhaust valve, and then everything starts again.

In an **Otto engine**, a spark plug ignites the mixture of petrol and air shortly before top dead centre. In a diesel engine, the air is compressed so strongly that it becomes very hot and the injected diesel ignites by itself. Between exhaust and intake, the inlet and exhaust valves are both open for a short moment; this is called **valve overlap**. A **turbocharger** uses the energy of the exhaust gases to force more air into the cylinder.

The **engine capacity** is the volume that all the pistons push aside in one stroke. A four-cylinder engine with a bore of 80 millimetres and a stroke of 90 millimetres has an engine capacity of about 1.8 litres. Power is calculated from torque and speed of rotation. An engine with 200 newton metres at 3000 revolutions per minute delivers about 63 kilowatts.

In 1876 the German inventor **Nicolaus August Otto** built the first usable four-stroke engine. In the 1890s Rudolf Diesel developed the engine named after him. Since then, four-stroke engines have powered cars, lorries, ships and lawnmowers. Because they give off exhaust gases and CO2, they are increasingly being replaced by **electric motors** today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A moving part of the cylinder that is pushed down by the gas pressure.
A shaft that turns the up-and-down movement of the pistons into a rotation.
The highest or lowest position of the piston, where it briefly stands still.
The volume that the pistons push aside in one movement.

gewusst: The camshaft turns only half as fast as the crankshaft.
At high revs, a car engine fires many times per second in each cylinder.
The sequence is often learnt by heart as “suck, squeeze, bang, blow”.

teile.einleitung: A viaduct is a long bridge that carries a road or railway line across a valley. In the Grisons stand some of the most famous viaducts in the world, which the trains of the Rhaetian Railway cross every day.
wichtigste: A viaduct is a long bridge across a valley.
It rests on tall supports called piers.
The old viaducts of the Rhaetian Railway are built of stone.
The Landwasser Viaduct near Filisur is about 65 metres high.
There, the train runs straight into a tunnel in the rock face.
At the Brusio spiral viaduct in the Valposchiavo, the railway goes round in a circle to gain height.
The Albula and Bernina lines have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Latin: via means way and ducere means to lead. So a viaduct leads a way across a valley or a gorge. It usually consists of many arches that rest on tall **piers**. A similar Roman structure that carried water into the towns, on the other hand, is called an **aqueduct**.

The famous **Landwasser Viaduct** near Filisur in the Grisons was built in 1901 and 1902. It is about 65 metres high and stands in an elegant curve. On one side, the train runs straight into a **tunnel** in the vertical rock face. The picture of the red train on the viaduct is one of the best-known photo subjects in Switzerland.

Near Brusio in the Valposchiavo, the Bernina railway has to climb a lot of height in a small space. That is why it goes round in a full circle on the **spiral viaduct**, passing under its own track as it does so. In this way the train gains height without the line becoming too steep. The stone viaduct is an attraction for travellers from all over the world.

The old viaducts of the **Rhaetian Railway** are built of natural stone, which often came from the surrounding area. During building, wooden **centring** supported the arches until the stones were firmly in place. Stone bridges last a very long time and fit beautifully into the mountain landscape. Since 2008 the Albula and Bernina lines, with their many viaducts, have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

Other countries also have impressive viaducts. The **Millau Viaduct** in southern France was opened in 2004 and is one of the highest bridges in the world. The Göltzsch Viaduct in Saxony is regarded as the largest brick bridge on Earth. Modern viaducts are mostly built of concrete and steel.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tall support on which a bridge rests.
A curved shape that spreads the weight sideways onto the piers.
A bridge that carries a water channel, known from Roman times.
A temporary wooden framework that supports an arch while it is being built.

gewusst: The highest point of the Millau Viaduct is higher than the top of the Eiffel Tower.
Some of the piers of the Landwasser Viaduct were built up without a fixed scaffold, with the help of steel towers and cranes.
On the Albula line, the railway overcomes big differences in height with spiral tunnels and viaducts.

teile.einleitung: A gearwheel is a wheel with teeth around its edge that meshes with another gearwheel and so passes on a turning movement. Gearwheels are found in clocks, bikes, cars, machines and even in mountain railways. Without them, a large part of our technology would come to a standstill.
wichtigste: A gearwheel passes on a turning movement to another gearwheel.
Several gearwheels that mesh with each other form a gear system.
Two gearwheels that mesh directly turn in opposite directions.
A small gearwheel turns faster than a large one that it meshes with.
For two gearwheels to fit together, their teeth must be the same size.
On a bike, a chain connects the front and rear gearwheels.
Many tiny gearwheels work in mechanical watches.

abschnitte.text: A gearwheel is a round disc with evenly spaced teeth around its edge. When the teeth of two wheels mesh, one pushes the other round. In this way a **turning movement** is passed from one axle to another. Several such wheels together are called a **gear system**. For everything to run smoothly, the teeth of both wheels must be the same size; otherwise they do not fit into each other.

If one gearwheel turns to the right, the wheel that meshes directly with it turns to the left. With three wheels in a row, the third one therefore turns in the same direction as the first again. If a small wheel with 10 teeth meshes with a large one with 30 teeth, the small one has to turn three times before the large one has gone round once. This ratio is called the **gear ratio**. A large wheel turns more slowly, but it can pass on more force.

On a bike, the gearwheels at the front by the pedals and at the back on the wheel are connected by a **chain**. With the **gears**, the chain moves onto other gearwheels. A small wheel at the front and a large one at the back make pedalling easy, which helps uphill. A large wheel at the front and a small one at the back give plenty of speed on flat stretches. This way you can choose the right gear ratio for the terrain.

In a mechanical watch, many tiny gearwheels mesh with each other and make the hands move at exactly the right speed. Switzerland is world-famous for its **watchmaking**, especially in the Jura Arc around La Chaux-de-Fonds and the Vallée de Joux. You can also find gearwheels at home, for example in a tin opener with a handle, where a small gearwheel turns the tin along its edge. Other examples are hand mixers, wind-up toy cars and the cranks on blinds and awnings.

On a **rack railway**, a gearwheel under the train meshes with a toothed rack between the rails. This lets the train climb very steep lines without slipping. The Vitznau-Rigi railway was opened in 1871 and was the first mountain railway of this kind in Europe. The Pilatus railway near Lucerne, with gradients of up to 48 percent, is regarded as the steepest rack railway in the world.

Gearwheels have existed since ancient times. A famous find is the **Antikythera mechanism**, a Greek device with many bronze gearwheels that is more than 2000 years old. In the Middle Ages, gearwheels drove mills and the first tower clocks. Since industrialisation, steel gearwheels have been made in large numbers and very precisely.

begriffe.erklaerung: Several gearwheels that work together and pass on a movement.
The ratio of how often one wheel turns while the other turns once.
A straight bar with teeth that a gearwheel can mesh with.
The rod in the middle around which a wheel turns.

gewusst: The Antikythera mechanism is often called the oldest known calculating machine in the world.
The Pilatus railway has a special rack in which the gearwheels mesh horizontally from both sides.
Some mechanical wristwatches consist of several hundred individual parts.

teile.einleitung: An inverter is an electronic device that turns direct current into alternating current. It is found in every solar installation on a roof, in electric cars and in emergency power systems.
wichtigste: An inverter turns direct current into alternating current.
Solar panels supply direct current, but the household network needs alternating current.
With MPP tracking, the inverter keeps looking for the point of greatest power.
Before feeding electricity in, it matches frequency and phase with the grid.
If the public grid fails, it must switch itself off automatically.
Modern solar inverters reach about 95 to 98 percent efficiency.
The basic form of a single-phase inverter is the H-bridge made of four switches.

abschnitte.text: Batteries and solar panels supply **direct current**, which always flows in the same direction. Our power grid, on the other hand, works with **alternating current**, which in Europe changes direction 50 times per second. The inverter turns one into the other. The counterpart, which turns alternating current into direct current, is called a rectifier and is found, for example, in every mobile phone charger.

Inside, electronic switches, usually **transistors**, switch the current on and off very fast and reverse its direction. The basic circuit of four switches is called an **H-bridge**, because on a diagram it looks like the letter H. By clever switching in many short pulses, an almost clean waveform is produced. Finally, filters smooth the current.

In a **photovoltaic installation**, the inverter converts the electricity from the panels for the household network. With **MPP tracking**, it keeps looking for the operating point at which the panels give the most power, for instance when clouds pass by. Before feeding electricity in, it matches frequency and phase exactly with the grid. If the public grid fails, it switches itself off automatically so that engineers can work safely on the lines.

An **off-grid inverter** forms its own small power network without the public grid, for example in a remote mountain hut with a solar panel and a battery. A **microinverter** is small and sits directly on a single solar panel. Such devices are also used in plug-in mini solar systems for the balcony. Large central inverters in solar power plants, on the other hand, are as big as a cupboard or a container.

An electric car also needs an inverter. The battery supplies direct voltage, but many motors run on **three-phase current**, an alternating current with three phases. The inverter produces the right current from this and so controls how fast the motor turns. When braking, it works the other way round, and the motor charges the battery again.

begriffe.erklaerung: Current that always flows in the same direction, for example from a battery.
Current that keeps changing direction, as in a socket.
Automatic search for the greatest power output of the solar panels.
A tiny electronic switch with no moving parts.
Alternating current with three wires, which drives motors well.

gewusst: An inverter often switches its transistors many thousands of times per second.
Inverters feel warm when they are working, because a small part of the energy is lost as heat.
Trains and modern trams also use inverters to control their motors.

teile.einleitung: A torch is a small, portable lamp that shines using batteries or a rechargeable battery. It helps in the dark, when camping, in a power cut or even in an emergency in the mountains. Today almost every torch has an economical LED.
wichtigste: A torch gets its electricity from batteries or a rechargeable battery.
Most modern torches have an LED.
A shiny mirror behind the bulb directs the light forwards.
When the batteries run low, the torch shines more weakly.
With a wind-up torch you make the electricity yourself by turning a handle.
A head torch is worn on the head with a strap.
For the alpine distress signal, you give a light signal six times a minute.

abschnitte.text: In a torch, the **battery**, the switch and the bulb form a closed circuit. When you press the switch, electricity flows from the battery through the light source and it lights up. Behind the bulb there is a curved, shiny **reflector**, which focuses the light forwards like a mirror. At the front, a pane of glass or plastic protects the inside.

In the past, torches had a small light bulb that used a lot of electricity and often burnt out. Today almost always **LEDs** are used, that is light-emitting diodes, which are much brighter and need much less electricity. An LED also lasts tens of thousands of hours and is not easily damaged by knocks. How bright a torch is is given in **lumens**.

Most torches use batteries or **rechargeable batteries**, and many can now be charged with a USB cable. When the batteries run low, the voltage drops and the light gets weaker. Wind-up torches need no battery at all: a small **dynamo** inside produces electricity when you turn the handle. Empty batteries do not belong in the rubbish but back in the shop at the collection point.

A **head torch** is worn on the head with a strap, so both hands stay free when hiking, climbing or putting up a tent. There are small keyring torches, waterproof diving torches and powerful torches for the police and fire brigade. Many mobile phones have a built-in torch function. The first battery torch was built in the USA around 1900.

In the Alps you can use a torch to give the **alpine distress signal**: a light signal six times a minute, then a minute’s break. The rescuers reply with three signals a minute. A torch also belongs in the emergency supply at home, so that you have light in a power cut. You never shine a torch into anyone’s eyes, because bright light dazzles and can harm the eyes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A curved mirror that directs the light forwards.
Light-emitting diode, an economical electronic light source.
A battery that can be charged again.
A unit that measures how much light a lamp gives off.
A small generator that turns movement into electricity.

gewusst: In American English a torch is called a “flashlight”, because early torches could only give short flashes of light before the weak batteries had to recover.
Modern LED torches are often much brighter than the best torches of thirty years ago and still use less electricity.
For the alpine distress signal you can also use whistles or shouts instead of light.

teile.einleitung: The screen is the device on which a computer, a mobile phone or a television shows pictures, texts and videos. Another word for a computer screen is monitor. It consists of millions of tiny picture points that together make a picture.
wichtigste: Another word for a computer screen is monitor.
A screen puts the picture together from many small picture points, the pixels.
After starting up, you see the desktop with a background picture.
If the computer is not used for a while, a screensaver often appears.
The distance between your eyes and the screen should be about an arm’s length.
Breaks and looking into the distance are good for your eyes.
It is best to clean a screen with a soft cloth.

abschnitte.text: A **screen** shows what a computer, tablet or smartphone is doing at the moment. For a computer it is also called a **monitor**. The picture consists of many tiny **pixels**, each of which can glow red, green and blue. From these three colours the screen mixes all the other colours. A Full HD screen has 1920 by 1080 pixels, which is more than two million picture points.

In the past, screens were thick, heavy boxes with a **picture tube**, in which an electron beam drew the picture on glass. Today flat screens are usual, mostly with liquid crystals, abbreviated LCD. In **OLED** screens, each pixel lights up by itself, which is why they are particularly thin and show a deep black. With a **touchscreen**, you can operate the picture directly with your finger. The size is usually given as the diagonal in inches; one inch is 2.54 centimetres.

After the computer starts, the **desktop** appears, the area with the little pictures for programs and folders. The picture in the background is called the wallpaper and you can choose it yourself. With the **brightness** setting, the screen becomes brighter or darker. If the computer is not used for a while, a screensaver appears or the screen switches off to save electricity. At the top of the screen there is often a small camera for video calls, the webcam.

The screen should be about an **arm’s length** away from your eyes. It is best placed so that you look down slightly and no window is reflected in it. Anyone who looks at a screen for a long time blinks less often, which can make the eyes dry and tired. That is why regular **breaks** are important, in which you look into the distance or move about. In the evening, bright screen light can make it harder to fall asleep.

It is best to clean a screen with a soft, dry or slightly damp cloth. Harsh cleaning products and paper towels can scratch the surface. Before cleaning, you switch the screen off; that way you can also see the dust better. Old screens do not belong in the rubbish; in Switzerland they are taken back free of charge by shops or collection points and recycled.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny picture point that the picture is made of.
How many pixels a screen has across and down.
A screen that you can operate with your finger.
The start area of the computer with icons for programs and folders.

gewusst: Screensavers were invented because otherwise a picture shown for a long time could burn into old tube screens.
If you look at a screen with a magnifying glass, you can often see the small red, green and blue points of light.
A 4K screen has four times as many pixels as a Full HD screen.

teile.einleitung: Abstraction means leaving out unimportant details and keeping only what matters. It is one of the most important thinking tools in computer science. Without abstraction, nobody could write large programs or operate complicated devices.
wichtigste: Abstraction means leaving out unimportant details and keeping what matters.
A simplified picture of reality with the important properties is called a model.
A network map of bus and tram lines is a good example of abstraction.
What matters depends on the task; for a bike tour, for example, distance and height climbed.
Through an interface you operate a device or program without knowing what is inside it.
If you use print() in Python without knowing how the output works inside, you are using abstraction.
A program for all regular polygons turns the turtle by 360 : n degrees after each side.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “abstrahere”, which means “to draw away” or “to take away”. In **abstraction**, you take away everything that is not important for a particular task. What is left is the essential part. What is important always depends on the purpose. For a bike tour, for example, you need the distance and the height to climb, while the colour of the houses along the way does not matter.

A good example is the **network map** of bus and tram lines. It shows only stops, lines and places to change, but no houses, trees or exact distances. Even so, you can find your way with it. Such a simplified picture is called a **model**. A globe, a building plan or a character in a computer game are also models.

A game stores, for example, only the position, health points and equipment of a character. It leaves everything else out. Commands are abstractions too: if you call print() in Python, you do not need to know how the computer gets the letters onto the screen. Programmers build **functions** out of small parts that can be used again. In this way a large program is built up layer by layer.

A turtle is a small figure that draws lines on the screen. Instead of writing a separate program for a triangle, a square and a hexagon, you can write a **general program** for every regular polygon with n corners. The turtle turns by 360 : n degrees after each side. For the square it is 90 degrees, for the hexagon 60 degrees. So the special case is replaced by a number, and that is abstraction.

An **interface** is the part through which you operate something without knowing what is inside it. In a car, these are the steering wheel, accelerator and brake. On a mobile phone, they are the screen and the icons. You do not need to know how the engine or the processor works. Thanks to such interfaces, people can use very complicated technology quite easily.

begriffe.erklaerung: A simplified picture of reality with the important properties.
The part through which you operate a device or program.
A named piece of a program that you can call again and again.
A solution that fits not just one case but many cases.

gewusst: The first London Underground map that showed only lines and stations was made in 1933 and became the model for many network maps.
Words are abstractions too: the word “dog” stands for all dogs, whether big or small.
A computer consists of many layers of abstraction, from tiny switches to the colourful app.

teile.einleitung: In a power cut, electricity suddenly stops flowing through the lines. Lights go out, fridges get warm and often the mobile network, traffic lights and trains fail too. Usually a power cut lasts only a short time, but big outages can affect millions of people.
wichtigste: The great power cut in Italy on 28 September 2003 began with a flashover from a Swiss high-voltage line to a tree.
On 22 June 2005 the SBB railway power network failed across the whole of Switzerland for several hours.
On 28 April 2025, Spain and Portugal above all were hit by a widespread power cut.
When, after an outage, more overloaded lines switch off one after another, this is called a cascade effect.
A power station with black start capability can start up on its own without electricity from the grid.
Hospitals bridge the first seconds with an uninterruptible power supply from batteries.
In Switzerland the organisation OSTRAL prepares measures for an electricity shortage.

abschnitte.text: Power cuts happen, for example, when a storm blows trees onto lines or lightning strikes. Technical faults, diggers that damage a cable or errors in control systems can also be to blame. When one line fails, the electricity has to flow through other lines. If these become overloaded and switch off as well, a **cascade effect** occurs, spreading like dominoes.

On 28 September 2003, a high-voltage line on the Lukmanier in Switzerland came too close to a tree, and there was a **flashover**. As a result, the power failed in almost the whole of Italy. On 22 June 2005, the SBB **railway power network** collapsed across the whole of Switzerland, and in the middle of the evening rush hour many trains came to a standstill. On 28 April 2025, Spain and Portugal were almost completely without electricity.

Grid operators plan their network according to the **(n-1) criterion**. This means that the failure of any one part, for example a line or a transformer, must not lead to a power cut. Hospitals and data centres have an **uninterruptible power supply** with batteries that steps in immediately. After a few seconds, emergency generators with diesel engines take over.

After a big outage you cannot simply switch everything on at the same time. First, power stations with **black start capability** start up; these need no electricity from the grid, for example hydroelectric power stations. Then the grid is rebuilt step by step and one area after another is connected again. With big outages, this can take many hours.

In Switzerland, the electricity industry’s organisation **OSTRAL** prepares measures in case there is ever too little electricity, for instance in winter. The federal government recommends that every household keeps an **emergency supply** of water, food and important things. These include a torch, spare batteries and a battery-powered radio through which the authorities can give information. You should only light candles under supervision and never near curtains.

begriffe.erklaerung: A widespread power cut that lasts a long time.
A chain reaction in which one failure triggers further failures.
A generator with an engine that produces electricity during a power cut.
Starting up a power station without electricity from the grid.

gewusst: Because Rome was celebrating the culture night Notte Bianca that very night, many people suddenly found themselves sitting in the dark in the middle of the city.
In a power cut, a fridge keeps food cool for a few more hours if you keep the door shut.

teile.einleitung: A tractor is a powerful vehicle that does heavy work, above all on the farm. It pulls ploughs, mowers and trailers and drives many machines directly with its engine.
wichtigste: A tractor is a pulling vehicle that works mainly in farming.
On many tractors the back wheels are much bigger than the front wheels.
Deep grooves in the tyres stop it from slipping in the field.
Most tractors run on diesel.
It pulls, for example, a plough, a mower or a hay wagon.
On the road it goes slowly, so you often have to wait behind it.
The word tractor comes from the Latin trahere, which means to pull.

abschnitte.text: A tractor has a powerful **diesel engine**, a driver’s cab and usually big back wheels. The wide tyres with deep grooves, the **tread**, grip even in soft, wet soil. Big wheels spread the weight and press the ground down less. Many tractors have four-wheel drive so that they do not get stuck on slopes or in mud.

With a **plough**, the tractor turns over the soil before sowing. It pulls seed drills, fertiliser spreaders and mowers that cut the grass. In summer it brings the **hay** into the barn with a trailer. In winter it sometimes pushes snow or carries wood out of the forest.

At the back of the tractor there is a turning shaft, the **power take-off**. With it, the engine drives attached machines, such as a hay tedder or a baler. A **hydraulic system** raises and lowers machines using oil pressure, so that the driver can operate them comfortably from the seat. Modern tractors even steer almost by themselves in dead straight lines using satellite navigation.

In the past, horses and oxen pulled the plough; later, heavy steam engines helped. At the end of the 19th century, the first tractors with petrol engines appeared in the USA. From 1917 Ford built one of the first tractors in large numbers, the Fordson. In Switzerland, makes such as **Hürlimann** and Bührer were well known, and the company Aebi still builds vehicles for steep mountain slopes today.

Because many Swiss farms lie in hills and mountains, small, nimble vehicles are often needed. For steep meadows there are special **slope mowers** and transporters with a low centre of gravity. In Switzerland, young people may drive agricultural vehicles up to 30 km/h from the age of 14 with a category G driving licence. On the road, drivers should be patient and only overtake when it is safe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A vehicle that mainly pulls other machines or trailers.
A turning shaft on the tractor that drives attached machines.
Technology that lifts and moves heavy parts using oil pressure.
Grooves in the tyre that give grip on the ground.

gewusst: The big back tyres of some tractors are taller than a primary school child.
Some of the tyres are sometimes filled with water so that the tractor is heavier and pulls better.
There are tractors that can drive across the field without a driver.

teile.einleitung: The power grid is a huge web of lines, substations and transformers that brings electricity from the power stations to every socket. It ranges from mighty high-voltage lines over the Alps to the cable under the road outside your house. For everything to work, production and consumption have to be exactly the same at every moment.
wichtigste: The power grid connects power stations with all consumers.
The Swiss power grid is divided into 7 grid levels.
Over long distances, electricity is transmitted at a very high voltage, because the losses are then smaller.
Transformers change the voltage, for example from high voltage to 230 volts.
The Swissgrid transmission network is about 6700 kilometres long.
In 1958, the grids of Germany, France and Switzerland were connected for the first time at Laufenburg in Aargau.
Production and consumption must always be the same so that the frequency stays stable.

abschnitte.text: Electricity is produced in power stations, for example in hydroelectric power stations in the Alps or in solar panels on roofs. Through the **power grid** it reaches factories, railways and households. Because electricity can hardly be stored, it has to be used at the very moment it is produced. So the grid is like a cycle that must never stop.

The Swiss grid is divided into **7 grid levels**. At the top is the **transmission network** with 380 000 and 220 000 volts, which transports large amounts of electricity across the country like a motorway. Below it come supra-regional and regional distribution networks, and at the very bottom the local network with 400 and 230 volts. In between are levels with substations, where the voltage is converted.

In every line, part of the energy is lost as heat. The higher the voltage, the smaller the current that has to flow for the same power, and the smaller the **losses**. That is why electricity is transported over long distances at high voltage. A **transformer** then steps the voltage down bit by bit until it is 230 volts at the socket.

The European power grid works at a **frequency** of 50 hertz. If more electricity is used than produced, the frequency falls; if more is produced, it rises. That is why power stations constantly have to adjust, so that production and consumption are exactly the same. If the balance is badly upset, there is a risk of a **blackout**, a widespread power cut that lasts a long time.

The Swiss transmission network belongs to the national grid company **Swissgrid** and is about 6700 kilometres long. Switzerland is closely connected with its neighbours and lies right in the middle of the European power network. It all began in 1958 with the so-called **Star of Laufenburg** in Aargau, where the grids of Germany, France and Switzerland were connected for the first time. This means the countries can help each other out when electricity is short somewhere.

More and more electricity comes from solar panels and wind turbines, which supply different amounts depending on the weather. That is why the grid is becoming more modern and digital; this is called a **smart grid**. An important building block is the **smart meter**, a digital electricity meter that sends the consumption data automatically. This way grid operators know better when how much electricity is needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device that raises or lowers the voltage of electricity.
A facility where electricity is converted from one voltage to another.
How often alternating current changes direction per second, measured in hertz.
A digital electricity meter that reports consumption automatically.

gewusst: The European interconnected grid links many countries from the Atlantic to the Black Sea and is one of the largest power grids in the world.
If you measure the frequency of the power grid precisely, you can tell from the value whether too much or too little electricity is being produced in Europe at that moment.

teile.einleitung: A transistor is a tiny electronic component that can switch or amplify electric current. It is the most important building block of all computers, mobile phones and games consoles. A modern computer chip contains billions of transistors on an area smaller than a fingernail.
wichtigste: A transistor can switch current on and off like a switch, or amplify it.
The name is made up of the English words “transfer” and “resistor”.
Shockley, Bardeen and Brattain received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956 for inventing the transistor.
A bipolar transistor has three terminals: base, emitter and collector.
In a field-effect transistor, a voltage at the gate controls the current.
Bipolar transistors come as NPN and PNP types.
CMOS technology combines two kinds of MOSFET so that almost no current flows when they are at rest.

abschnitte.text: A **transistor** is a component made from a **semiconductor**, usually silicon. With a small current or a small voltage, you can use it to control a much bigger current. So it works either as an **amplifier**, for instance in a radio, or as a lightning-fast switch that only knows “on” and “off”. Every computer calculates using this on and off, that is 1 and 0.

A semiconductor conducts electricity only under certain conditions. By deliberately adding foreign atoms, called **doping**, layers with different properties are created; in bipolar transistors they are in the order NPN or PNP. In a **bipolar transistor**, a small current at the base controls a large current between the collector and the emitter. If it has, for example, a current gain of 150, a base current of 0.2 milliamperes lets 30 milliamperes flow at the collector.

Most transistors in computer chips are **MOSFETs**, a kind of field-effect transistor. In them, a voltage at the terminal called the gate controls the current, and almost no control current flows. In **CMOS** technology, two kinds of these transistors are combined so that almost no current flows when they are at rest. That is why mobile phones and laptops last so long on their batteries.

At the end of 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain built the first working transistor at Bell Labs in the USA; shortly afterwards William Shockley developed the bipolar transistor. For this invention the three received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956. Before that, large, hot and fragile **vacuum tubes** were needed. In the 1950s the first small transistor radios came onto the market, which people could take anywhere.

From the 1960s, people learnt to connect many transistors on a single small piece of silicon to make an **integrated circuit**. Since then transistors have become smaller and smaller; today they are only a few nanometres in size, which is a thousand times thinner than a hair. A modern mobile phone processor contains many billions of transistors. That is why the transistor is regarded as one of the most important inventions of the 20th century.

begriffe.erklaerung: A material such as silicon that conducts electricity only under certain conditions.
Deliberately adding foreign atoms to a semiconductor to change how well it conducts.
The control terminal of a field-effect transistor.
A chip on which many transistors and other components are built together.
A circuit that turns a weak signal into a strong one.

gewusst: John Bardeen later received a second Nobel Prize in Physics, for explaining superconductivity.
Probably more transistors have been made than all other objects built by humans put together.
If you connect two bipolar transistors as a Darlington pair, their current gains roughly multiply.

teile.einleitung: Public-key cryptography, also called an asymmetric cryptosystem, is an encryption method with two different keys: a public one and a private one. Anyone may know the public key, but only its owner knows the private one. This brilliant idea protects almost every connection on the internet today.
wichtigste: Every person has a public key and a private key.
You encrypt a message to Bob with Bob’s public key.
You create a digital signature with your own private key.
The Diffie-Hellman method of 1976 makes it possible to agree on a shared key over an open channel.
Rivest, Shamir and Adleman published the RSA method in 1977.
The security of RSA depends on the fact that large numbers are hard to factorise.
With HTTPS, a certificate authority confirms that a public key belongs to a website.

abschnitte.text: In **symmetric** encryption, both sides use the same secret key. The problem: how do you get this key safely to the other person? In an **asymmetric cryptosystem**, every person has two keys. Anyone may know the **public key**, while the **private key** is kept secret. Whatever has been encrypted with one key can only be opened again with the other.

You can imagine it like a letterbox. Anyone can drop a letter through the slot; that is the public key. But only someone with the letterbox key can take it out. So if Alice wants to write to Bob, she encrypts the message with Bob’s public key. Only Bob can read it again with his private key.

The method can also be used the other way round. Anyone who processes something with their own private key creates a **digital signature**. Everyone else can use the public key to check that the message really comes from the sender and has not been changed. With **HTTPS**, a certificate authority confirms with a certificate that a public key really belongs to a particular website. The padlock symbol in the browser shows this protected connection.

In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a method with which two parties can agree on a shared key over an open channel. In 1977 Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman presented the **RSA** method. It is based on the fact that you can easily multiply two large prime numbers, but can hardly split the result back into its factors. A tiny example: with p = 3 and q = 11, n = 33, and the exponent e = 3 goes with the private exponent d = 7. In reality, numbers with hundreds of digits are used.

In 1994 Peter Shor described an algorithm for **quantum computers**. With **Shor’s algorithm**, a large enough quantum computer could break RSA. Such quantum computers do not exist yet. Even so, researchers are already developing new methods that should also stand up to quantum computers. These are called post-quantum cryptography.

begriffe.erklaerung: A key that anyone may know and that is used for encrypting.
A secret key that only its owner knows.
An electronic signature that shows who sent a message.
Splitting a number into its prime factors, such as 33 = 3 times 11.
A digital identity card that confirms who a public key belongs to.

gewusst: At the British intelligence service, researchers had a similar idea a few years before RSA, but they were not allowed to publish it.
In explanations, the two people communicating are almost always called Alice and Bob.
Because asymmetric methods are slow, they are often used only to agree on a key, and the rest is encrypted symmetrically.

teile.einleitung: The Swatch is a plastic wristwatch that came onto the market in Switzerland in 1983. With bright colours, cheeky patterns and low prices, it became a cult object around the world. At the same time it helped the Swiss watch industry out of a severe crisis.
wichtigste: A Swatch is a wristwatch.
The first Swatch came out in 1983.
The case of the classic Swatch is made of plastic.
The name is made up of the English words Second and Watch.
The Swatch company has its headquarters in Biel.
Nicolas G. Hayek is regarded as the father of the Swatch.
The Swatch was invented to help the Swiss watch industry.
The Swatch is known above all for its bright colours and patterns.

abschnitte.text: The Swatch is a **quartz watch** with a case made of **plastic**. It consists of only 51 individual parts, far fewer than traditional watches. The parts are assembled by machine and the case is welded shut instead of screwed. That is why the watch could be made cheaply in Switzerland.

In the 1970s, cheap **quartz watches** from Japan and Hong Kong came onto the market. Many Swiss watch companies could not compete with these prices. Tens of thousands of jobs were lost, especially in the Jura Arc. Today this hard time is called the **quartz crisis**.

Engineers at the company ETA in Grenchen, including Elmar Mock and Jacques Müller, developed a watch that could be made very cheaply. On 1 March 1983 the first Swatch was presented. The name comes from **Second Watch**, because people were meant to own several and change them depending on their mood. The watch was marketed like a fashion item.

The businessman **Nicolas G. Hayek** helped to reorganise the struggling Swiss watch companies. He brought them together in one large group, which today is called the **Swatch Group** and has its headquarters in **Biel**. It also includes well-known brands such as Omega, Longines and Tissot. That is why Hayek is regarded as the father of the Swatch and the saviour of the Swiss watch industry.

Every year, new Swatch models come out in bright **colours** and patterns. Many were designed by artists. Some rare models are now sought-after collector’s items and worth much more than when they were bought. In 2013 Swatch also brought out a mechanical watch with automatic winding, the Sistem51.

begriffe.erklaerung: A watch in which a vibrating quartz crystal measures the time precisely.
The severe crisis of the Swiss watch industry in the 1970s.
An object that a great many people enthusiastically collect or wear.
The large Swiss watch group to which the Swatch brand belongs.

gewusst: The Sistem51 has this name because its mechanical movement also consists of only 51 parts.
Swatch’s new headquarters in Biel has a huge curving wooden roof that looks like a snake.

teile.einleitung: A rack railway is a railway that uses a gearwheel to grip a toothed rail, so that it can climb very steep mountains. Without this technology, the wheels would spin on the steep slope. Switzerland is the land of rack railways: in 1871 Europe’s first mountain railway ran up the Rigi here.
wichtigste: A steep mountain railway needs a gearwheel so that it does not slip on the slope.
The rack usually lies in the middle between the rails.
In 1871 Europe’s first mountain railway ran up the Rigi.
The Swiss engineer Niklaus Riggenbach built rack railways such as the Rigi railway.
The Gornergrat railway starts in Zermatt and offers a view of the Matterhorn.
The Brienz Rothorn railway still often runs with steam locomotives.
Rack railways go more slowly than normal trains.

abschnitte.text: Normal trains hold on to the rails only through the friction of their smooth steel wheels. On steep lines they would slip. That is why a rack railway has a **gearwheel** under the locomotive. Its teeth mesh with a **rack**, which usually lies in the middle between the rails. In this way the train can pull itself up the mountain and brake safely on the way down.

On 21 May 1871 the **Vitznau-Rigi railway** was opened. It was the first mountain railway in Europe. It was built by the Swiss engineer **Niklaus Riggenbach**, who had invented his own rack. The Rigi railway was a great success and attracted many tourists. After that, many more rack railways were built in Switzerland and all over the world.

There are several kinds of rack, named after their inventors. The **Riggenbach** rack looks like a ladder lying down. In the **Abt** system, two racks with staggered teeth lie side by side. The Pilatus railway has a special system by Eduard Locher, in which the gearwheels grip from the side. With it, the railway manages gradients of up to 48 percent.

The **Pilatus railway** of 1889 is regarded as the steepest rack railway in the world. Since 1898 the **Gornergrat railway** has run from Zermatt up to a height of more than 3000 metres, with a view of the Matterhorn. The **Brienz Rothorn railway** on Lake Brienz still often runs with steam locomotives. The Wengernalp railway and the Jungfrau railway in the Bernese Oberland are rack railways too.

Rack railways go much more slowly than normal trains. This is because of the steep gradient and the rack, which does not allow high speeds. But they are very safe, because they have several independent **brakes**. Many railways only use the rack on part of the line and otherwise run like a normal train. They are then called mixed railways.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with points around its edge, called teeth.
A straight rail with teeth that the gearwheel meshes with.
How steeply a line climbs, often given in percent.
The force that stops things from simply sliding past each other.

gewusst: The Pilatus railway is so steep that its carriages are built like a staircase.
The world’s first rack railway ran up Mount Washington in the USA as early as 1869.
With a gradient of 48 percent, the line climbs almost 50 metres over 100 metres.

teile.einleitung: An automatic door opens by itself as soon as someone comes near. A sensor notices the person, and a motor slides the door open. Such doors are found in shopping centres, stations, hospitals and airports.
wichtigste: An automatic door opens by itself.
With an automatic sliding door, a motor opens the door.
On many automatic doors, the sensor sits above the door.
A light barrier often notices whether someone is standing in the doorway.
If someone is standing in the doorway when it is closing, it opens again.
Automatic doors help wheelchair users in particular.
You should not play with an automatic door, because you can get knocked.

abschnitte.text: An **automatic door** opens and closes without you having to touch it. The most common are **sliding doors**, where the door panels glide to the side. But there are also automatic swing doors and revolving doors. You often find them in shopping centres, stations, hospitals or airports. Very many people go in and out there, often with bags or suitcases.

Above the door there is usually a **motion detector**. It sends out invisible rays, such as infrared light or radar waves, and notices when something moves. Then it sends a signal to a control unit. The **control unit** switches on an electric motor, which pulls the door panels to the side with belts. After a few seconds without movement, the door closes again.

So that nobody gets trapped, automatic doors have extra sensors. A **light barrier** is an invisible beam across the doorway. If it is interrupted, the door knows that someone is standing in it and opens again. In a power cut or a fire, many doors can be pushed open by hand so that they can serve as an **escape route**. Even so, you should not play with automatic doors, because you can get knocked.

Automatic doors are a great help especially for **wheelchair** users. Anyone with a pushchair, a walking frame or heavy shopping also gets through more easily. In hospitals they also help with **hygiene**, because nobody has to touch door handles. In Switzerland, public buildings should be as barrier-free as possible. Automatic doors contribute to this.

As early as ancient times, the Greek inventor **Hero of Alexandria** described temple doors that opened as if by magic. He used fire, heated air and water to drive them. Modern automatic sliding doors appeared in the USA in the 1950s. Today large buildings can hardly be imagined without them. Many doors even save energy, because they only stay open as long as necessary.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that notices something in its surroundings, such as a movement.
A sensor that notices when someone moves.
An invisible beam of light that reports when something interrupts it.
A way to leave a building quickly in an emergency.

gewusst: Some automatic doors open only halfway when a single person comes, and fully when many people come.
In great cold, automatic doors often stay open for a shorter time so that less heat is lost.
Almost 2000 years ago, Hero of Alexandria built a kind of machine that gave out holy water in return for a coin.

teile.einleitung: A wind turbine is a machine that turns wind into electricity. You can see the big white towers with their three long blades on hills, passes and at sea. They are the modern descendants of the old windmills.
wichtigste: The wind makes the rotor blades of a wind turbine turn.
Most large wind turbines have three blades.
A generator in the nacelle turns the rotation into electricity.
Wind turbines often stand on hills and mountain ridges, because the wind blows more strongly there.
In a very violent storm, wind turbines are stopped so that they are not damaged.
The largest wind farm in Switzerland is on Mont-Crosin in the Bernese Jura.
In the past, windmills were needed mainly to grind grain.

abschnitte.titel: How a wind turbine is built
abschnitte.text: A wind turbine consists of a tall **tower**, with the **nacelle** sitting on top. At the front of the nacelle, the **rotor** is fixed, usually with three rotor blades. Inside the nacelle are the generator and often a gearbox. On large turbines the tower is more than 100 metres high, and a single rotor blade can be more than 50 metres long.

The wind flows past the rotor blades and makes them turn, similar to an aircraft wing. The rotation is passed on to the **generator**, which turns it into electricity. A computer always turns the nacelle into the wind. The turbine starts to run in a light breeze. In a very violent storm it is stopped and the blades are turned out of the wind so that nothing breaks.

Long before there was electricity, people used **windmills**. They used them mainly to grind grain into flour or to pump water away. The Netherlands is famous for its windmills, for instance at Kinderdijk. Only from the end of the 19th century did people build wind turbines that produce electricity. You know a very simple wind wheel as a toy: the **pinwheel**, which turns when you blow on it.

The largest wind farm in Switzerland is on **Mont-Crosin** in the Bernese Jura. Other wind turbines turn, for example, on the Gütsch near Andermatt and at the Nufenen Pass. Since 2020, five large wind turbines have stood on the **Gotthard Pass**. In Switzerland they are often built on the Jura heights and on passes, because the wind blows strongly there.

Wind turbines produce electricity without giving off exhaust gases. But they can make noise and change the look of the **landscape**. Birds and bats can collide with the rotor blades. That is why some turbines are switched off at certain times, for example when a lot of bats are out and about. Before building, experts check carefully whether a site is suitable.

begriffe.erklaerung: The turning part of the wind turbine with the rotor blades.
The machine housing on top of the tower.
The machine that turns the rotation into electricity.
Several wind turbines standing together in one place.

gewusst: The tips of the rotor blades of large wind turbines move as fast as a car on the motorway, or even faster.
In the towers of many wind turbines there is a ladder or a small lift for the technicians.
Wind turbines with three blades run more smoothly and evenly than those with two blades.

teile.einleitung: The Swiss Light Source, SLS for short, is a large research facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Aargau. There, electrons circle in a ring at almost the speed of light and produce extremely bright X-ray light as they do so. With this light, researchers study materials, medicines and tiny structures.
wichtigste: The SLS has been in operation at the PSI since 2001.
Its storage ring has a circumference of 288 metres.
The X-ray light is produced when electrons are steered onto curved paths.
From 2023 to 2025 the storage ring was renewed in the SLS 2.0 upgrade.
According to the PSI, SLS 2.0 improves the emittance, that is how tightly the beam is bundled, by up to a factor of 40.
Pharmaceutical companies use the SLS especially for protein crystallography.
In top-up operation the ring is constantly refilled so that the current stays constant.
There are about 20 experiment stations at the SLS.

abschnitte.titel: What is a synchrotron light source?
abschnitte.text: In a synchrotron light source, **electrons** are accelerated to almost the speed of light. Then they circle in a large ring, the **storage ring**. Whenever magnets steer the electrons onto a curved path, they give off light. This **synchrotron light** ranges from infrared to hard X-rays and is much brighter than the light from an X-ray tube in hospital.
